Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Śramaṇa Subject Dharmapāla and others, Great Masters of the Transmission of the Dharma, recipients of the purple robe, of the Office of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices. Chapter One, Part Two: The Secret Body of the Bodhisattva. "Furthermore, Śāntamati!..."

All the physical forms and modes of conduct of all sentient beings abide within the physical forms and modes of conduct of the Bodhisattva, yet the Bodhisattva never gives rise to realization nor engages in conceptual discrimination.

By means of that bodhisattva’s equanimous mind of non-discrimination, he manifests bodily postures in accordance with his body; yet the bodhisattva’s body is by its very nature immovable, and because it is immovable, he manifests the activity of the body.
Although his body is free from signs, he does not impair the purity of the bodhisattva’s body.
Having manifested radiant light that shines universally upon the hells, he causes all sentient beings to attain peace and happiness.
Furthermore, O Bodhisattva!
For the sake of all sentient beings without exception, you do not spare even your own body or life.

If any sentient beings should come individually seeking to eat the flesh of your body, the Bodhisattva manifests before them and cuts off the flesh to give it to them, even extending to the marrow, blood, and vital essence, granting them all as they require.

Śāntamati, you should know that when a bodhisattva gives away his own body, flesh, and so forth to sentient beings according to their needs, because that bodhisattva knows the body to be immeasurable, he is thereby able to know the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) to be immeasurable accordingly.
The immeasurable is the inexhaustible body and the inexhaustible gate; it is precisely the inexhaustible dharma-gate of dependent origination.
Whatever body a bodhisattva manifests is solely for the purpose of bringing all sentient beings to maturity.

If there should be someone with a mind of greedy attachment who is enamored by exquisite and dignified physical forms, the Bodhisattva will immediately manifest before them in the form of a beautiful woman.
Following that man’s heart of lustful attachment, she fulfilled every one of his desires.

At that time, because of her own passionate clinging, the woman’s physical form became withered and emaciated; she soon met her end, her sense faculties perished, and her body became foul, putrid, and impure. Then, due to his own lack of wisdom, that man felt revulsion and departed.

From the very body of that deceased woman, a voice spontaneously issued forth to expound the essentials of the Dharma, causing that man’s mind to attain awakening and ensuring he would never retreat from his resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!

A bodhisattva manifests a vast body within this trichiliocosm, appearing either within a precious canopy or upon the tip of a finger; even when the kalpa-fire blazes with fierce, flaming intensity, he can completely cover it with his fingers, yet the bodhisattva’s body remains entirely unharmed."

Furthermore, they are able to manifest physical forms to universally perform acts of offering for all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; they pile up exquisite flower canopies as vast as Mount Sumeru, and gather precious flowers as high as mountain peaks, offering them all to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.

Furthermore, taking this trichiliocosm as one great vessel, he filled it with fragrant oil equal in volume to Mount Sumeru, arranged lamp-wicks throughout it, and lit the lamps so that they blazed with vast and intense radiance, thereby performing acts of offering for all the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, he accumulated vast quantities of lamps, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, blazing everywhere as an offering to the Tathāgata.
Moreover, the Bodhisattva covered his own limbs with the garments he wore and poured ghee over them to kindle lamps, universally performing acts of worship for the Tathāgata.

That lamp blazed intensely with great radiance, its vast illumination reaching Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; therein, sentient beings were able to see one another and witness the miraculous manifestations of supernatural power displayed by the Bodhisattva.
Having seen this, immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Among them, for those classes of sentient beings who were arrogant and conceited, the Bodhisattva immediately manifested the body of the powerful Nārāyaṇa, or the formidable form of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
Upon seeing him, those sentient beings were struck with terror; they immediately humbled their minds before the Bodhisattva, taking refuge, prostrating, and entreating him to hear the Dharma.

Furthermore, in great kingdoms, cities, and various charnel grounds, the Bodhisattva saw countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings filling them everywhere. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva manifested a vast body and displayed the signs of death and dissolution, causing those sentient beings who had previously fallen into the animal realm and whose karmic retributions as animals were exhausted to take the flesh from the body he had manifested and eat it. Having eaten it, they passed away and were all reborn in the heavens; by means of this cause, they eventually entered parinirvāṇa.

Therefore, you should know that once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has purified their past vow-power, they are able to fulfill that vow throughout the long night by performing deeds for the benefit of others, vowing that when sentient beings approach the end of their lives, they may eat the flesh of their body and thereby be reborn in the heavenly realms.

By these causes and conditions, until finally entering parinirvāṇa, they cause all sentient beings to accomplish what they have thought of, accomplish what they have sought, and accomplish the power of their vows.
“Śāntamati, you should know that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess such extraordinary practices and vows.

I recall that in the past, throughout the four directions of this Jambudvīpa, there were eighty-four thousand vast kingdoms and cities, as well as many hundreds of thousands of villages, towns, and districts, where hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of people resided.”

At that time, a great calamity and an epidemic plague arose within the city and kingdom; the people therein were afflicted with various diseases, such as ailments affecting the body’s tissues—whether in their raw or ripened stages—each with distinct symptoms. Whether they were boils, sores, scabs, or leprosy, or disorders of wind, bile, and phlegm, patients of all sizes filled the land in every direction.
Although thousands of highly skilled and eminent physicians were sought out and excellent medicines were employed, none were able to cure any of those sufferings of disease.
Because those people had no remedy for their illness, they were without protection or refuge; raising their voices in a great cry, they wept piteously and said:
"Who can extinguish this suffering of our disease?"
"Whether they be devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, or others—
whether human or non-human—
whoever is able to pacify and eliminate my illness, I shall relinquish all my wealth and treasures to offer them entirely; I shall follow their instructions and repay their profound kindness."
"Śāntamati, you should know that at that time, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Tathāgata was the Lord of Devas, Śakra, named Sunetra.
Within that celestial realm, with his pure divine eye which surpasses that of humans, he was able to perceive all those multitudes of people suffering from manifold illnesses;
furthermore, with his pure divine ear, he heard everywhere the sounds of the weeping of all those people."
Having seen and heard this, he gave rise to a heart of compassion and reflected to himself:
"I should now act as a refuge, a protector, and a resort for these people who are without refuge, without protection, and without a resort."

Having formed this thought, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately transformed himself into the form of a man named Śānta and went to a great city in this Jambudvīpa called Sukṛta, which was not far from there.
Abiding in the midst of space, he universally revealed [the truth] to all the people within Jambudvīpa, speaking these verses:
"The Great City of Good Action is not far from here; Within it dwells a man named Śānta.
If one takes the flesh from his body and eats it, It will completely pacify and eliminate all illnesses."
Do not be startled or terrified, nor harbor fear; take the flesh of my body as you please with joyful hearts.
This is a sublime medicine to save all people; herein there is no harm and no ill will.

"At that time, all the people throughout the kingdoms, cities, villages, and towns who were afflicted by illness, having heard the sound of those verses in the air, immediately went together to the place where the man Śānta was in the great city of Kalyāṇakāra."
Having arrived, each person cut off some of his flesh and ate it to cure their illness.
Although they took from him one after another, the flesh of his body was inexhaustible.
At that time, Śānta again spoke these verses for the sake of the multitude:
"If I shall attain the Bodhi of a Buddha, this true Dharma shall be inexhaustible for me;
because it is true, I pray that even the flesh of this body of mine shall be inexhaustible."

"At that time, all those people throughout the four directions who were afflicted by illness and suffering each took pieces of flesh from the body of the man Śānta according to their own desires; yet Śānta’s body remained peaceful and as it was before, neither increasing nor decreasing.
As they continued to cut away, the flesh grew back again immediately."

At that time, all the people in that city who ate this meat were completely cured of every illness and suffering they possessed; free from disease and filled with happiness, they were entirely without grief or affliction.
In this manner, in succession, all the people within Jambudvīpa ceased their various ailments and attained complete ease and tranquility.
At that time, all the people—men and women, boys and girls—reflected to themselves: "That man, Śāntamati!"
"You are able to pacify and eliminate all our illnesses, so that we may be free from disease and our bodies attain ease and tranquility.
At this time, what should we offer as an act of worship?"
Thereupon, many people gathered together and went as one to the place where Śānta was.
Having arrived, they each joined their palms in respectful faith and, with one voice, spoke this verse:
"You are our excellent refuge and our great protector; You are the King of Physicians and the wondrous medicine."
"Following your instructions, my illness has been cured; what may I do to offer you my service?
At that time, the man Śānta concealed his manifested form and returned to his body as Śakra, and spoke this verse for the entire assembly:
"Gold, silver, wealth, and food and drink— I have done none of these things."
Solely for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings, may the ten paths of virtuous action be brought to fulfillment.
May the vows and practices for enlightenment be cultivated with steadfastness, serving as the cause for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
May they give rise to one another’s hearts of loving-kindness and compassion, so that all matters of benefit may grow.
Having heard this, one should resolve upon bodhicitta, And further give rise to the supreme intention of great compassion;
May all universally accumulate sublime and wondrous causes, So that the ten paths of wholesome action are entirely purified.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati! At that time, after Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had spoken these verses, he returned to his celestial palace.

At that moment, among all the men and women, boys and girls, and the entire multitude of beings in Jambudvīpa—whose number was beyond reckoning—not a single person fell into the evil realms; upon the end of their lives, they were all reborn in the common lot of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the happy realms."

Once they have been born in that heaven, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately preaches the Dharma to them, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, causing them all to become non-retrogressive from the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; among those sentient beings, some may even distance themselves from dust and leave behind defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!

Therefore, you should know that once a bodhisattva’s bodily actions performed through the secrecy of the body have attained purity, they can sacrifice their own life to bring immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings to maturity, ultimately enabling them to attain the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati, saying:
"Śāntamati, you should know that the body of a bodhisattva is indestructible, firm, true, and a body that is neither born nor extinguished."
If there are sentient beings who can be transformed and delivered by means of a perishable body, he manifests such a body to transform and deliver them;
if there are sentient beings who can be transformed and delivered by means of an imperishable body, he manifests such a body to transform and deliver them.
It is entirely indestructible in every respect; fire cannot burn it, and a blade cannot sever it. This body is firm and solid, composed of the truly indestructible diamond.
Therefore, Śāntamati!
The physical forms manifested by a bodhisattva serve solely to bring about the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings through their ripening.

Yet, this bodhisattva has no such thoughts, nor does he make any discrimination as to "this is the body" or "this is the form. Because he knows that the body is devoid of characteristics, he immediately attains the state where phenomena are devoid of characteristics; furthermore, there is no distinction between the body being devoid of characteristics and all phenomena being devoid of characteristics.

If the characteristic is the very body yet free from characteristics, and that characteristic is the very dharma yet free from characteristics, it is because one can thus enter accordingly into this freedom from characteristics.
Thus, the freedom from characteristics of one's own body and the freedom from characteristics of the bodies of all sentient beings are both equally so.

Why is this? Because by virtue of one's own body being free from marks and all sentient beings' bodies being free from marks, one enters the marklessness of the entire dharma-realm; because the dharma-realm is free from marks, one enters the marklessness of dharmas. Yet, within this, there is in reality not even the slightest dharma to be apprehended.

That is to say, one enters the suchness of the bodies of all sentient beings by means of the suchness of one's own body; and one enters the suchness of one's own body by means of the suchness of the bodies of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, the suchness of one's own body enters the suchness of all phenomena; because it enters the suchness of all phenomena, it enters the suchness of all Buddhas.

Furthermore, by virtue of the suchness of one's own body, one enters directly into the suchness of the past, future, and present; nor does the suchness of the past conflict with that of the future or the present.

The suchness of all past, future, and present phenomena is itself the suchness of the aggregates, bases, and elements; the suchness of the aggregates, bases, and elements is itself the suchness of purity.
The *tathatā* of defilement and purity is the *tathatā* of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa; the *tathatā* of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa is the *tathatā* of non-activity;
the *tathatā* of non-activity is the *tathatā* of all activity.
“Good son! That which is called *tathatā* (suchness) is precisely the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); the true nature is precisely the nature of suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*).

It is a nature without differentiation, a nature without categories, a nature without arising, a nature without contention, and a nature without grasping. Because there is no dharma that can be grasped within *tathatā*, it is said that *tathatā* is a dharma without grasping.”
Because that suchness is without anything to be grasped, it is grasped in just this way;
yet among all forms of grasping, the Bodhisattva manifests as if there were dharmas to be grasped, though in suchness there is neither grasping nor activity.
Because there is no grasping, there is no contention; because there is no contention, although that which is grasped appears within all forms, that suchness remains unmoved.

Therefore, with wisdom that accords with reality, one should investigate the true body of the Tathāgata; by contemplating the equality of the Tathāgata’s body, one should then investigate the *tathatā* (suchness) of one's own body.

To state the essential point: one should carefully observe that all bodies lack the nature of being a body and are ultimately unarisen, for one knows that all bodies are formed from dharmas produced through dependent origination.
Having understood this, one is then able to awaken to and enter the gateway of that Dharmakāya.
By entering this gateway of the Dharmakāya, one immediately becomes the Dharmakāya, which is not a body of aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), or elements (dhātu).

One should contemplate that very Dharmakāya as extensively expanded and supremely exalted according to reality; from this, one manifests a body to perform acts of benefit and happiness for all sentient beings, until all that is seen, heard, sensed, and known serves to accomplish the welfare and happiness of sentient beings.

"Śāntamati, you should know that it is like the physician-king Jīvaka, who gathers all the most excellent medicines and, through their refined and skillful compounding, fashions the form of a woman—exquisite in color, dignified in appearance, and delightful to behold. He establishes her in various activities as required, whether coming or going, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, and in distinguishing various phenomena; yet this is neither conceptualization nor free from conceptualization."

Whosoever among the sick—whether they be kings, ministers, elders, or householders—come to the presence of Jīvaka, the King of Physicians, and unite with the woman produced by his wondrous medicine, once they have united, all their suffering from illness is entirely pacified and eliminated; free from disease and at ease, they obtain happiness.

Śāntamati! Observe this King of Physicians, Jīvaka; by means of his skillful wisdom, he is able to pacify and eliminate all diseases for the world, a power of wisdom that other physicians do not possess.

The preeminence of the Bodhisattva’s dharmakāya is likewise so: if those men, women, boys, or girls who are consumed by their bodies with greed, hatred, and delusion can contemplate the dharmakāya according to reality and truth, they will be able to extinguish all afflictions;
their minds will attain pliancy and their bodies will be freed from burning.

Therefore, one should know that the bodhisattva’s power of past vows is pure, and the bodhisattva’s dharma-body is vast, increased, and superior; to contemplate this according to reality is the purity of the bodhisattva’s body-secret.
“Śāntamati, you should know that the Dharma-body of a bodhisattva is not accomplished through the power of food and drink, nor can it be nourished by morsel food.

Having realized such characteristics, the bodhisattva manifests the acceptance of food and drink out of compassion for all sentient beings; though there is taking, there is no sign of attachment. Nor is there any taking for the sake of cherishing the body; within that which is taken, the Dharma-body neither increases nor decreases.”

Therefore, one should know that the Dharma-body of a bodhisattva is neither born nor extinguished, nor does it arise; yet within it, birth, extinction, and activity are manifested solely for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity.
Cessation is itself non-cessation and is without volitional construction; all phenomena should be understood in this way.
That which has arisen is the meaning of conditioned conjunction; all phenomena should be understood in this way.
Furthermore, it should be known that the arising of all those dharmas is non-arising.
The body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body, the Dharma-food, the Dharma-power, and the ultimate refuge of the Dharma.
The body of the Tathāgata is the body of space, the unequaled body, the supreme and most excellent body above all in the three realms,
the body through which all Tathāgatas have attained penetration, the incomparable and peerless body that is pure,
stainless, and undefiled, the body of self-nature luminosity, the body of self-nature non-arising, and the body of self-nature... [non-existence].
The body that has arisen, the body apart from mind and consciousness, the body whose intrinsic nature is like an illusion, a mirage, or the moon reflected in water,
the body accomplished through emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the body most supreme throughout the ten directions and as vast as space,
the body equal to all sentient beings, the boundless and limitless body, the body without category or discrimination, the body without...
A body that is not distinct from non-existence; a body that is immovable through abiding in non-abiding; a body whose intrinsic nature is formless;

a body whose intrinsic nature is devoid of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; a body not composed of the earth element; a body not composed of the water, fire, or wind elements;
a body not produced from seeds, nor from the combination of seeds, nor from the great elements; a body not produced from seeds.

The body that is comparable to all phenomena in the world is peerless; it is not produced by the eye, does not rely on the ear, is not known by the nose, is not discerned by the tongue, is not a composite of the body, and is not constituted by the mind.
It is not turned by the mind, nor is it turned by the mental consciousness; furthermore, it is neither non-turning nor following-turning.
“Good son! For this reason, you should contemplate the body of the Tathāgata as it truly is.

This bodhisattva dwells in the state of equality regarding the body of the Tathāgata; having attained purity, he practices the bodhisattva conduct and manifests his body everywhere throughout the trichiliocosm—whether in the four great continents, Jambudvīpa, or in all royal capitals, villages, towns, and districts. In every such place, the bodhisattva universally manifests his form.”
Yet within this, there is nothing manifested and no obstruction.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva can manifest the bodies of various Māras throughout the ten directions; within that which is manifested, they manifest without obstruction, and within that which is not manifested, they manifest without obstruction. Because of this, there is nothing seen and nothing heard, nothing perceived and nothing known; all that is manifested serves solely to bring all sentient beings to maturity.

Within the application of mindfulness to the body, the bodhisattva likewise experiences neither increase nor decrease; although the bodhisattva knows the body to be impermanent, knows the body to be suffering, and knows the body to be selfless, they nevertheless manifest their bodies for the sake of sentient beings to perform deeds of benefit and happiness.
The Bodhisattva knows that the nature of the body is inherently quiescent; yet, for the sake of sentient beings, they manifest a conceptualized body to perform various acts of benefit and happiness.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva understands that the body is formed through causes and conditions, and thus observes those respective causal factors as they truly are: there is neither a creator nor an experiencer. Moreover, they are able to observe that this body is insentient, like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles.
Although the physical actions of a bodhisattva are already pure, they manifest their body for the sake of sentient beings.

Śāntamati, you should know that from the moment the Śākya Bodhisattva first generated the mind of enlightenment in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, his actions of body, speech, and mind were entirely pure.

Furthermore, the physical actions of the body possess immeasurable and boundless merit; even if one were to spend eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, whether speaking on them by the Tathāgata or by myself, the vast purity of all the bodhisattvas' physical secrets and physical actions could not be fully exhausted.
The Buddha-spoken *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśamahāyānasūtra*, Fascicle Two.
The Buddha-spoken *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśamahāyānasūtra*,
Fascicle Three.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Dispersing Grandee, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of Sanskrit Transmission, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject, under Imperial Edict. Chapter Two: The Secret Speech of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati, saying: “Noble son!
What is called the purity of the bodhisattva’s vocal secrecy and vocal karma?

Śāntamati, you should know that wherever a bodhisattva arises is the very birth-story (jātaka) of that bodhisattva; and according to the birth-story of that bodhisattva, one enters into the bodhisattva’s voice.

All vocal sounds and languages of every sentient being, all paths of speech and modes of expression used for communication, the collection of all phenomena of coming and going, and the subtle investigation of words concerning suffering, pleasure, and so forth—all enter into and abide within the voice of the Bodhisattva; therein they encounter no obstruction, and through unattached wisdom and vision, they all proceed in accordance with it.

Even the subtle sounds of mosquitoes, insects, flies, and butterflies, the Bodhisattva is able to articulate and express them all, causing the bodies and minds of all sentient beings who hear the Bodhisattva’s voice to become light and tranquil.
Whatever they hear, expressed exactly as it was articulated, all issues forth from the gateway of the Bodhisattva’s mouth.
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
“In accordance with the infinite limits of sentient beings, The varieties of their types are likewise immeasurable.”
Though one might speak for a hundred eons of that which is boundless, how could this inconceivable be fully described?
By employing analogies and speaking according to the meaning, there is no error in explaining the Dharma of the Great Being;
it neither increases nor decreases, like space, as he brings forth a vast mind and expounds it.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati Bodhisattva!

All the various kinds of sounds belonging to the Brahma Kings, all the various kinds of sounds belonging to Śakra, all the various kinds of sounds belonging to the World-Protecting Heavenly Kings, as well as the various kinds of sounds belonging to devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and even all the various kinds of sounds belonging to sentient beings—the Bodhisattva enters into them all by means of his own voice."
Furthermore, a verse says:
“The Bodhisattva speaks with joy in the Brahma-voice, Surpassing even the voice of the Brahma King;
What he teaches accords with the practices of compassion, And the four dharmas of sympathetic joy and equanimity are all in harmony.”
The delightful songs and melodies of Śakra are eclipsed by the voice of the Bodhisattva;
following whatever exquisite musical tones he produces, he discerns the meanings of all phenomena accordingly.
The exquisite voices of the hosts of kinnaras are all utterly surpassed by the voice of the Bodhisattva;
it extinguishes the blazing fire of craving, and one feels love and joy for that which he speaks.
The delightful sounds of the gods in the desire realm, And the various songs and chants of the celestial beings,
Proclaim the meaning of the Dharma in accordance with reality, Causing all of them to give rise to joy.
Sentient beings who possess greed, hatred, delusion, pride, arrogance, flattery, doubt, and their like,
upon hearing the Bodhisattva’s voice that accords with reality, are all able to bring their greed, hatred, and other afflictions to rest.
All the hosts of devas in the realm of form, having heard the voice of the Supreme Person,
all gave rise to hearts of joy, aspiring for bodhi and rebirth in the happy realms.
The sounds of the exquisite music of the mahoragas, gandharvas, nāgas, and others,
upon hearing the proclamations of the Ocean of Merit, all experience vast and great joy.

In various places throughout the boundless realms, including this Jambudvīpa among the lands of men, beings hear the wondrous voice of the Bodhisattva according to their capacity; having heard it, they all attain liberation.
The realms of the gods dwelling on earth and those dwelling in space—all enter into the Bodhisattva’s voice;
according to the specific types of beings they encounter, he proclaims the definitive and true Dharma.
Kalaviṅkas and kokilas, geese, wild ducks, parrots, and śārikas;
peacocks, jīvañjīvakas, and kunālas, auspicious birds, ruddy sheldrakes, and the like;
lions, tigers, leopards, bears, deer, and elk; elephants, horses, rhinoceroses, cats, dogs, and pigs.
These running beasts and flying birds, upon hearing these sounds, all rejoice.
All four-footed and two-footed beings, as well as those with many feet or no feet— sentient beings of every kind—
the Bodhisattva enters into their various voices, awakening them and inspiring in them love or awe as is appropriate.
Among all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm, With their various distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior natures,
Whether in the three miserable realms or among humans and devas— The Bodhisattva’s voice universally enters into them all.
Within this, the bodhisattva is without discrimination, without grasping, without bondage, and without conceptual thought;
abiding in a state of non-distraction and meditative equipoise, they manifest various signs as appropriate to the task at hand.
The pure aspirations sought by sentient beings, expressed through sounds throughout millions of lands,
and likewise those exceeding the sands of the Ganges— all these, this mind neither grasps nor awakens to.
All the hosts of Māras within the three thousandfold world-system, having heard the Bodhisattva’s vast and magnificent voice, were struck with awe and fear;
they quickly turned their hearts toward him, joining their palms in reverent faith and prostrating themselves in worship.
Sentient beings who were always fond of contentious debate and possessed of overweening pride did not take refuge or have faith;
yet, upon hearing the pure words of the Great Being, they joined their palms in respectful faith and prostrated themselves.
Those who are deaf or mute, those without tongues, and all sentient beings with stammering or impaired speech,
by means of the Bodhisattva’s exquisite words, are immediately able to hear and speak.
Afflictions burn and further oppress them, as they commit hundreds of kinds of sinful deeds;
yet by hearing the virtuous and pure words of the Bodhisattva, their minds attain coolness and all evils are stilled.
If sentient beings hear the sound of impermanence, they shall likewise hear the sounds of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
the same applies to the dharmas of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience, as well as diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, all of which they shall hear.
All oceans of merit, though one were to speak for many koṭis of eons, could not exhaust them;
with boundless voice and boundless wisdom, they all abide in the Buddha’s sound without interruption.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!
You should know that within the speech and sounds of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, there is no speech of attachment, no speech of ferocity,
no speech of delusion or confusion, no speech of defilement, and no speech of bondage or liberation."
No speech that is high or low; no harsh or abrasive speech; no malicious or perverse speech;
no defective or leaking speech; no rigid or stubborn speech; no speech that is discordant or compliant; no regressive speech; no speech following evil;
no contradictory speech; no speech following defilement; no indeterminate speech; no agitated speech; no...
There is no speech of arrogance; no speech of anger or resentment; no untimely speech; no speech of mixed desires;
no speech of regional attachment; no speech of longing; no excessively slow speech;
no excessively rapid speech; no speech that impairs the faculties; no speech that impairs the voice; no speech that destroys the mind.
There is no speech that is crooked or perverse; no speech that is inferior or weak; no speech that is concealed or hidden;
no speech that is decayed or withered; no speech that is disloyal or antagonistic; no speech that is deep or treacherous; no speech that does not lead to liberation;

no speech that lacks compassion; no speech that harms others; no speech that creates discord between oneself and others; no speech that involves coming and going [in distraction]; and no speech that is grasping.
He utters speech that is pure, not impure; not irrational, not intolerant, not confused, not slanderous, not unrighteous,
not arrogant, not base, not untimely, not mistimed, and not false.
Speech that is not false; speech that does not seek gain or offerings; speech that is not unencompassing; speech that is not deluded or bewildered;
speech that is not characterized by doubt; speech that is not unpleasant; speech that is not slanderous;
speech that is not contemptuous; speech that is not self-aggrandizing; and speech that does not cause division among others.
There is no speech that functions to praise oneself; no speech that functions to disparage others;
no speech of derision; no speech of subjugating others; no speech regarding what should not be done; no speech that contradicts what has been done;
no speech that destroys secrets; no speech that fails to guard [one's words]; no speech that treats the wise with contempt; no speech that destroys...
There is no speech that slanders the noble ones; no speech that fails to praise; no speech that fails to extol;
no speech that exposes the faults of others; no speech that is as piercing as a shot arrow; no speech that speaks of the wrongs of others; no speech that fails to rescue and uplift;
no speech uttered out of overweening pride (*adhimāna*); no speech of sinful karma; and no speech that is not beneficial.
He said:

"Śāntamati, you should know that every word and sound uttered by a bodhisattva is established through the power of supernormal knowledge and wisdom, as the fruit of meritorious conduct. It proceeds from the continuity of well-planted seeds without interruption, such that whatever is spoken is entirely accomplished."
At one time, while a bodhisattva was walking, standing, sitting, or lying down beneath a tree, if someone were to come to where the bodhisattva was and ask this question:
"Do you know how many leaves there are on this tree?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva did not examine the tree nor count its leaves, but answered immediately:
"This tree possesses such-and-such a number of leaves."
Just as the Bodhisattva had spoken, there was neither increase nor decrease in the number of those tree leaves.
Furthermore, someone asked:
"How many grains of sand are there in the Ganges River?"

How many hundreds, how many thousands, how many hundreds of thousands, how many koṭis, how many ayutas, how many nayutas, how many kankaras, how many bimbaras, how many vivāhas, how many akṣobhyas, how many immeasurables (aprameyas), how many asaṃkhyeyas, how many ardhaghaṭas, how many vahas, how many nāgabala-s, or how many incalculable (asaṃkhyeya) numbers?
At that time, the Bodhisattva did not examine the river nor count its sands, but replied immediately:
"This river possesses such-and-such a number of sands."
Just as the words spoken by that bodhisattva, so too the sands of those rivers neither increase nor decrease, being equal in number to what is known by the wisdom of the Tathāgata.

What the bodhisattva says is true and without falsehood; it does not require the testimony of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and the assemblies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, but is to be realized and known solely by the Buddha-Tathāgata.
Śāntamati! You should understand all such conditions in this way.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!"
I recall that in the distant past, there was a seer named Mitrāyu and a brahmin named Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.

At that time, there was a great nyagrodha tree named Bhadraśāla, which possessed many branches and leaves that spread out in all directions to provide shade, covering an area of one krośa in length and breadth.
At that time, the seer Priyā was dwelling beside the tree; by means of his supernormal powers, he had spent seven days closely observing and counting its leaves.
Later, on one occasion, the brahmin Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana entered the city to beg for alms, and after wandering about and finishing his meal under that tree, he went to the dwelling of the seer Priyā.
Having arrived, they were filled with joy; they greeted one another with pleasant words, and through various conversations, they all experienced great delight.
Then the seer said: "O Great Brāhmaṇa!..."

"You should certainly know this: among those in the human world, is there anyone who could, by carefully observing and examining, know the exact number of branches and leaves on this great nyagrodha tree?
The brāhmaṇa replied, "Venerable One!"
"There are also such people in the world. The seer asked again,
"What kind of people are they?"
The brahmin said: "O Venerable One! You should explain this to me."
The rishi replied: "Great Brahmin! Tell it to me."
At that time, the brahmin did not examine the tree nor count its leaves; in response to the request, he immediately spoke this verse:
“Eight thousand nayutas in number, And ninety-two koṭis more;
Know that there are sixty akṣobhyas, With sixteen equaling the number of its branches.”
Furthermore, there are thirty nayutas, ninety-six kankaras, and thirteen vibhāṣas; these are all the number of its leaves.
All the branches and leaves that this tree possesses remain exactly as previously stated, neither increasing nor decreasing;
I speak thus according to my wisdom as it truly is, and those who doubt may count for themselves and find no error.
At that time, having heard these words, the seer Subhūṣita was deeply struck with wonder and spoke in verse:
“O Brahmin, by your supernormal knowledge, you have spoken well with words of truth;
you know exactly as they are all the branches and leaves of this noble and excellent King of Nyagrodha trees.”
You have never observed those trees, nor have you ever calculated their number;
yet the branches and leaves therein are immeasurable, and you are able to comprehend and enter them with a mind of wisdom.
After the seer had spoken these verses, he asked again:
"Great Brahmin! As you have said, is it through your own intellectual power that you know this?"
"Are the various noble sages assisting you to speak this? The brahmin replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"Listen well now!
I speak according to reality with the wisdom of those among humans; this space may be shattered, but these words are not false.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati, saying:
"You should know this now: the seer Priyangu at that time was none other than the present Great Wise Śāriputra;
the brahmin Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana was none other than the present World-Honored One, the Śākya Lion."
Because of this, the ocean of verbal qualities possessed by a bodhisattva is able to abide in the true qualities of the Dharma and its meaning according to reality. Śāntamati!
These are called the purity of the bodhisattva’s vocal secrecy and vocal karma.
Among them, if there is anyone who enters even slightly into understanding, I declare that person to be one of supreme wisdom.
Chapter Three: The Secret Mind of the Bodhisattva, Part One. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati, saying:
“What is meant by the purity of the secret mind and mental karma of a bodhisattva?”

Śāntamati, you should know that all actions performed by a bodhisattva are performed through wisdom and not through pride; they are entirely manifested as a playful display of the indestructible, wondrous wisdom of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), established through all manner of karmic activities and accomplished by means of vast power.
Furthermore, the characteristic of that supernormal knowledge can establish all modes of activity;
moreover, the sublime wisdom of that supernormal power can perceive all phenomena.
Furthermore, the wisdom of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-jñāna*) is itself an inexhaustible characteristic, for it is able to accord with all places.
Moreover, the wisdom of supernormal powers is able to manifest all forms as they appear, because it pervades each and every such form.
Furthermore, the wisdom of supernormal powers is able to enter into all those sounds because sounds are equal across the limits of the past and the future.
Moreover, the wisdom of supernormal powers is universally able to observe the minds of all sentient beings, because the intrinsic nature of the mind can be perceived through investigation.
Furthermore, the wisdom of supernormal powers is well able to recollect the events of boundless eons, because there is no interruption between the prior and subsequent limits.
Moreover, the wisdom of supernormal powers can know all types of phenomena, as they are all the characteristics of the practice of liberating wisdom.

Furthermore, the knowledge of supernormal powers (abhijñā-jñāna) accords with what is sought at the appropriate time regarding the dharma of the exhaustion of outflows (āsrava-kṣaya), for it does not transcend that specific temporal occasion.
Moreover, the knowledge of supernormal powers is itself supramundane (lokottara), as it constitutes the noble stage of decisive discernment (ārya-nirvedha-bhāgīya).
Furthermore, as for the wisdom of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), neither Śrāvakas nor Pratyekabuddhas can fathom its source or depth.
Moreover, this wisdom of supernormal powers is the meaning of profound depth; it is fully capable of subduing all Māras and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Furthermore, the wisdom of supernormal powers can reach the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and directly realize all the supreme Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, the wisdom of supernormal powers is fully capable of turning the sublime wheel of Dharma in accordance with [the needs of beings].
Furthermore, the wisdom of supernormal powers skillfully accomplishes the task of taming all sentient beings.
Furthermore, through the wisdom of supernormal powers, they attain great empowerment and achieve mastery over all phenomena. "Śāntamati!
This is what constitutes the purity of the bodhisattva’s mental secrets and mental activities."

Because the mind is pure, it is free from defilement; being immaculate, bright, and clear, it is detached from all afflictions. It is able to skillfully subdue [the senses], skillfully perform all karmas, and skillfully enter into dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, and samāpatti, yet it does not ultimately fall into any of them.

Upon the complete recollection of the dharma of non-arising, it arises; furthermore, it is not moved by the desire realm, nor does it arise through bondage, nor does it cease through bondage, nor does it originate through bondage.

Why is this so? It is because one is able to liberate oneself from all conceptual discrimination, liberate oneself from all bonds of defilement, and liberate oneself from the basis of inverted grasping; that very liberation is birth, that very liberation is cessation, and that very liberation is arising. Although there is birth, there is nothing that is born. In this way, one is able to fully perfect all the Buddha-dharmas of the Mahāyāna.

However, if one carefully and thoroughly investigates those Buddha-dharmas throughout the ten directions, nothing at all is found, yet it is not that nothing is found; because all Buddha-dharmas are neither found nor not found, one is thus able to accordingly attain all those dharmas and all Buddha-dharmas.
Therefore, regarding all phenomena and all Buddha-dharmas, there is no phenomenon that is not a non-phenomenon.
Why is this? Because when one thoroughly and critically investigates all phenomena, nothing at all is apprehended, yet it is also not the case that nothing is apprehended.

If one seeks all phenomena as they truly are and finds nothing at all, yet it is not that there is no finding, then there is no phenomenon that can be reckoned by number, because all phenomena have already transcended the measure of calculation.

If one can thoroughly understand the equality of all those phenomena, therein there is no phenomenon, nor even the absence of a phenomenon, that can be grasped or clung to; this is the meaning of the non-clinging to all phenomena.
If one were to comprehend this meaning, it would be utterly meaningless;
yet if there is no comprehension, that [meaning] is neither non-meaningful nor not non-meaningful, because the establishment of non-meaning is visible before one's eyes.
If there were any wisdom that could be fully comprehended, it would constitute an obstacle to that unimpeded wisdom.
If, however, there is no obstruction regarding wisdom, this is precisely non-attachment.

If there is no attachment, there is no dwelling; if there is no dwelling, there is no exhaustion; if there is no exhaustion, there is neither exertion nor falling away; if there is neither exertion nor falling away, there is no non-self; if there is no non-self, then there is also no self; if there is no self, there is no grasping; if there is no grasping, there is no contention; if there is no contention, there is no dispute. This absence of dispute is what is called the Dharma of the śramaṇa—this is the Dharma of the śramaṇa.
It is like space, which is fundamentally equal.
Because space is equal, it is not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm.
Because it is thus, there is nothing whatsoever to which one is bound in any place.

Because there is no binding, there are no forms, colors, or various characteristics. Because there are no color-forms, one is able to accord with and awaken to them; because one can thus accord with and awaken to them, one is able to differentiate all distinctions.
The Bodhisattva Śāntamati asked:
"What is meant by 'conforming realization' (anuloma-bodha)?
Furthermore, what is meant by 'discriminative differentiation' (vibhāga-vikalpa)?"
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva said:
"There is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended; this is called 'conformity with awakening. Because it is awakening, it is itself differentiated discernment.
Therefore, these two explanations are made regarding dharmas."
"Śāntamati, you should know that these are called the purity of the mind and mental activities of the bodhisattva’s secret mind.
Thus ends the third fascicle of the *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa Mahāyāna Sūtra* spoken by the Buddha.
[End of Fascicle Three] of the *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa Mahāyāna Sūtra* spoken by the Buddha.

The Fourth [Section], translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, the Great Master of Sanskrit Transmission, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Dharmapāla, and others, by imperial decree. The Remainder of the Third Chapter, "The Secret Mind of the Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati, saying:
“Good son! Regarding the secret of the bodhisattva’s mind: when practicing loving-kindness, one knows there is no self; when practicing compassion, there are no sentient beings;
when practicing sympathetic joy, there is no life-principle; when practicing equanimity, there is nothing [to be grasped].”
If a person cultivates the practice of giving, their mind is subdued; if they cultivate the practice of ethical discipline, their mind is tranquil;
if they cultivate the practice of patience, their mind possesses the characteristic of inexhaustibility; if they cultivate the practice of diligence, their mind is free from signs;
if they cultivate the practice of meditative concentration, their mind is stable; if they cultivate the practice of wisdom, their mind is without [conceptualization].
In investigation: if one practices the four foundations of mindfulness, the mind is without recollection and without mental application;
if one practices the four right efforts, the mind is perfectly balanced; if one practices the four bases of psychic power, the mind is free from conceptual proliferation;
if one practices the faculty of faith, the mind is without attachment; if one practices the faculty of diligence, the mind is without exertion.
Awakening: if one cultivates the faculty of mindfulness, one attains the mind of spontaneous wisdom; if one cultivates the faculty of concentration, one attains the mind of the wisdom of equality;
if one cultivates the faculty of wisdom, one attains the rootless mind; if one cultivates the five powers, one attains a mind that is not subject to subjugation;
if one cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment, one attains the mind of discerning wisdom; and if...
By cultivating the Eightfold Noble Path, one attains a mind that has nothing to cultivate; by cultivating śamatha, one attains a mind of tranquil stillness;
by cultivating vipaśyanā, one attains a mind that has nothing to observe; by cultivating the Four Noble Truths, one attains a mind that ultimately has no cognition;
and by cultivating the mental attention of the Buddha, one attains a mind free from mental attention.
If one cultivates the mental attention on the Dharma, one immediately attains the mind of equality with the dharma-realm;

if one cultivates the mental attention on the Sangha, one immediately attains the non-abiding mind; if one cultivates the practice of maturing sentient beings, one immediately attains the mind that is primordially pure;

if one cultivates the practice of upholding the true Dharma, one immediately attains the mind of non-differentiation within the dharma-realm; if one cultivates the adornment and purification [of the Buddha-fields]...

By practicing the conduct of Buddha-fields, one immediately attains a mind equal to space; by practicing the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one attains a mind of non-apprehension;
by practicing the conduct of the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), one attains a mind that turns without turning;
by practicing the conduct of accomplishing all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), one attains a markless mind; and by practicing the adornment of the fruit of enlightenment (*bodhi-phala*).

One immediately attains the mind of perfect fulfillment within the three realms; if one cultivates the practice of subduing all māras, one attains the mind that universally gathers all sentient beings;
if one cultivates the practice of proceeding toward bodhi, one attains the mind that realizes the self-nature of the dharmadhātu;
if one cultivates the practice of turning the wheel of Dharma, one attains the mind that neither turns nor does not turn; if one cultivates...
Through the practice of Great Nirvāṇa, one immediately attains the mind that contemplates the self-nature of saṃsāra. "Śāntamati!
You should know that all these are the secret dharmas of the minds of Bodhisattvas who have attained forbearance (kṣānti-pratilabdha), and whose mental karma is purified."

When that bodhisattva has thus become purified, they immediately attain the purification of the minds of all sentient beings; this bodhisattva is then able to enter into the minds of those sentient beings, for all those minds of sentient beings emerge from the radiance of the great bodhicitta.
Just as space abides in all places and enters into all places, so too is the bodhisattva’s mind: it abides in all places and enters into all places.

When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, had thus proclaimed this inconceivable true Dharma of the secrets of the body, speech, and mind of all bodhisattvas, seventy-two thousand devas and humans in the assembly gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); eighty-four thousand people were distanced from dust and free from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; and eight thousand bhikṣus, through the exhaustion of outflows regarding all dharmas, attained liberation of mind.

At that time, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways; a great radiance shone everywhere, and from the void there naturally rained down various celestial flowers. Furthermore, in the sky, hundreds of thousands of kinds of exquisite music resounded spontaneously without being played.
From within that music, these words emerged:

"Only those sentient beings who have already received the prediction of enlightenment shall be able to hear this True Dharma spoken by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets."

Having heard this therein, they shall uphold, recite, and practice it according to the principle; they shall extensively proclaim it to others as appropriate, and never forget the mind of great enlightenment.

One should know that such a person has not achieved this through meager roots of virtue; rather, they have deeply planted the roots of goodness under many, many Buddha-Bhagavāns, diligently cultivated all supreme meritorious deeds, and shall bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
Chapter Four: The Arrival of the Bodhisattva Ghoṣeśvararāja. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Śāntamati, saying: "Good son!
“Did you hear the various kinds of musical instruments and wondrous sounds in the air?
The Bodhisattva Śāntamati addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One, [I did].”
"I have already heard this;
what kind of exquisite and wonderful sound is this?
I pray that the Buddha will explain it for me."
The Buddha said, “Śāntamati!

You should know now that there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Ghoṣeśvararāja who has come from the world-system Mahāmegha, from the presence of the Tathāgata Meghasvara-rāja, to this Sahā world in order to behold, pay homage to, and attend upon me with offerings; furthermore, he wishes to hear and receive the sublime Dharma proclaimed by the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, and also desires to see the great assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas gathered from the ten directions.”
That Bodhisattva Vighuṣṭaśabda concealed his physical form and dwelt in mid-air, raining down various exquisite flowers and playing sublime music as an offering to me.
From within the sounds of that music, such a voice emerged:
"The World-Honored Tathāgata will, before long, proclaim the vast and sublime Dharma within this great assembly.

Having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ghoṣeśvararāja immediately descended from the sky into the Buddha’s assembly. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and standing before the Buddha, addressed him, saying:

“The Tathāgata Meghasvara-rāja of the Mahāmegha World inquires after the World-Honored One: Are you free from illness and affliction? Are your daily activities light and easy? Is your physical strength at peace?”
That Buddha-Tathāgata further spoke thus:

"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, possesses great skillful means and is adept at preaching the True Dharma; established by the majestic spiritual power of that Buddha, he is thus able to penetrate all immeasurable Buddha-dharmas."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ghoṣeśvararāja, saying:
"Excellent, son of good family!
You have come well to this great assembly, desiring to hear Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, proclaim the inconceivable secret Dharma of the Tathāgata."
"You should listen to this attentively and receive it with careful heed.
Chapter Five: The Preceding Deeds of the Cakravartin King Dhṛtarāṣṭra At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas within the gathering all had this thought:

"In the presence of which Buddha, World-Honored One, did this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, personally attend and receive teachings to plant deep roots of goodness? Furthermore, what kind of vast vows did he cultivate, such that he is now able to possess such great eloquence and skillfully expound all dharmas?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the doubts and reflections in the minds of the bodhisattvas, addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati, saying: "Good son!

I recall that in the past, after an incalculable kalpa (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) and further beyond an incalculable number of immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas, there was a kalpa named Bhadra and a world named Vyūha."

A Buddha appeared in the world, named Anantaguṇaratnavyūharāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

Śāntamati, you should know that that world, Adorned, is vast, wondrous, peaceful, and prosperous; its population is flourishing, its ground is as level as the palm of a hand, free from sand, gravel, thorns, and impurities, and its grasses, trees, and forests are lush green and lovely.

Furthermore, there were famous flowers, and soft grasses covered the ground, lush green and exquisite, like the right-turning *śrīvatsa* mark on a peacock's neck; they possessed both color and fragrance, bringing delight to those who beheld them.
When the foot is placed upon the ground, it sinks down four finger-widths; when the foot is lifted, it rises back up by four finger-widths.
It is free from extreme cold or heat, being perfectly balanced with moderate warmth and coolness, while a soft, beautiful, and pure breeze brings joy to all who encounter it.
The ground was adorned like vaidūrya.

At that time, the people were handsome in appearance; they had little greed, anger, ignorance, or other afflictions. They were filial and affectionate, possessed of strength, and were able to understand and enlighten themselves upon hearing well-spoken words.

And within the Dharma of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata King Adorned by a Multitude of Jewels of Boundless Merit, there were twelve nayutas of śrāvaka assemblies and thirty-two koṭis of bodhisattva assemblies.
At that time, the lifespan of humans was thirty-six koṭis of years, and among them were those who passed away from their lives.
Śāntamati, you should know that within that world-system of the Well-Manifested Eon (Bhadrakalpa), there existed four great continents.
Each of the four great continents is eighty-four thousand yojanas in extent, and within each yojana there are a thousand kingdoms, cities, districts, towns, and villages surrounding it.

In that adorned world, there is a great city named Supreme Purity; the dimensions of that city are vast and expansive, measuring sixty-four yojanas to the north, forty yojanas to the south, and the same distance from east to west.
There were ten thousand gardens and groves as adornments, and within the capital city there were further ten thousand provinces, cities, districts, and towns.
In that most pure capital city, there was a great wheel-turning sage king named Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who possessed the seven treasures and was the sovereign of the four great continents.

Having deeply planted roots of goodness in the presence of previous Buddhas, he was the most excellent among kings in terms of merit and majestic radiance, and he never regressed from his mind set upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

“Śāntamati! The royal city where that Cakravartin King Dhṛtarāṣṭra dwells is sixteen yojanas square, vast and exquisite. It has sevenfold walls made of the seven precious substances, and above them are sevenfold pavilions with sevenfold jeweled nets from which various jeweled bells hang.”
Within the enclosure, there are four great gardens on all sides:
the first is named Many Flowers, the second Joy of Virtue, the third Joy of Peacocks, and the fourth Happiness of the Seasons.
Within each of these gardens there is a great pond:
the first is named Joy, the second Joy-Surpassing, the third Fragrance-Surpassing, and the fourth Flowing-Along.

These ponds are each half a yojana in length and breadth; their steps are paved entirely with various jewels, their bottoms are made of Jāmbūnada gold, and their floors are strewn with golden sand. They are filled with water possessing the eight virtues, covered throughout by precious lotus flowers, and frequented by swans, geese, mandarin ducks, and various other birds swimming therein.

Furthermore, that Cakravartin King Dhṛtarāṣṭra had seventy thousand palace ladies and maidservants, all of whom were endowed with exquisite and sublime physical beauty; they served as his "jewel of women" (strī-ratna) to attend upon him, and all these palace ladies had already resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The king had a thousand sons, whose physical forms were upright and majestic; they were courageous and fearless, capable of subduing the armies of others, and each was adorned with the twenty-eight marks of a great man. With deep hearts of pure faith, they were devoted to the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Śāntamati! At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata King Adorned by the Multitude of Jewels of Boundless Merit, resided in the city of the Great Kingdom of Utmost Purity.

That Cakravartin King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with his ministers, brahmins, elders, and all the people, all with deep respect, reverence, and offerings, and with pure faith, served and made offerings to that Tathāgata King Adorned by the Multitude of Jewels of Boundless Merit and the assembly of bhikṣus for a full one koṭi of years. They extensively maintained joyful intent, offering all kinds of food and drink, exquisite and wonderful clothing, and even all articles of enjoyment, presenting them all as offerings.”
Furthermore, the assembly of bhikṣus each offered three gardens for his residence. "Śāntamati!

That wheel-turning king had several crown princes whose minds were each pure and free from negligence; they drew near to that Buddha to hear the sublime Dharma with courageous resolve, and did not become defiled by or attached to sensual pleasures."

Through heedfulness, their minds became tranquil; by listening to the True Dharma, these princes soon attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Immediately, each leaped into the air like a king of geese soaring with ease, traveling from garden to garden and from city to city, even wandering throughout the four great continents. As they moved through the sky, they spoke these verses:
"What benefit is gained when the Buddhas appear in the world?"
The collective benefit for humanity is profound once more.
O Benevolent One, a pure faith that listens to the Dharma is extremely difficult to find even throughout a hundred kalpas.
Now this Sage among Men has appeared in the world to proclaim the True Dharma, the path of tranquility.
I have now approached that Blessed One; by hearing the Dharma, I am born into a happy realm.
Having heard the true Dharma, I have destroyed the miserable realms; having heard the true Dharma, I am born into a happy realm.
Through hearing the Dharma, afflictions are eliminated, and the mind attains the supreme bliss of cooling tranquility.
While this verse was being spoken in the sky, this great earth shook in six ways;
gods and humans emitted sublime sounds from the air, and a great rain of various flowers fell, producing delight:
"If a person were to behold the Great Teacher, the Buddha, his merits could not be fully described."
One should pay homage to the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, joining palms with sincere and respectful faith.
That Buddha knows the intentions within the minds of people and teaches the Dharma to each according to what is appropriate.
Upon hearing the Dharma, thirty-six koṭis of people all abided in the path to supreme bodhi;
furthermore, three hundred koṭis of people attained the most sublime and pure Dharma-eye.
All gave rise to a mind of weary detachment, took refuge in the Buddha, left the household life, and relied upon the true teaching.
Furthermore, forty quadrillion nayutas of people received the pure precepts and performed the work of Buddhas;
having heard the Dharma and made offerings to the World-Honored Buddha, they each returned to their respective places.
After those princes had spoken these verses, they collectively performed acts of offering for their father, the Cakravartin King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

They selected the finest and most exquisite *nāgakesara* sandalwood to construct a multi-storied pavilion, vast, magnificent, and exquisitely adorned, measuring ten *yojanas* in both length and breadth. Its four sides and four corners were perfectly symmetrical, and the gates and passageways of the tower were likewise made entirely of the finest *nāgakesara* sandalwood;
its craftsmanship was complete and perfect, like that of a celestial palace.
A half-tael of that Dragon-Firm Incense was worth more than the price of Jāmbūnada gold, and those pavilions were exquisitely constructed with marvelous craftsmanship and beautifully adorned.

At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King Dhṛtarāṣṭra desired to go to the presence of the Tathāgata Infinite Merit Jewel-Assembly Adornment King to behold and pay homage to him, to draw near to him, and to hear and receive the True Dharma.
At that time, the king’s sons, along with the palace ladies and their retinues, attended upon the father king and entered the great sandalwood pavilion.

The king sat upon a lion throne adorned with lotuses; the crown prince, the palace ladies, ministers, and the common people all paid him their respects, making extensive offerings of every kind of flower garlands, scented unguents, exquisite garments, precious banners, pennants, and canopies, as well as sublime music.

Furthermore, with jeweled nets draped over the pavilions, the multitude together lifted them up and proceeded forward; immediately, they soared into the midst of the sky, moving with sovereign ease like the king of geese.

Arriving at the place where the Buddha was, they slowly set the pavilion down upon the ground. Then, the Wheel-Turning Sage King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with his crown prince and palace ladies, descended gracefully from the pavilion. They proceeded to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated themselves with their heads touching the ground at the Buddha’s feet, and after each member of the bhikṣu saṃgha had likewise paid their respects, they circumambulated him seven times to the right. Returning to stand before the Buddha, they joined their palms with sincere devotion to listen to and receive the True Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata King Adorned by the Multitude of Jewels of Boundless Merit, knowing that the holy Wheel-Turning King Dhṛtarāṣṭra had come to the Buddha’s assembly desiring to hear the Dharma, immediately preached the sublime Dharma to him as was appropriate, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him.
The Buddha said: "Great King!

You should now know that there are four kinds of dharmas; if one practices them according to the principle, one will be able to abide securely in the Mahāyāna and proceed toward the supreme path, so that all wholesome dharmas shall not be lost or destroyed."
What are the four? Great King,
the first is that one who has faith in the Dharma is able to progress toward the supreme path.
Furthermore, what is called faith?
It means that because one possesses faith, one is able to accord with the lineage of the noble ones and refrain from doing whatever ought not to be done.
Second, it is to respect and incline toward the supreme path.
Out of respect, one is able to listen to and receive the sublime Dharma spoken by the noble ones; because one receives the Dharma with earnest attention, the ears do not wander to external sounds.
Third, being free from pride, one is able to advance toward the supreme path.
Because they are free from pride, they are able to show reverence, faith, and prostration toward all those who are worthy and noble.
Fourth, through diligence, one is able to advance toward the supreme path.
By means of diligence, both body and mind attain pliancy, and all wholesome dharmas that are undertaken are successfully accomplished.
"Great King!
If one practices these four dharmas according to the principle, one will be able to abide securely in the Mahāyāna and advance toward the supreme path.
