Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu.

Translated by the Imperial Preceptor for the Transmission of the Dharma, the Great Master, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Dharmapāla, and others, by imperial decree. From the remainder of the fifth chapter, "The Preliminary Practices of the Wheel-Turning King Dhṛtarāṣṭra": "Furthermore, O Great King!..."

There are four dharmas; if one is perfected in them, one will be able to abide securely in the Mahāyāna, accomplish the practice of non-negligence, and remain without mental distraction. What are these four?

First, guarding the sense faculties through ethical discipline; second, contemplating the faults of sensual desires; third, embracing all conditioned things with the perception of impermanence; and fourth, regarding certainty in the Dharma as the supreme life-force.
"Great King!
If these four dharmas are perfected, one will be able to abide securely in the Mahāyāna, accomplish the practice of non-negligence, and remain free from mental distraction."
“‘Great King! There are four kinds of dharmas; if a king practices them and is fully endowed with them, he is called a benevolent king.
What are these four?’”

First, never abandoning the great mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); second, instructing others in the teachings of enlightenment; third, dedicating all roots of virtue toward enlightenment; fourth, having seen or heard of the great majestic power of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, one likewise gives rise to a heart of joy regarding the power possessed by all devas, humans, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, yet seeks only the great majestic power of the Buddha.
"Great King!
If a king fully cultivates these four dharmas, he is called a 'benevolent king.
Therefore, Great King!"

One should constantly cultivate the practice of heedfulness, maintain pure faith, and aspire to the True Dharma; one should give rise to a desire for the Dharma, diligently seek the True Dharma, and always sport within the garden of the True Dharma without becoming attached to sensory realms.
Why is this so? Great King, you should know that desire is never satiated; that which brings true satisfaction is called noble wisdom.
"Furthermore, Great King!
One's lifespan is extremely short and life does not endure for long; the karmic retribution for offenses committed when proceeding to the next world is terrifying.

Therefore, you should know that you must always draw near to, make offerings to, and revere the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas. By means of these roots of goodness, you should dedicate them toward four goals."
What are these four?

First, dedication toward inexhaustible karmic fruition; second, dedication toward inexhaustible Dharma-gates; third, dedication toward inexhaustible sublime wisdom; and fourth, dedication toward inexhaustible eloquence.
“Great King! Furthermore, there are four dharmas:

first, because the body is pure, one is able to accomplish the practice of wisdom; second, because speech is pure, one is able to accomplish the practice of learning; third, because the mind is pure, one is able to accomplish the practice of precepts; fourth, because wisdom is pure, one is able to accomplish the practice of knowledge.”
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:

first, because their skillful means are perfected, they are able to bring sentient beings to maturity; second, because their wisdom is perfected, they are able to subdue all māras; third, because their vows are perfected, they are able to act exactly as they have spoken; fourth, because they encounter the Buddhas, they attain the perfection of all Buddha-dharmas.

“At that time, the Cakravartin King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having heard the True Dharma from that Buddha—which was taught for his benefit and brought him joy—gave rise to a heart of rapture, delight, and exultation. He took priceless, exquisite pearls and all the royal possessions he had for his own use, offering them all to the Buddha as an act of worship. Furthermore, for the remainder of his life, he practiced the various holy conducts and upheld the five precepts.”

At that time, the king’s palace ladies, having heard the True Dharma from that Buddha, their hearts were filled with great serenity, leaping with joy and delight; each covered the Buddha with the garments they wore and their ornaments, and for as long as they lived, they practiced the various holy conducts (*brahmacarya*) and upheld the five precepts, all of them vowing to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, having attained great benefit and increased his Dharma-wealth, the Cakravartin King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with his palace ladies and retinue, each with utmost sincerity prostrated at the feet of the Buddha. Having likewise paid homage to the assembly of bhikṣus and circumambulated them seven times, he immediately entered the great multi-storied pavilion, leaped up into the air, and traveled with sovereign ease back to the city of the Great Kingdom of Utmost Purity.

"Furthermore, at a later time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King Dhṛtarāṣṭra selected a day of the full moon, prepared his carriage, and went out to the Great Garden of Many Flowers to enjoy himself. There, with the clear sounds of drums and flutes playing exquisite music, he indulged in whatever pleasures he desired, sporting and strolling about."
At that time, there were two supreme palace ladies, one named Akṣobhyā and the other named Anupamā;
they went together to the Lake of Joy, bathed themselves in its pure waters, and having emerged, covered themselves with garments and sat upon lion-thrones of lotuses.
Within those two palaces, there were two youths who had each been spontaneously born while seated; they sat cross-legged.

The youths were upright and majestic, their complexions wondrous beyond compare, endowed with all the primary and secondary marks of perfection, and a sight for which all people longed to behold them. In an instant, they each leaped upward from their seats and remained suspended in the air.
At that time, voices of sages and saints spoke from the air, saying:
"These two youths—one named Dharmamati and the other named Dharmaprajña.
Thus, these two names were established on this account.
The youth Dharmamati was born by transformation upon the seat of the palace lady Akṣatā;
the youth Dharmamati was born by transformation upon the seat of the palace lady Anupamā.
At that time, the two youths were also sitting cross-legged in mid-air, and with one voice they spoke these verses:
“O Noble One, we have now attained a sublime benefit, namely, the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Having already aroused this mind, we have encountered the World-Honored One; with pure hearts, we offer our faith and prostration.”
The great ocean is deep and vast, its bottom difficult to fathom; The wheel of birth and death revolves without rest.
To ferry sentient beings across the broad stream of saṃsāra, One must never abandon that bodhicitta.
There is a world named Undestroyed Body, where there is a World-Honored One named King of Time.
I have come from there seeking the Dharma-gate, desiring to behold the Sage, the mass of merit.
At that time, each of us sat cross-legged, having been born from the seats of our two mothers;
our father, the Great Holy King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, came here with palms joined to pay his respects, saying:
"May my father examine and listen to what I have to say."
Having skillfully attained the Dharma throughout *ayuta* eons, until the ultimate realization of Great Bodhi, one does not abandon what has been gained therein.
It is most difficult for all but a Buddha to appear in the world; it is rare to have parents who establish one in the position of the Dharma.
To encounter a virtuous friend within the Dharma for even a single moment is as rare as pure, wondrous jewels appearing at will.
Possessing desire for the Dharma, diligence, and heedfulness, Having left the household life, they gain benefit and perfect clear comprehension;
Exerting themselves in what is beneficial, their minds are pliant and gentle, Endowed with shame, modesty, great learning, and virtuous precepts;
With compassion, they tame and pacify sentient beings, Causing them all to attain the profound patience of the Dharma.
With diligence, vigor, and an unattached mind, they bring all classes of beings to maturity and gather them in.
Because their minds are free from signs, they attain composure; they do not begrudge even their own bodies or lives.
Contemplating the True Dharma as if saving themselves from a fire, they vow to obtain the supreme merits of all Buddhas.
That which is most supreme and difficult to obtain for my father, the King, is the supreme Dharma that I praise;
I have come from that buddha-field to return to the original source of that Buddha.
We have already established ourselves in the bodhisattva stage, Universally able to embrace all wholesome dharmas;
In a single kṣaṇa we have attained the five supernormal powers, And our minds are able to understand through mindfulness and contemplation.

Then that Cakravartin King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with his queens, retinue, and the two youths—the wise Bodhisattvas—by means of their supernormal powers, remained in mid-air and proceeded together to the assembly of the Tathāgata Anantaguṇaratnavyūharāja.
Having arrived, they each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and the entire assembly extended their respectful homage.
At that time, the Buddha perceived that the two youths were true sons of the Buddha, who desired to hear and receive the teachings of the path to enlightenment.
The Buddha, knowing his intention, immediately proclaimed for him the profound and true Dharma.
The Buddha said:
"O son of good family!

One should know that all phenomena arise from conditions; within them there is no sovereign and no agent. Knowing that the internal is empty and the external has no objective sphere of action, one realizes that all phenomena are empty, provisional, and without reality. Regarding both seeing and acting, one should be entirely pure, like space, with nothing to be grasped.

When that Buddha, the World-Honored One, had thus extensively proclaimed the Dharma of purity in these many ways, seventy-six nayutas and three koṭis of people within the assembly attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

At that time, after the Cakravartin King Dhṛtarāṣṭra had performed offerings within the Buddha’s assembly for seven days and nights, he returned to his own residence in an instant, together with his sons, palace ladies, and retinue.
"At that time, on a later occasion, while the Wheel-Turning King was dwelling alone within a sandalwood pavilion and seated upon a lotus lion-throne, he thought to himself:
'These thousand sons of mine have all already established themselves in the dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; yet among them, which one shall first attain the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?'"
"I ought to devise a method to verify this matter.
Having thought thus, he immediately commanded his attendants to fashion a vase with exquisite craftsmanship using the seven precious gems.

Once it had been well-crafted according to the required proportions, he ordered that the names of each of the thousand sons be written down and placed inside the precious vase. He then fashioned a magnificent lotus flower out of the seven precious gems and set the vase within its center. Thereafter, for seven days and nights, he extensively offered worship to the names within the vase, utilizing subtle and exquisite incense, flowers, ointments, powdered perfumes, as well as the sounds of drums, flutes, and songs.
At that time, ten thousand devas and humans in the air assisted in performing various kinds of sublime offerings.

After making such offerings for seven days and nights, he summoned all his palace ladies, retinue, and the king’s one thousand sons, as well as the two youths, to assemble before him; he then placed the precious vase upon an exquisite golden couch.
Once the King had settled in, he immediately commanded his attendants to draw names from the precious jar.

Following his orders, the attendants first drew one name from within the jar and presented it before the King; that name was none other than Prince Viśuddhamati. Thereafter, they drew the names in succession until all had been taken.

Immediately, in that very instant, this great earth shook in six ways; all the palace ladies, each previously holding various exquisite musical instruments, had them sound spontaneously without being struck, producing wondrous songs.
"Śāntamati! You should know that the prince Viśuddhamati, who at that time first drew his own name from the jar—could he have been anyone else?
He was none other than the Tathāgata Krakucchanda of the past within this Bhadrakalpa."
Next, draw one name from within the vase; the one named Prince Varasena was none other than the Tathāgata Kanakamuni of the past.
Next, a name was drawn from the vase; it was the name Prince Śāntendriya, who was the Tathāgata Kāśyapa of the past.
Next, a name was drawn from the vase; it was the name Prince Sarvārthasiddha, O Śāntamati!
"You should know that this is none other than my own person.
Next, take one name from within the jar; the one named Prince Ratnacandra shall attain Buddhahood under the title Maitreya Tathāgata."
Next, draw one name from the jar; the one named Prince Ox-King shall become a Buddha named Lion Tathāgata.
Next, draw one name from the jar; the one named Prince Lightning-Heaven shall become a Buddha named Great Banner Tathāgata.
Next, draw one name from the vase; the one whose name is Prince Bhadrapāla shall become a Buddha named Ratnapuṣpa Tathāgata.
Next, draw one name from the vase; the one whose name is Prince Śrīprabhaśuddha shall become a Buddha named Puṣpānta Tathāgata.
Next, draw one name from the jar; the one named Prince Padmanetra shall become a Buddha named Suvimalaprabha Tathāgata.
Next, draw one name from the jar; the one named Prince Vimalaprabha shall become a Buddha named Sunetra Tathāgata.
Next, draw one name from the vase; the one named Prince Viśuddhahrada shall become a Buddha named Suratna-bāhu Tathāgata.
Next, draw one name from the vase; the one named Prince Prajñārāja shall become a Buddha named Jvalanaprabha Tathāgata.
Next, take one name from within the jar; the one named Prince Well-Adorned shall become a Buddha named Tathāgata Light-Taste.
Next, take one name from within the jar; the one named Prince Increasing Portion shall become a Buddha named Tathāgata Guide.
Next, draw one name from within the vase; the one named Prince Pure Adornment King shall immediately attain Buddhahood under the title Tathāgata Upholder of Supreme Merit.
Next, a name was drawn from the vase; the one named Prince Śrīguhya shall become a Buddha named Jinaśrī Tathāgata.
Next, a name was drawn from the vase; the one named Prince Sudarśanagātra shall become a Buddha named Jñānakoṣa Tathāgata.
Next, draw one name from the jar; the one named Prince Vīrabala shall become a Buddha named Ratnākara Tathāgata.
Next, draw one name from the jar; the one named Prince Ratnakīrti shall become a Buddha named Samantaprabha Tathāgata.

Śāntamati! You should know that, as extensively explained, from among those thousand sons they were taken up in succession until only one name remained; the one named Prince Mahāśṛṅgavyūha shall attain buddhahood under the name Tathāgata Anantaguṇaratnayaśas.

"Śāntamati! From among all the names, the single name remaining in the precious jar was drawn last; it was 'Prince Anantamati,' and this prince held the position of the youngest among the thousand sons."
At that time, his elder brothers spoke with contempt, saying:
"When we, your elder brothers, have attained Buddhahood, we shall have already performed the works of a Buddha and delivered sentient beings.
What will you do at the very end?"
Then the Crown Prince Anantamati spoke these verses:
“The Buddha-dharma is boundless like space; Sentient beings and wisdom are likewise inexhaustible.
Through pure conduct and vows, cultivated by the fragrance of the precepts— Listen now as I speak of this course of conduct and vow.”
Whatever the lifespan of my elder brothers may be, and whatever the number of assemblies of kings may be—
if one were to aggregate all my lifespans together— may there be a community of śrāvakas equal to that number.
After the Prince had spoken this verse, the devas in the sky praised him, saying:
"The noble one’s aspiration is pure and perfect; he shall bring benefit to sentient beings without end."
"Śāntamati! You should know that at that time, the youngest prince Anantamati shall attain Buddhahood under the name of Rucirarāja Tathāgata, becoming the final Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa."
Śāntamati! All the lifespans of the Buddhas and the assemblies of śrāvakas throughout the Bhadrakalpa shall be fully attained by that Tathāgata Sukākāṅkṣin;
because that Tathāgata possesses such excellent aspiration, he is therefore named Sukākāṅkṣin (Desire for Joy).
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!
Observe this bodhisattva mahāsattva, who is endowed with skillful means and perfect pure ethical discipline, whose great vows are unimpaired, and whose sublime practices are fulfilled."
Those nine hundred and ninety-nine princes, up to and including Prince Anantamati, had all fully accomplished the aforementioned merits.
At that time, those thousand princes together addressed the two young sons of good family, the Bodhisattvas, saying:
"O you two, Dharmamati and Dharmaprajña! You sons of good family!"
"What kind of extraordinary power of aspiration did you cultivate in the past that it has now resulted in this?
The youth Dharmacintin replied: "O noble ones!"

I and all of you shall possess a continuity of supreme practice like that of Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva; we shall not depart from the unsurpassed secrets of all Tathāgatas, nor shall we depart from the hearing, receiving, faith, and understanding of all Buddha-dharmas.
The youth Dharmamati said:
"Now that my elder brothers are endowed with the power of supreme vows, I pray that you and I may all realize bodhi.
Once we have attained bodhi, I shall exhort each of you to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma."
"By the power of his vow, he received the prediction of awakening from that Buddha.
"Śāntamati, you should know: who else could the Wheel-turning Sage King Dhṛtarāṣṭra have been at that time?"
He is none other than the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara.
Those thousand princes of that wheel-turning king (cakravartin) during his former causal stage were precisely these thousand Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, of this Bhadrakalpa.
From the Tathāgata Krakucchanda to the Tathāgata Ruci, these names were not translated in the ancient scriptures, but are simply referred to as Louti (Lokiteśvara).

At that time, the youth Dharmamati, who was born by miraculous transformation amidst the assembly of the irreproachable palace ladies, was none other than the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, manifested through his supernatural power.
At that time, the youth Dharmamati, who was born by transformation amidst the incomparable palace women, was none other than the Brahma King Śikhin.
O Silent Wisdom!
Those who were the palace ladies of the Universal Monarch Dhṛtarāṣṭra at that time are the assembly of bodhisattvas present in this gathering today.

At that time, those palace ladies, having been brought to maturity and transformed by the King’s thousand sons, all became non-retrogressive in their resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and dwelt securely in the Mahāyāna.
Those palace ladies shall, in due order, receive the prophecy of enlightenment within this Bhadrakalpa. Śāntamati!

You should further observe that the principle of dependent origination is not contradictory: the causes, which are the roots of virtue, and the results, which are the superior practices of generating the bodhicitta, are never lost or destroyed.
Now, all the bodhisattva mahāsattvas in this assembly are able to increase their most supreme resolve.
Thus concludes the fifth fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa-mahāyāna-sūtra*.
The Buddha-spoken *Tathāgatācintyaguhya-mahāyāna-sūtra*, Fascicle Five.

The Sixth Translation, by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Imperial Court, Driven-in-Dust Official, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Dharma Master of Light and Sanskrit, Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Weijing and others, translated by imperial decree. Chapter Six: The Path to Enlightenment. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati, saying:

“If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should study the practices of those great beings; for the most excellent path is not attained through mere words, but must be realized through genuine practice to obtain the true path to bodhi.”
In this context, what is called the path to enlightenment?
It refers to being free from all harm toward any sentient being, diligently cultivating the *pāramitās* while giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness;
universally gathering all beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and practicing the four sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
Diligently practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
perfecting the activities of the six supernormal powers to gather and transform sentient beings through skillful means;
and nurturing all roots of goodness and dharmic practices.
This is called the path to great enlightenment.
Furthermore, Śāntamati, the path to enlightenment consists of a resolute intention of faith and reverence, a profound mind that is pure, upright, and free from deceit.
Because the mind is equanimous, one practices the Dharma of equanimity;
because one does not commit any transgressions, one is free from all fears;
and because it causes that path to enlightenment to increase, it is the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā).
Because that path to enlightenment leads toward the path of peace and happiness, it is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*);
because that path to enlightenment is free from harm, it is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*);
because that path to enlightenment establishes all phenomena, it is the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Because that path to enlightenment is free from confusion, it is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*);
because that path to enlightenment is thoroughly understood, it is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);
because that path to enlightenment penetrates and gives rise to unimpeded knowledge, it is great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).
Because that path to enlightenment is irreversible, it is great compassion;
because that path to enlightenment brings forth joy, it is great sympathetic joy;
because that path to enlightenment enters into reality, it is great equanimity.
Because that path to enlightenment clears away thorns, one is able to remain far removed from defiled states such as greed, hatred, malice, and doubt;
because that path to enlightenment accords with the dharma of peace and happiness, the mind is free from obstacles;
because that path to enlightenment is free from peril and evil, one does not become attached to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles.
Because that path to enlightenment is free from heterodox and external dharmas, it consists in skillfully observing the aggregates, bases, and elements;
because that path to enlightenment can subdue all Māras, it is able to eliminate all afflictions;
because that path to enlightenment is the vast Dharma, it is able to remain far removed from the mental orientations of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Because that path to enlightenment accords with the True Dharma, it is able to conform to the former Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas;
because that path to enlightenment is extensively able to accumulate the great treasure of the Dharma, it skillfully conforms to the jewel of omniscience;
because that path to enlightenment is ever-illuminating, it is able to manifest the light of unimpeded wisdom.
Because that path to enlightenment is well-expounded, it is embraced by all spiritual friends;
because that path to enlightenment is free from notions of high and low, it is devoid of opposition or compliance;
because that path to enlightenment is free from the darkness of defilement, it is devoid of anger, resentment, weariness, or indolence.
Because that path to enlightenment leads toward the higher realms,
it is able to bring about the complete distancing from all unwholesome dharmas.
Because that path to enlightenment is firmly established in the direction of peace and bliss, it ultimately leads to the realization of the dharma of great parinirvāṇa.

“Śāntamati! You should know that all such things as these are the path of great bodhi traversed by bodhisattvas—whereas those who do not proceed toward it nor follow its path are the so-called śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Within this [path], the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are truly established, and they are caused to fully accomplish the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
Chapter Seven: The Inconceivable Secret of the Tathāgata’s Body, Part One. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, saying:
“Great Lord of Secrets!
"Please explain briefly for me the secret of the Tathāgata.
In this regard, what constitutes the secret Dharma of the Tathāgata?
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati, saying:
“Good son! Listen attentively, listen attentively.
Now, relying upon the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, I shall proclaim for you the secret of the Tathāgata.”
There are three kinds. What are the three?
First, the secret of body; second, the secret of speech; and third, the secret of mind.
“What is called the secret body of the Tathāgata? O Śāntamati,
you should know that it refers to the Tathāgata’s ability to manifest all modes of dignified conduct within a state of non-conceptualization and non-discrimination.”
"Good son! Whether gods or humans, if there are those who see the Tathāgata sitting and thereby conceive respect, I cause them to see the Tathāgata sitting.
If there are gods or humans who delight in seeing the Tathāgata walking, I cause them to see the Tathāgata walking."
If there are devas or humans who wish to see [the Tathāgata] dwelling, he immediately causes them to see the Tathāgata dwelling.
If there are devas or humans who wish to see him reclining, he immediately causes them to see the Tathāgata reclining.
If there are devas who delight in hearing the Dharma and give rise to reverence, he immediately causes them to see the Buddha preaching the Dharma.
If there are devas who delight in seeing him in silent composure, he immediately causes them to see the Buddha in silent composure.
If there are devas who delight in meditative concentration, he causes them to see the Buddha remaining in concentration;
if there are devas who delight in emerging from concentration, he causes them to see the Buddha emerging from concentration.
If there were devas who delighted in seeing the Buddha with an unblinking gaze, he would cause them to see the Buddha with an unblinking gaze.
If there were devas who delighted in supernatural transformations, he would cause them to see the Buddha’s supernatural transformations.
If there are devas who desire to behold the Buddha’s golden-colored form, he immediately causes them to see his golden body.
Or if there are those who wish to see it as the color of white silver, crystal, lapis lazuli,
agate, coral, amber, ruby, or white pearl— [he causes them to see it accordingly].
As for the colors of the jewels—colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white; colors like those of the moon, like those of the sun, like those of fire, and like the color of a mass of light;
colors like those of Śakra, like those of Brahmā, like the color of snow, like the color of orpiment, and like the color of vermilion.
As for their color, it is like the color of water; it is like the color of the *aśoka* tree flower,
like the color of the *campaka* flower, like the color of the *sumana* flower, like the color of the *vārṣika* flower,
like the color of the *kumuda* flower, like the color of the *padma* flower, and like the color of the *punnāga*.
The color of the *kāśa* flower; the color of various exquisite flowers; the color of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa;
the color of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra; the color of a newly blossomed lotus;
the color of the jewel of the Auspicious Treasury (*śrīgarbha-ratna*); the color of a *maṇi* jewel; the color of an *indranīla* sapphire; and so forth.
Regarding the color of the pure light of space: such various forms and characteristics, up to and including the forms and characteristics of boundless merit,
the Tathāgata causes each of those beings, according to their respective inclinations and faiths,
to perceive all the bodily forms and characteristics of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!

Suppose all sentient beings throughout a trichiliocosm, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, were to attain human bodies; each of those sentient beings would be able to accomplish whatever they contemplate or resolve with faith regarding the Tathāgata’s physical form, color, marks, and majestic deportment."

Just as it is for one sentient being, so it is for all others; every single sentient being, by contemplating and resolving with faith upon the Tathāgata’s physical form, color, marks, and majestic deportment, shall achieve fulfillment.
Furthermore, sentient beings differ according to what their minds believe and understand. O Śāntamati!

For this reason, the Tathāgata causes all sentient beings to each rejoice in their hearts through various matters such as conduct and activities, in accordance with their respective beliefs and understandings.

Having accorded with their inclinations and understandings, [the Tathāgata] causes all sentient beings to comprehend such matters as the Tathāgata’s majestic deportment; yet the Tathāgata’s body or mind is not subject to agitation or distraction, nor does he undergo any conscious effort of awakening, while still being able to skillfully know the differences in the mental dispositions and past karmic actions of all sentient beings. Therefore, the Tathāgata universally manifests his majestic deportment and other such matters in accordance with what is appropriate for each.

For example, when a pure, circular mirror is placed in various locations, its light illuminates all forms; wherever it is hung, all reflections appear within it. That which is illuminated is equal, without increase or decrease, yet this circular mirror has no volition and no discrimination.

Śāntamati! The Tathāgata is likewise in this regard: he thoroughly knows the minds and intentions of all sentient beings and causes them all to rejoice according to the manifestations he displays; yet the Buddha-Tathāgata has no volitional thought, no discrimination, and no further awakening.
This is what is called the secret body of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, Śāntamati, the body of the Tathāgata is not established by the aggregates, sense bases, or elements; it is not produced by karma, nor does it arise from afflictions. It is not born from the womb of a mother and father, nor is it produced by the primary elements such as the *kalala* stage; it is not produced by the nourishment of blood, flesh, impurities, tendons, bones, or the inhalation and exhalation of breath.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati! The body of the Tathāgata is no body at all.
It is what is called the Dharma-body, which is like the body of space; it is not a body of material form, a body free from all conceptual proliferation, and a body that has no sphere of activity."

If there are sentient beings who delight in seeing physical forms and thereby give rise to faith and reverence—those who are to be delivered by such means—the Tathāgata then manifests a form-body with all its tangible, obstructive characteristics.

If there are sentient beings who delight in the Dharma and give rise to faith and reverence by departing from signs, then in all places and of all kinds, there is no tangible, obstructive characteristic; even the divine eye cannot perceive it.
Śāntamati! You should know that within a single assembly of a Buddha, the perceptions of all the great multitude differ:
some sentient beings see the body of the Buddha while others do not; some see him from afar while they do not see him when nearby.
Or it may be seen when near but not seen when far; or it may be seen neither when far nor when near;
or it may be seen with a concentrated mind but not seen with a distracted mind;
or it may be seen with a distracted mind but not seen with a concentrated mind; or it may be seen when observing another but not seen when observing oneself; or...
One may see it when observing oneself but not when observing another; one may see it within a dream but not after waking;
one may see it while awake but not in a dream; one may see it within meditative absorption (*samādhi*) but not upon emerging from it;
one may see it upon emerging from absorption but not while in it; or one may see a virtuous sign but not an unvirtuous one.

One may not see a sign; or one sees an unwholesome sign but does not see a wholesome sign; or one sees with a mind that has been aroused to awakening but does not see with a mind that has not been so aroused;
or one sees with a mind that has not been aroused to awakening but does not see with a mind that has been so aroused;
or one sees with a mind of application but does not see with a mind without application; or one sees with a mind without application.
Furthermore, they do not perceive the mind of application; in these and other such ways, they contemplate the body of the Tathāgata through immeasurable varieties of signs.

Those sons of the gods of the form realm—whose physical forms are tranquil, whose conduct is tranquil, who abide in a state of meditative equipoise through excellent deportment, and who are well-pacified and well-disciplined—yet even with their eyes blinking and moving, they are likewise unable to perceive the proportions, color, or marks of the Tathāgata’s body.
Why is this? Because the body of the Tathāgata is endowed with immeasurable kinds of adorned physical marks; it is equal to space, for its nature is constituted by the Dharma-body.
Just as space is vast and boundless, so too is the physical form of the Tathāgata vast.
Furthermore, just as space pervades all places and penetrates everywhere, so too does the physical form of the Tathāgata pervade all places and penetrate everywhere.
Furthermore, just as space is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), so too is the physical form of the Tathāgata free from all conceptual proliferation.
Moreover, just as space can universally nourish all sentient beings, so too can the physical form of the Tathāgata universally nourish all sentient beings.
Furthermore, just as space has no categories and no discrimination, so too is the physical form of the Tathāgata: it has no categories and no discrimination.
Furthermore, just as space enters into all forms and luminosity, so too does the physical form of the Tathāgata enter into all forms and luminosity.

Furthermore, just as all forms and radiances whatsoever abide within space, so too it is with the physical form of the Tathāgata: the forms and radiances of all sentient beings abide within the Buddha’s body.

Furthermore, just as all medicinal herbs and forests depend upon space for their growth and flourishing, so too is the physical form of the Tathāgata; it is likewise able to cause all the roots of goodness possessed by all sentient beings to grow and flourish.

Furthermore, just as space is neither permanent nor impermanent and cannot be expressed in words, so too is the physical form of the Tathāgata neither permanent nor impermanent; it cannot be expressed in words, nor can its cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) be perceived.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!
I do not see anyone among all the gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas in the world who is able to behold the supreme uṣṇīṣa of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."

Why is this so? Śāntamati, you should know that I recall a time not long after the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, had attained enlightenment, when he was turning the sublime Wheel of Dharma at the Deer Park in Ṛṣipatana, near the city of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, in the eastern direction named Campaka Flower Color; his world was named Like an Illusion, and his land was named Subduing Enemies.
There was a bodhisattva there named Wind-Bearer who came to this Sahā world to behold, pay homage to, and draw near to the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and stood before the Buddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vāyudhara, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, had this thought:
"The physical marks of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, are now vast, immeasurable, and boundless; I am unable to behold the mark of his crown."
"I shall now attempt to measure the physical dimensions and limits of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

Having formed this thought, the Bodhisattva Vāyudhara saw his own body to be sixty-eight thousand yojanas in height, and he saw the physical marks of the Buddha’s body to be eight hundred and forty thousand yojanas in height.
Again, he thought:
"Could I now, by means of the playful supernatural powers I have attained, measure the extent and limits of the Tathāgata’s physical form?"

Having formed this thought, the Bodhisattva immediately, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and by his own supernormal powers, traveled upward to a buddha-field passing beyond as many worlds as there are grains of sand in a hundred koṭis of Gaṅgā rivers. There was a world named Mahāpadma, where the Buddha, named Padmaśrīgarbharāja Tathāgata, currently resides, teaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings.
Having arrived, the Bodhisattva observed with meticulous scrutiny, yet he was unable to see the mark of the Tathāgata’s crown, nor could he measure the dimensions or boundaries of the Buddha’s body.

Then the Bodhisattva Vāyudhara approached the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Padmaśrīgarbharāja; he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, stood before the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"How far is it from where I have come to here?
That Buddha replied, "Good son!..."
"Having passed through as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in more than a hundred koṭis of Gaṅgā rivers, we have arrived at this world.
The Bodhisattva Vāyudhara addressed that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

Because I am unable to perceive the cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, nor can I perceive the dimensions or limits of that Buddha’s body, I have come from afar to pose this inquiry.
That Buddha replied: "Good son!

Even if you were now to exhaust all your supernatural powers and travel through all worlds in the zenith for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, you still would not be able to know the limits or the measure of that Buddha’s body."
Furthermore, noble son!

Even if one were to exhaust all possible analogies, they could not illustrate the various merits of that Buddha-Tathāgata—his morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; whether his body, speech, or mind, or his form or characteristics, no analogy whatsoever can describe them, for that Tathāgata transcends all measurable phenomena.

Only by means of space can it be illustrated; for the Tathāgata’s morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are all like space. Whether it be body, speech, or mind, or whether it be form or characteristics—all these are said to be entirely like space.
"Therefore, you should know that because space is immeasurable, the bodily marks of the Tathāgata are likewise immeasurable. "Śāntamati!

Having heard this teaching from that Buddha, the Bodhisattva Vāyudhara conceived a sense of rare wonder; he leaped for joy, feeling delight, gladness, and exhilaration. Immediately, he prostrated with his head at the feet of that Buddha, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic power, vanished from that buddha-field in an instant. He returned once more to this Sahā world, stood before the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and with palms joined in sincere devotion toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke these verses:"
"All Buddha-dharmas are most vast, equal to space and without limit;
if a person intends to measure their boundaries, they will bring harm upon themselves."
I have traversed hundreds of koṭis of Buddha-fields, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
to go to a single Tathāgata’s field, desiring to observe the dimensions of the Tathāgata’s body.
Once I had arrived at that buddha-field, the world was named Great Lotus;
I could not perceive the height of the Buddha’s cranial protuberance, nor did I know the measure of his body.
The World-Honored One, the Master of Transformations, dwells in that land; his name is the Honored One, King of the Auspicious Treasury.
That Buddha, knowing the thoughts in my mind, spoke these words for my sake:
"If one wishes to use the method of analogies to illustrate the boundless teachings of all Buddhas,"
That Buddha cannot be known through superficial characteristics; such a person would instead incur the sin of slandering the Buddha.
Only one dharma may serve as a metaphor, equal and no different from all the Buddhas' dharmas:
namely, the vast and expansive empty space, whose measure and boundaries cannot be found.
Just as space is vast and expansive, so too is the mass of the Buddha’s merit—
namely, his morality, concentration, wisdom, the doors of liberation, and his knowledge and vision of liberation.
Just as empty space has no dimensions, so too are the Buddha’s physical marks;
his uṣṇīṣa is so lofty and vast it cannot be beheld, for he is no different from the realm of empty space.
Just as space is vast and expansive, so too is the Buddha’s body vast;
because the measure of his body is boundless, his radiance is likewise vast.
Because his radiance is vast and expansive, the secrecy of his speech is likewise vast.
The vastness of the secret of speech is immeasurable and boundless; The vastness of the secret of mind is likewise so.
Because the secret of mind is vast, The vastness of the Buddha’s compassion is also thus.
The vastness of the Buddha’s compassion is immeasurable and boundless; The vastness of the Buddha’s wisdom is also thus.
Because the Buddha’s wisdom is vast and great, so too is the Buddha’s body vast and great;
the gate of supreme merit from which awakening arises is likewise vast and boundless.
The merit born from the bodhicitta gives rise to supreme marks;
From that gateway of merit, they arise, filling the boundless realm of space, And producing all manner of most excellent virtues.
All classes of sentient beings whatsoever, And all aggregates of merit universally gathered— Even all bodhisattvas are likewise so; They all arise from the bodhicitta.
All the assemblies of bodhisattvas, Proclaiming that the mass of merit is exceedingly vast—
If one can protect and uphold this gateway of the True Dharma, The mass of merit obtained will be even greater than theirs.

Even if all Buddhas, through their wisdom of application, were to proclaim it together for ten million eons, the merit of upholding the True Dharma would be boundless; ultimately, its limit could never be known.
The merit born from the great bodhicitta, and the boundless merit of upholding the true Dharma—
when compared with the gate of liberation through emptiness, they do not equal even one-sixteenth part of it.
The gate of liberation of emptiness is subsumed herein; likewise, it is not separate from the bodhicitta.
All gates of merit for upholding the true Dharma are likewise entirely subsumed within this.
If one can thoroughly understand this wondrous dharma-path, This is the great renown of a bodhisattva;
Boundless merits of enlightenment will be attained— This indeed is the cultivation of the bodhisattva practice.
When I now spoke these verses, billions of world-systems all shook;
there were thousands of billions of devas and humans, with thousands of billions of sounds from drums, pipes, and songs,
and beings numbering in the thousands of billions, all of whom gave rise to the vast mind of enlightenment.
Having heard of the Buddha’s such great majestic power, Vāyu now speaks to me as it truly is:
the Buddha possesses such inconceivability—immeasurable, boundless, and unsurpassed.
"The Buddhas universally manifest the gateway of manifold forms; this is the true secret of spontaneous wisdom. "Śāntamati!
You should know that such teachings as these are what is called the 'secret of the Tathāgata'."
The Sūtra on the Inconceivable Secret Mahāyāna of the Tathāgata Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Six.
The Sūtra on the Inconceivable Secret Mahāyāna of the Tathāgata Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll Seven.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Grand Master of Light and Sanskrit, and Saṃgha-member of Purple Robes, the Subject Wei Jing, by Imperial Decree. The Remainder of Chapter Seven: The Inconceivable Secret of the Tathāgata’s Body. "Furthermore, Śāntamati!..."
Regarding the physical marks of the Tathāgata, within a single assembly there are those who see them and those who do not;
those who see them gaze upon him with joy, while those who do not see them remain silent and bewildered.
Śāntamati, you should know that the Tathāgata does not sustain himself with solid food.

Should there be sentient beings who see the Buddha partaking of worldly food, they may think: "He possesses complete majestic power and has fully cultivated the practices for awakening; the assembly of noble sages constantly follows behind the Buddha, receiving his food within their own vessels."
This is how sentient beings see the Buddha-Tathāgata repeatedly taking food and placing it into the food vessels.

Once those noble ones have accepted the food, if there are sentient beings who are to be transformed and delivered within the Buddha-Dharma and whose karmic obstructions have been exhausted by virtue of roots of goodness planted in past lives—even if they are in every place of their rebirth unable to obtain food or drink and are emaciated by hunger and thirst—by the power of their past merit, those sentient beings are able to eat the remains of the food of the Buddha-Tathāgata.

Having eaten until full, his mind attained lightness and ease; his limbs were nourished and moistened, and his deep mind became pure, whereby he immediately resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Śāntamati! If sentient beings have fallen into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or other evil destinies, they are unable to give rise to the mind of great bodhi.
For this reason, [this applies] until the very end of the realm of nirvāṇa.
Therefore, you should know that the Tathāgata does not partake of worldly food and drink; the sustenance of the Tathāgata is what is called the "Dharma-food.
The Buddha’s body is as firm and solid as Nārāyaṇa, because it is real and indestructible, being composed of vajra.
Śāntamati! The body of the Tathāgata is not formed or nourished by the matured internal organs, nor is it composed of mucus, saliva, or various impurities.
The body of the Tathāgata is like Jāmbūnada gold—without flaw, without fracture, and free from all defects.

The body of the Tathāgata possesses great majestic power because its substance is firm and heavy like a vajra; yet it is also extremely supple like kācilindika cloth, so that wherever it touches the body, all obtain sublime bliss.

Śāntamati, you should know that once, there were certain devaputras and devakanyās of great majestic power who prostrated at the feet of the Buddha; as they performed their prostrations, their hands touched the Buddha’s feet, and having touched them, they immediately gave rise to the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, you should know that the Tathāgata does not arise from defilement.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!
When sentient beings who are dominated by desire see the body of the Tathāgata for even a moment, they immediately conceive the thought of detachment from desire within themselves.
Sentient beings of a wrathful temperament, upon briefly beholding the body of the Tathāgata, immediately give rise to a mind of loving-kindness;
sentient beings of a deluded temperament, upon briefly beholding the body of the Tathāgata, immediately obtain the illumination of the light of wisdom;
and sentient beings of an equal-temperament, upon briefly beholding the body of the Tathāgata, immediately become free from all afflictions within their own bodies.
When sentient beings who are stingy and miserly briefly behold the body of the Tathāgata, they are immediately able to believe in and understand the Dharma of relinquishment;
when sentient beings who have broken the precepts briefly behold the body of the Tathāgata, they are immediately able to believe in and understand the purity of the Dharma of the precepts;
and when sentient beings with minds of anger and resentment briefly behold the body of the Tathāgata, they immediately attain the Dharma of patience.
Sentient beings who are indolent immediately arouse diligence upon briefly beholding the body of the Tathāgata;
sentient beings with distracted minds immediately attain tranquil concentration upon briefly beholding the body of the Tathāgata;
and sentient beings who are ignorant immediately attain supreme wisdom upon briefly beholding the body of the Tathāgata.

"Good son! To speak in brief, if any sentient beings should even momentarily behold the body of the Tathāgata, they shall not abandon any wholesome dharmas; all unwholesome and defiled states such as doubt will be completely eliminated, and their minds will be established in goodness. Yet, the Buddha, the Tathāgata, always abides in non-conceptual equanimity."
This is called the secret body of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!

It is as when the Tathāgata creates an emanated person who performs various buddha-deeds; yet the mind of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, involves no preparatory application, no arousal of thought, and no volitional attention."
The Buddha likewise does not form this thought:
"I am able to transform those beings who are to be transformed.

Nevertheless, for the sake of bringing to maturity all sentient beings—whether in this world, in other worlds, or even across hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya worlds—who are ready to be delivered, he performs various beneficial acts.
This is called the secret of the Tathāgata’s body.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!

The Tathāgata’s body emits a vast radiance, possessing countless hundreds of thousands of colors; this light universally illumines all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, extensively bringing all sentient beings to maturity.
Yet the Buddha-Tathāgata has no awakening, nor any preparatory application, nor any mental engagement.
These are called the Tathāgata’s secret of body and the purity of bodily action.

"Śāntamati, you should know that what has been taught here is but a brief and concise explanation of the Tathāgata’s secret of the body and the purity of bodily action. Were it to be explained in detail, even if one were to spend an eon or more than an eon, one could not reach its limit."

When the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, had spoken this inconceivable Dharma of the Tathāgata’s body-secret, ten thousand people in the assembly resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).
At that time, there were devas and humans in the assembly who scattered various exquisite flowers over the Buddha and made offerings to the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his right golden arm, placed it upon the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Mahāguhyapati Vajrapāṇi, and spoke these words of praise:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Lord of Secrets!
You have excellently expounded the inconceivable dharma of the Tathāgata’s secret body; I understand it all.
Regarding the dharma you have taught, I now rejoice."
Chapter Eight: The Inconceivable Secret of the Tathāgata’s Speech. Part One. Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati, saying:
"Furthermore, what is meant by the purity of the Tathāgata’s secret speech and vocal karma?"
That is to say, the Tathāgata realizes the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within a single day and night, and enters great parinirvāṇa within a single day and night.
Yet, during that interval, the Tathāgata has never uttered a single word, nor has there been any expression. Why is this?
Because the Buddha, the Tathāgata, is constantly in samāhita.
The Tathāgata likewise has neither exhalation nor inhalation, nor vitarka nor vicāra; because he is without vitarka and vicāra, the speech he utters is free from all error and falsehood.

Yet the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is without vitarka and vicāra, without discrimination or extensive discrimination, without speaking, without demonstrating, and without expression; nevertheless, sentient beings hear the Tathāgata proclaiming teachings, while the Tathāgata remains ultimately in meditative concentration.
In all ways and at all times, although he is able to express [the Dharma] through words and letters, there is ultimately nothing expressed.

If there are sentient beings who, by means of these words and letters, give rise to faith and reverence, those beings may say to themselves, "The Tathāgata is preaching the Dharma for me. Yet, the mind of the Buddha-Tathāgata always abides in non-conceptual equanimity (*upekṣā*).
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!

The Tathāgata does not produce sounds from his lips, teeth, tongue, throat, or mouth, nor is there anything heard or listened to [as such]. The sounds produced by the Tathāgata emerge from space; it is only because sentient beings think that the sounds of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, emerge from the opening of the mouth."
Śāntamati, you should know that the speech of the Tathāgata possesses sixty-four kinds of sublime characteristics. What are these sixty-four?
First, it is flowing; second, it is soft; third, it is pleasing to the mind; fourth, it is delightful.
Fifth, pure; sixth, free from defilement; seventh, luminous; eighth, sweet;
ninth, pleasant to hear; tenth, not inferior; eleventh, complete and perfect;
twelfth, well-disciplined; thirteenth, without harshness; fourteenth, without wickedness; fifteenth, virtuous and gentle.
Sixteenth, it is pleasing to the ear; seventeenth, it is suitable for the body; eighteenth, it gives rise to courage and vigor in the mind;
nineteenth, the mind is joyful; twentieth, there is delight; twenty-first, there is no feverish distress;
twenty-second, it is like a command; twenty-third, it is well understood; twenty-fourth...

Clearly, twenty-fifth is "loving-kindness," twenty-sixth is "causing joy to arise," twenty-seventh is "causing others to act according to instructions," twenty-eighth is "causing others to understand well," twenty-ninth is "in accordance with principle," thirtieth is "beneficial," and thirty-first is "free from the fault of redundancy."
Thirty-second, his voice is like the roar of a lion; thirty-third, like the sound of a dragon;
thirty-fourth, like the thundering roar of clouds and lightning; thirty-fifth, like the voice of a nāga king;
thirty-sixth, like the exquisite song of a kiṃnara; thirty-seventh, like that of a kalaviṅka...
38. The sound of Brahmā; 39. the sound of the *saṃjīva* bird;
40. the exquisite sound of Śakra; 41. the sound of a drum being beaten;
42. not too high; 43. not too low; 44. following [the capacity of the listener].
Entering all sounds: forty-fifth, without deficiency; forty-sixth, without destruction;
forty-seventh, without defilement; forty-eighth, without longing for gain;
forty-ninth, complete; fiftieth, adorned; fifty-first, manifesting; fiftieth...
Second, the perfection of all vocal sounds; fifty-third, the delight of the sense faculties;
fifty-fourth, freedom from censure; fifty-fifth, freedom from frivolity; fifty-sixth, freedom from agitation;
fifty-seventh, entering into all assemblies; fifty-eighth, the possession of all marks.
[The Buddha] said: "Furthermore, Śāntamati!

The fifty-ninth [mark] is that the speech uttered by the Tathāgata causes the minds and hearts of all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions to rejoice, yet the Buddha does not form such a thought."
"I am able to proclaim all dharmas," namely:

the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, jātaka-s, vaipulya-s, adbhuta-dharma-s, upadeśa-s, and nidāna-s; furthermore, the teachings on secret prior practices, the teachings on past origins, and the teachings on former causes; as well as brief explanations, extensive explanations, and detailed explanations; the instruction, establishment, classification, and differentiation of stages; and the elucidation and clarification of that which was spoken by the Tathāgata.

Regarding such dharmas as these, within all those great assemblies—whether the assemblies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās; or the assemblies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth—the Buddha is able to provide the gift of Dharma to each according to their respective faculties, diligence, and capacity, acting in accordance with what is appropriate for them.
When that assembly hears the teaching of the Dharma, they all believe that what is spoken issues from the mouth of the Buddha, the Tathāgata.
Yet, although the Dharma taught contains no mutual redundancy of speech, each member of the assembly understands all phenomena according to their own respective voices.
Śāntamati! This is what is called the secret speech of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!"

Regarding the "sixty": although all sentient beings are infinite in number and the conduct of all sentient beings is likewise infinite, the mental activities of sentient beings as taught by the Tathāgata are briefly categorized into eighty-four thousand types. This is merely for the sake of sentient beings of inferior faculties and natures, so that they may understand and enter into what the Tathāgata has taught.
Śāntamati, you should know that the mental activities of sentient beings are without measure.

Whether they be sentient beings of greedy temperament, those of hateful temperament, those of deluded temperament, or those of equal temperament, as for the distinctions among the mental activities of each and every such being—even if a Buddha-Tathāgata were to spend an eon, or more than an eon, or even if the Tathāgata were to remain in the world for hundreds of thousands of eons, reaching the limit of his maximum lifespan, he would still be unable to describe the ultimate boundaries of the mental activities of all sentient beings.

If the Buddha were to speak only of the boundless nature of the mental activities of sentient beings, those beings would be unable to understand or enter into them and would instead give rise to further delusion. Therefore, the Tathāgata, through skillful means, briefly explains that within the immeasurable activities of sentient beings, there are eighty-four thousand categories.

Furthermore, O Śāntamati, all the dharmas taught by the Tathāgata accord with the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings, causing them all to attain awakening as is appropriate for each.
This is what is called the Tathāgata’s secret of speech.

Furthermore, Śāntamati, the sixty-first is the Tathāgata’s secret wisdom of speech: it enters into the minds and intentions of all sentient beings, yet his words do not issue from the opening of the Tathāgata’s mouth, but emerge from space alone.
If there are sentient beings who think that all the speech of the Buddha-Tathāgata issues from the opening of his mouth, let them not give rise to such a view. Why is this?
There may be sentient beings who see the Buddha’s speech issue from the *uṣṇīṣa* mark, or from the crown of his head.
They emerge, either from the hairline, or from the shoulders, or from the forehead,
or from between the eyebrows, or from the *ūrṇā* mark, or from the eyes, or from the ears,
or from the nose, or from the cheeks, or from the mouth, or from the neck, or from...
They emerge from the arms, or from the hands, or from the fingers,
or from both sides, or from the chest, or from the back, or from the navel, or from the private organ,
or from the eyes, or from the knees, or from the calves, or from the ankles, or from...
They may emerge from the feet, or from the various marks and signs of excellence, or from all the pores of the skin;
such beings have differing ways of knowing and understanding them.
Śāntamati! This is what is called the secret speech of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!

Sixty-second: The speech uttered by the Tathāgata accords with the various inclinations and understandings of sentient beings and accords with the ripening of the mental dispositions of sentient beings, causing them all to understand accordingly; yet the Buddha, the Tathāgata, always abides in non-conceptual equanimity.

For example, just as various musical instruments produced through conventional worldly methods are all exquisitely skillful according to how they were crafted—neither touched by hands nor dependent on human effort, yet when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produce beautiful sounds—the sounds thus produced are all the result of being struck by the winds of the differentiation of prior karma.

The speech of the Tathāgata is also like this: it is stirred by the wind of wisdom according to the various inclinations of all sentient beings, yet it does not issue forth through the exertion of the Tathāgata’s own effort.
The Tathāgata accords with the distinctions of the prior karma of all sentient beings and speaks to them according to their respective spheres of experience as appropriate. Śāntamati!
It is, for example, like an echo which follows whatever it expresses; the sound that issues forth is neither internal, nor external, nor in between.

The speech of the Tathāgata is likewise: whatever issues forth serves only to manifest the mental intentions of sentient beings; yet the voice of the Tathāgata is neither internal, nor external, nor in between.
Furthermore, within the great ocean there is a wish-fulfilling jewel named "Fulfiller of All Intentions," which, when suspended upon a high banner, spontaneously emits a sound.
It is said that this jewel can fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings, yet this precious gem itself is without discrimination.

The Tathāgata is also like this: his wondrous jewel of speech is pure in its profound mind; suspended upon the banner of great compassion, the Tathāgata utters sublime words according to the various aspirations of all sentient beings, causing them all to understand clearly. Nevertheless, the Buddha-Tathāgata constantly abides in non-conceptual equanimity.
Śāntamati! This is what is called the secret speech of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!
Sixty-third: The voices of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas have no limit.
I do not see any among all the devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas in the world who can know the boundaries or the measure of the Tathāgata’s voice.

Why is this? I recall that at one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the great city of Rājagṛha, surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattvas, proclaiming the Dharma-gate of the Purification of the Wheel of Sound, extensively manifesting and revealing it for the sake of sentient beings.
At a later time, through the power of the empowerment of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"To what extent does the range of the Tathāgata’s pure wheel of sound extend?"

Having formed this thought, he vanished from his original seat and, by means of his own supernatural power, immediately went to the summit of Mount Sumeru to hear how far and near the voice of the Buddha-Tathāgata could be heard.

Again, exerting his supernatural power, he traveled throughout the trichiliocosm, further west beyond Mount Sumeru, across the realms of the four great continents, and beyond the Iron Ring Mountains and the Great Iron Ring Mountains, even unto the very limits of the world-system; returning to the summit of the Iron Ring Mountains, he listened intently to the extent of the Tathāgata’s voice, finding that this sound was uniform, without increase or decrease.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having understood the matter, thought to himself:
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana intends to measure the extent of my voice; I should now withdraw my supernormal power."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal powers. Then, empowered by the majestic spiritual authority of the Buddha, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, through his own supernormal power, traveled westward from this world across as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in ninety-nine Ganges Rivers. He arrived at a world named Prabhāketu, where a Tathāgata named Prabhārāja currently resides, dwelling and teaching the Dharma to transform sentient beings.

At that time, after the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had arrived in that land, he carefully listened to the extent of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni’s voice; it was as if, within a space of ten cubits, one were hearing the voice spoken by a person there.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana heard the Buddha’s voice in that world in exactly the same way; the sound was uniform, without any increase or decrease.
The physical stature of that Tathāgata King of Radiance was one hundred yojanas high, while the bodies of the bodhisattvas were fifty yojanas high.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, by means of his own supernatural power, traveled in a circle among the alms bowls used by those bodhisattvas.
When those bodhisattvas saw this phenomenon, they were overcome with derisive laughter and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Now, how is it that a tiny insect with the appearance of a śramaṇa has come into this bowl and is crawling about?
That Buddha replied: "O sons of good family!..."
You should not give rise to thoughts of contempt or arrogance. Why is this?

The practitioner within this bowl is the foremost disciple among the Śrāvakas of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni; he is the most preeminent in supernormal powers among the great assembly of Śrāvakas.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana approached the presence of the Tathāgata King of Radiance, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and stood before the Buddha.
That Buddha said: "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana! These bodhisattvas have mocked us;

you should now, by virtue of being sustained by the empowerment of that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, manifest various supernatural transformations through your own supernormal powers."
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed that Buddha, saying:
"In accordance with the Buddha’s instruction, I shall now sit cross-legged and perform a miraculous transformation upon this jewel-island."
The Buddha said,
"Now is precisely the right time. Thereupon,
the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately leaped into the air to a height of seven koṭis of tāla trees and performed a feat of supernatural transformation.

Within that seat, he manifested hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of vast adornments of pearl necklaces; from each of those necklaces issued forth hundreds of thousands of koṭis of rays of light, and from every gateway of light, lotus flowers were born.

Within each of these lotus thrones, there is an image of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, seated upon it; all those images of the Tathāgata proclaim the pure, true Dharma with the wheel of wondrous sounds.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Now, while sitting cross-legged, I am able to perform various supernatural transformations throughout all the worlds of these four great continents; I can even perform various supernatural transformations throughout this small chiliocosm, a medium chiliocosm, and a great trichiliocosm."
That Buddha replied,
"Now is indeed the right time. At that moment,
the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having manifested the miraculous transformations as was appropriate, withdrew his supernormal powers and returned to stand before the Buddha.
At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas all gave rise to a sense of wonder and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what purpose has this Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana come to this world?"
That Buddha replied: "O sons of good family!
This Mahāmaudgalyāyana has come here because he wishes to measure the extent of the sound-circle of that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni."
Then the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata King of Radiance, addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"From this day forward, do not again give rise to the thought of wishing to measure the extent of the Tathāgata’s wheel of sound."
This is because the Tathāgata’s pure voice is without measure and cannot be quantified.

Even if you were to employ your own majesty and supernatural powers to travel toward the western direction for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, you would ultimately never be able to reach the limit or boundary of the sublime wheel of the voice of that World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, for the sublime wheel of the Buddha-Tathāgata’s voice is without measure.

That I rashly attempted to measure the immeasurable, pure, and wondrous wheel of the voice of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni is a profound sin of mine.

How far is it from where I have come here?
That Buddha replied:
