If you now wish to return to your own buddha-field, you should offer devout prostrations to that Buddha.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana! You should know this now:

if you were to attempt to return to your native land by means of your own supernormal powers, even if it took an entire kalpa, you would not be able to reach it; or else, before arriving at that land, you might enter parinirvāṇa midway.
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana! Now that you have arrived here, from which direction do you come—east, west, south, or north?
Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied:
“My mind is bewildered and obscured; I do not know where I am now.

That Buddha told him, “For this reason, you should know now that even if you were to use your own supernormal powers for as long as an eon, you would ultimately be unable to return to that buddha-field.”
Mahāmaudgalyāyana asked:
"In which direction is that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, currently located?
That Buddha replied:
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana! That Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, is currently residing in the eastern direction.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately prostrated himself toward the east, touching the ground with his five limbs, and with the utmost sincerity and reverence paid homage to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, speaking these verses:

“The Holy One among bipeds has taken me under his care; Possessing great majesty, worshipped by gods and humans, Endowed with boundless wisdom and boundless voice, I now wish to return to my own land.”

“Śāntamati! Now, within this entire assembly on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, everyone hears the sound of the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s wailing.”
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As for this sound of wailing that is now heard, what does it portend?”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“This is the sound of the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana, who has gone to the western direction, passing through as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in ninety-nine Gaṅgā rivers. He has reached the world-system called Prabhāketu within the realm of the World-Honored One Prabhāpāla Tathāgata. Because he is currently about to return from there to this Sahā world, there is such a sound of wailing.”
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason has the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana gone to that world?”
The Buddha said,
“Ānanda! You yourself shall know the causes and conditions for why Mahāmaudgalyāyana is bringing [the relics] back to this land.”
At that time, the entire assembly on Vulture Peak Mountain joined their palms in reverent salutation and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We wish to behold that world, Banner of Light, and gaze upon the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata King of Light, as well as those bodhisattvas and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.”

At that time, having accepted the exhortation, the World-Honored One immediately emitted a great radiance from between his eyebrows called "Pervasive in All Places. This light shone universally and continuously across Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of ninety-nine Ganges Rivers, illuminating extensively the world-system known as Banner of Light.

At that time, the entire assembly in this gathering was able to see that world of Radiant Banner, behold the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata King of Radiance, and witness those bodhisattvas; they also saw Mahāmaudgalyāyana prostrating with his five limbs touching the ground, bowing toward the Buddha and wailing aloud.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"You should now follow the radiance of the light and return to this land."

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having received the great wheel of light from the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, returned immediately to this Sahā world in the space of a single thought. Standing before the Buddha, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and once again, with utmost sincerity, touched the ground with his five limbs (pañcamaṇḍalaka), speaking thus:
“World-Honored One!
I now repent my transgression!
I now repent my transgression!
Because I rashly attempted to measure the World-Honored One’s immeasurable, pure, and wondrous wheel of sound, I have committed this profound offense.
"I traveled far to another realm to hear the voice of the Buddha; having arrived there, the sound of the Buddha I heard was no different from this.
The Buddha said, "Maudgalyāyana!"
It is as you have said.
The voice of the Tathāgata has no measure; it is like space, which has no measure, is without limit, and cannot be quantified.
If space could be measured, the voice of the Tathāgata could also be measured. Why is this?
Because space is vast, the voice of the Tathāgata is likewise vast.
When this account of Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s past and future was being told in the city of Rājagṛha, ten thousand people resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati, saying:
“Śāntamati, you should know that this is the secret speech of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!”
"Sixty-fourth: all that is turned by the minds of every sentient being is surpassed by the mind of a single sentient being.
The Bodhisattva Śāntamati said, "O Great Lord of Secrets!"

If even the mental activities of a single sentient being cannot be conceived, measured, calculated, or scrutinized—even by all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm who have attained the stage of a pratyekabuddha—despite doing so for an entire kalpa, how much less could this be done by all sentient beings?
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva said: “Śāntamati!

I shall now inform you so that you may awaken to the fact that all the mental states and mental factors of all sentient beings are in constant flux. When the Tathāgata’s wondrous wheel of sound emits various voices to proclaim the Dharma, it causes all sentient beings to give rise to joy; yet the Buddha, the World-Honored One, abides eternally in non-conceptual equanimity.”
At that time, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva spoke these verses:
“If all sentient beings in the three thousandfold world-system were to realize the fruit of a pratyekabuddha,
and even if one were to spend an entire eon calculating them, one could not comprehend the mind of a single sentient being.”
Of all sentient beings in the world, only the Buddha can know their minds;
though he understands them in accordance with the minds of beings, the Buddha has no arousal of thought and no discrimination.
Even unto all classes of sentient beings, there are three ways of gathering and contemplating them;
the World-Honored One, according to their types and as is appropriate, proclaims the True Dharma with a pure and wondrous wheel of sound.
Mastery over the Dharma, he proclaims wondrous sounds; all who hear them are filled with joy.
According to the names and characteristics as they are proclaimed, he skillfully reveals all phenomena through their names.
All classes of sentient beings, their physical forms, names, and thoughts—
within a single pore the Tathāgata emits radiance, skillfully discerning each according to their needs.
All the transformations of the World-Honored One’s great compassion emit light from every pore;
this radiance surpasses that of all others, and from the wheel of his voice, he proclaims the wondrous Dharma.
Even if one were to skillfully proclaim the Buddha’s sūtras through various parables for an entire eon,
one would ultimately never reach the limit of the Buddha’s words or the wheel of his voice.
All afflictions are without form; the words spoken are likewise without form.
Because these words lack the cause of form, the formless afflictions naturally subside and cease.
Therefore, the various characteristics of forms expressed in language cannot be found anywhere;
because they are ultimately unattainable, the characteristics of the afflictions are likewise so.
Because their language is unreal, what they speak is neither internal nor external;
likewise, afflictions are unreal, and the nature of defilement is neither internal nor external.
Because not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended, the words spoken by the Buddha pervade the ten directions;
that afflictions cannot be apprehended is likewise so—therefore, there is that which the Buddha has proclaimed.
The linguistic paths of all sentient beings are divided into three grades: superior, middling, and inferior.
Language is neither body nor mind; herein there is neither abiding nor non-abiding.
For example, when musical instruments are formed from conventional phenomena, And various sounds are produced by being blown or struck by the wind,
Those sounds that emerge have no point of origin, And within them, there is likewise no creator.

Due to the power of their long-accumulated, pure natures, And stirred by the winds of the minds of all sentient beings, The Buddha, the World-Honored One, utters sublime sounds; Yet the Buddha remains free from any conceptual discrimination.
Just as an echo responds to a sound, The resonance is neither internal nor external;
So too, the wondrous speech uttered by the Honored One among Men Is neither internal nor external.
Furthermore, just as a wish-fulfilling jewel is free from discrimination yet causes all sentient beings to give rise to joy,
so too is the Buddha free from discrimination, yet all sounds are perfectly fulfilled within him.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!
You should know that the Tathāgata’s secret wisdom of speech enters into all sentient beings to proclaim all dharmas.

In all the various places of birth for all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, the Tathāgata enters into the languages and sounds of all sentient beings, establishing the Four Noble Truths through various names."
"Śāntamati! As it has been taught, there are the noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
All the gods dwelling on earth spoke thus:"

“*Kave kava-mūle kavana-ye kavadolu.* This is precisely what is taught as the noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.”
The gods dwelling in the sky spoke thus:

“*Tāre tāre tāretāre tārāvatī amoghe amoghapāśe*. This is precisely the teaching on the noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.”
The gods of the Four Great Kings spoke thus:
“*Ini mini nāpi nārāpi.*” This is precisely the teaching on the noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Those gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven spoke thus:

“Avartani, asvāti, kṣayāvati, kṣayanugāmini. This is precisely what is said regarding the noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

The Yāma gods spoke thus: “*Śūre śūrasenī śūrākṣye śūrākṣyabhave.*” This is precisely what is called the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

The Tuṣita gods spoke thus: “O-kā-li, Mu-kā-li, Vi-ba-nu, San-za-li. This is precisely the teaching on the Noble Truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
The gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven speak thus:

Those gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations spoke thus:

"Ha ha hu | Ha ha vinaye | Ha ha vigame | Harani game. This is precisely what is said regarding the noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
The celestial beings of that host of Māras spoke thus:

“Aṅgāraṃ, aṅgāramūlaṃ, aṅgāraparyantaṃ, aṅgāraniḥśritaṃ siddhānnaṃ. This is precisely what is meant by the Noble Truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Those gods of the Brahmakāyika heaven spoke thus:

“*Śubhe śubhe kare śubhe viśane śubhavardhane.*” This is precisely the teaching on the noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
The Brahmā-purohita devas spoke thus:

“Mahari, saṃhari, sarani, sarasarani. This is precisely what is said regarding the noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
The devas of the Brahma assembly spoke thus:

“*Māraṇa māraṇasanti māraṇa mṛhāṇa mṛhāṇu praśama.*” This is precisely the teaching on the noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
That Great Brahmā spoke thus: “*Taraṇe tarañjale tasta-pure kuruvahe.*” This is precisely what is said regarding the noble truths of suffering,
the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Those gods of Limited Radiance spoke thus:

“Hi hi, he hi, hu hu, ha ra nu san ti. This is precisely what is said regarding the noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Below this, there should have been the text explaining the Four Noble Truths for the Apramāṇābha and Ābhāsvara devas, but it is originally missing from the Sanskrit manuscript.
Those Parīttaśubha devas spoke thus:

That Sunirmita deva spoke thus: “Mukti muktavati muktamūli muktamatotsṛti. This is precisely what is said regarding the noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
“The gods of Akaniṣṭha spoke thus: ‘Niśce, atyanta-niśce, akṣarapaṇe, apratisandhite.

Śāntamati, you should know that these various gods each established the Four Truths by means of their respective celestial languages. Furthermore, the hosts of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, as well as the hosts of the *Dṛḍhakāya* yakṣas and the *Mālādharin* yakṣas, each established the Four Truths by means of the specific languages of their own kind.”

"Śāntamati! Within the various lands of this Jambudvīpa—speaking briefly, throughout a full thousand lands, and even across all the populations of the sixteen great nations—the Tathāgata enters into all their various languages, sounds, and mental conceptions according to their respective regions. He understands and fully comprehends the Four Noble Truths as they are established through the names and designations of all those languages and sounds."

From those dwelling in the land of Śakra to those dwelling at the very limits of the world—filling a thousand such realms within Jambudvīpa—all these multitudes of people, with their various languages, various sounds, and various mental conceptions, each establish names and speak of the Four Noble Truths.
The Tathāgata enters into all languages and sounds and is able to understand them completely, yet the mind-consciousness and speech of the Tathāgata do not become dispersed. Śāntamati!

Within this small chiliocosm, there are ninety-four *koṭi-nayuta* hundreds of thousands of varieties of speech, names, and terminology, each expounding the Four Noble Truths. All spoken sounds and expressions are subsumed within these, and they all ultimately converge upon the single meaning of the Four Noble Truths: that is, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the Truth of Non-arising (*anutpāda-satya*), the Truth of Suchness (*yathābhūta-satya*), and the Immovable Truth (*acala-satya*).
Śāntamati! This is precisely what constitutes the secret speech of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!"

The Tathāgata’s speech is able to sever all the doubts and indecisiveness of sentient beings; that is to say, throughout the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions, he universally encompasses all sentient beings, and according to what is known by the Buddha's wisdom, the realm of sentient beings is more vast than the realm of earth.

Śāntamati! Suppose every single sentient being were to attain a perfection of wisdom equal to that of the Venerable Śāriputra; for this reason, suppose all these beings, each possessing wisdom equal to that of Śāriputra, were to spend an eon or more than an eon together questioning, deliberating, weighing, and investigating matters of doubt, with each individual being superior to the next.
Having deliberated among themselves on the matters they doubted, these sentient beings all came at once to question the World-Honored One.
At that time, in the interval of a finger-snap, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, answered every question as it was asked.

Therefore, the World-Honored One, in accordance with the mental states arising in each sentient being, universally encompasses all beings and, using a single voice, proclaims for them all that which cuts through the web of doubt, causing all sentient beings to attain joy once their doubts have been severed.

Śāntamati! This is called the Tathāgata’s speech that is universally able to sever all doubts and indecisiveness of sentient beings; yet, there is no movement or fluctuation in the Tathāgata’s mind or speech, for everything is spoken exactly as it truly is.
Śāntamati, you should know that such explanations as these are all the secret words and rare words of the Tathāgata.
This is precisely what is called the purity of verbal action.

When the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, had spoken these words of the Tathāgata, thirty-two thousand beings within the assembly resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. All the bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa from every buddha-field throughout the ten directions—those who were each practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) in the presence of their respective Buddha-Bhagavats—desiring to make offerings to the Buddha and the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, lowered jeweled canopies and scattered exquisite flowers. These flowers circled around and came into this assembly, scattering over the Buddha and the body of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, and continued to scatter until they had completely filled the entire assembly for the duration of a kalpa.
Those various jeweled canopies revolved and remained suspended in the air above the Buddha’s head, and from those jeweled canopies issued a wondrous sound that spoke these words:
“We, the assembly of bodhisattvas of this Bhadrakalpa, have sent these to be used as offerings for the World-Honored One and the Great Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva.”
“May you graciously accept us.

Having heard all these unprecedented teachings proclaimed by the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the entire assembly felt even greater excellence and gave rise to a sense of rare wonder. They immediately prostrated themselves before the Bodhisattva Mahāguhyapati Vajrapāṇi with utmost reverence, conceiving the highest degree of faith and respect, and all spoke thus: “O Mahāguhyapati!...”
At this time, we have swiftly obtained a great benefit, having heard the inconceivable Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s secret speech as proclaimed by the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.

If any sentient beings hear what has been taught and believe it with understanding, free from doubt, the merit of their human existence will not have been in vain; they shall be those whom the Tathāgata is destined to transform and deliver, and they will attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa Mahāyāna Sūtra, Scroll Eight.
The Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa Mahāyāna Sūtra,
Scroll Nine.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Imperial Court, the Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, the Great Dharma Master of Sanskrit and Chinese, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Weijing, by Imperial Decree. The Remainder of the Eighth Chapter, “The Inconceivable Secret of the Tathāgata’s Speech. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the entire assembly, praising them, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
He then addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati, saying:

“Śāntamati, you should know that the true principle of all Tathāgatas, the True Dharma of the Tathāgatas, and the conduct of the Tathāgatas are truly difficult for all the world to believe and understand.”
And this True Dharma can be skillfully proclaimed by the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets.
If sentient beings are to soon come to possess this Dharma, they will, upon hearing this proclaimed True Dharma, give rise to faith and understanding accordingly.

Having given rise to faith and understanding, they are then able to receive and uphold [the teaching] without alarm or fear; they enter into its meaning and realize its true nature. Such a person shall receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When the Buddha-Tathāgata praised the Bodhisattva Mahāguhyapati Vajrapāṇi for his skillful exposition of the Dharma, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds in the ten directions shook in six ways; a great radiance shone everywhere, various exquisite flowers rained down spontaneously from the sky, and the sounds of drums, flutes, and songs resounded in all their variety.

Incalculable sentient beings resolved their minds upon Bodhi; incalculable bodhisattvas attained the patience of conformity (*anulomikī kṣānti*); incalculable bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and because the roots of goodness of incalculable bodhisattvas had matured, they attained the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

At that time, within a radius of sixty-eight thousand yojanas before the Buddha, the World-Honored One, amidst that great assembly, the earth suddenly split open everywhere. Great waters surged forth like clusters of akṣa fruits, rising high into the air and reaching as far as the Brahma realm; at that moment, this entire trichiliocosm was filled with fragrant water.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Śāntamati, saying: “Śāntamati!
Do you now see this water surging upward?”
The Bodhisattva Śāntamati addressed the Buddha,
saying: “I see them,
World-Honored One!”
"What is the prior sign of all that exists here?
The Buddha said, "Śāntamati!"
That this great earth should suddenly crack open and water surge upward is not something to be conceived by thought.

Those sentient beings who receive and uphold this True Dharma shall likewise be so: within the True Dharma, they will understand the reality of things as they truly are and achieve sudden, expansive awakening; all their gates of sinful karma, such as ignorance and false views, will be completely cleared away; and the teachings on principles expounded through inexhaustible Dharma-light, supreme wisdom, and eloquence will all manifest.
This is indeed the Great Being Vajrapāṇi skillfully proclaiming the True Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy in their hearts.
O Śāntamati! You should know that this True Dharma is entirely the unique, supreme characteristic of the Tathāgata.
Chapter Nine: The Inconceivable Secret of the Tathāgata’s Mind. Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati, saying:
“Furthermore, what is meant by ‘the inconceivable secret of the Tathāgata’s mind and the purity of his mental activity’?”
Śāntamati! For example, when the beings of the Formless Realm are born, they take a single consciousness as their common object of focus and remain there for eighty-four thousand kalpas.

That consciousness also does not follow other consciousnesses in their transformation; when it has ceased at the limit of one's lifespan, one is born in various places according to the ripening of karma.

The Tathāgata is likewise: by means of non-abiding consciousness, while during the day and night the Bodhisattva realizes the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, during that same day and night the Tathāgata enters *nirupadhi-śeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Relying upon the realm of Great Nirvāṇa, within that interval, the Buddha-Tathāgata has no mind to be turned;
there is no mind of investigation, no mind of non-investigation, no mind of understanding,
no mind of recollection, no mind of limitation, no mind of accumulation, no mind of dispersion, and no mind of agitation.
There is no mind to be exalted, no mind to be disparaged; no mind for defense,
no mind for pursuit, no mind for valor, no mind for observation, no mind for affliction, no mind for wandering,
no mind for meditative stillness, no mind for joy, no mind for oppression, and no mind for dwelling in peace.
There is no mind that acts universally, no mind that discriminates, no mind that differentiates,
no mind that conceptualizes, no mind abiding in calm abiding (*śamatha*), no mind abiding in insight (*vipaśyanā*), no mind flowing along with consciousness,
no establishment of one's own mind, no observation of another's mind, no mind relying upon the eye, and no mind relying upon...

The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind do not have the mind as their support; they do not have the mind as their support for forms, nor the mind as their support for sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects.

The mind does not abide in the objects of perception, nor does it abide in the sense-sphere of the mind, nor does it abide in the internal sense-spheres, nor does it abide in the external sense-spheres.
The mind does not act in reliance upon phenomena, nor does it act in reliance upon wisdom. It does not...
With the mind, one observes phenomena of the past, future, and present.
"Śāntamati! This is the purity of the Tathāgata’s mental activity."
The mind of the Tathāgata has not the slightest dharma to be grasped; among all dharmas, it functions solely through unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision.

Since the Tathāgata’s own mind is already pure, he likewise perceives neither the impure minds of sentient beings nor any view of existence or non-existence regarding them, remaining free from all discrimination.
Although there is seeing, there is no conceptual proliferation; this seeing of non-seeing is what is called "seeing.

That wisdom of the Tathāgata does not correspond with what is seen by the fleshly eye, nor with what is seen by the divine eye, nor with what is seen by the wisdom-eye, nor with what is seen by the Dharma-eye, nor with what is seen by the Buddha-eye. It does not correspond with what is heard by the divine ear, nor with what is known by the knowledge of others' minds, nor with what is contemplated by the knowledge of recollecting past lives, nor with what is performed by the knowledge of supernormal powers, nor does it correspond with any out-flowing (sāsrava) knowledge.
That which is appropriately associated with all phenomena refers to the unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena.

Yet, the Buddha-Tathāgata is without preparatory application (*prayoga*), without further realization, and without volitional mental engagement (*manasikāra*); dwelling well within the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, he observes the mental activities of all sentient beings and fully understands all phenomena, whether defiled or pure.
All the ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha possessed by all Tathāgatas are never abandoned by the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Yet, within these dharmas, the Buddha-Tathāgata exerts no application of effort, has no further awakening, and maintains no volitional attention.

The Tathāgata is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness, and constantly abides in samādhi; yet he does not abandon any of the Buddha-activities, remaining without attachment within the unimpeded wisdom regarding all Buddha-dharmas.

“Śāntamati! For example, suppose a Tathāgata were to manifest a transformed image of a Tathāgata. That manifested image would have no mind, intellect, or consciousness; it would not engage in the activities of body, speech, or mind. Yet, through the power of the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), it is able to perform all the works of a Buddha.”

The Tathāgata is likewise thus; because he is no different from the emanated images he creates, he perceives all phenomena as being entirely like emanations and is therefore free from conceptual discrimination. Without initiating any activity of body, speech, or mind, he is able to perform all Buddha-works; yet there is no preparatory application, no awakening, and no volitional attention.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata thoroughly understands that the self-nature of the characteristics of all phenomena is like a magical creation.
Therefore, having attained self-awakening, out of compassion, he employs skillful means to awaken all sentient beings.

“Śāntamati! You should know that the wisdom of that Tathāgata does not abide in the conditioned, nor does it abide in the unconditioned; it does not abide in the aggregates, the sense bases, or the elements; it does not abide internally, nor does it abide externally; it does not abide in wholesome dharmas, nor does it abide in unwholesome dharmas; it does not abide in the mundane, nor does it abide in the supramundane; it does not abide in what is faulty, nor does it abide in what is faultless; it does not abide in the outflowing, nor does it abide in the non-outflowing; it does not abide in the past, nor does it abide in the future, nor does it abide in the present; it does not abide in cessation through deliberation, nor does it abide in cessation not through deliberation; and so on, up to not abiding in consciousness.”

The Tathāgata, regarding the mental activities and inclinations of all sentient beings, proceeds solely by means of unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision; yet he is without preparatory effort, without further awakening, and without deliberate mental engagement.
Śāntamati! This is precisely the inconceivable secret dharma of the Tathāgata’s mind.
Therefore, you should know that the Tathāgata is constantly in samādhi, yet he does not abandon the mental activities and expressions of all sentient beings.
Chapter Ten: Praising the Merits of the Bodhisattva Mahāguhyapati Vajrapāṇi. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Among all the assemblies of Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa throughout the worlds of the ten directions who are currently practicing the holy life in the presence of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—whichever of those Bodhisattvas does the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, constantly follow?
The Buddha said: “Śāriputra, stop, stop!
This is the inconceivable practice; those among gods and humans in the world who do not give rise to faith in the bodhisattva practices will, on the contrary, encounter confusion.
If there are sentient beings who are sustained by a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they will, upon hearing of this, develop pure faith and feel no fear.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have conceived supreme pure faith in the Tathāgata; I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound this for me.
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, constantly follows behind me; can you see him?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have only now been able to see it through the majestic spiritual power of the World-Honored One; it was not something I could know or see by myself from of old.
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!..."

It is so, it is so. You should now know that throughout this Bhadrakalpa, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, constantly follows behind all those assemblies of bodhisattvas, manifesting the form of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi in every place; he is able to do so through the power of his past vows and his supernormal powers.

Śāriputra! Even for all classes of sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, constantly follows them manifesting his original form; yet, even so, the power of wisdom manifested through his sustaining grace (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not yet fully perfected.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
That Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi constantly follows behind the Bodhisattva Maitreya; are you able to see him?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I see this now for the first time; it is not what I have seen before.
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! He is always following behind him, yet you do not see him yourself.

From other world-systems, whether they be bodhisattvas, Brahmā kings, Śakra devānām indra, or the world-protecting deities, they constantly come to see that Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva holding his vajra, following behind Maitreya Bodhisattva.”
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

At one time, when the assembly of bodhisattvas of that Bhadrakalpa manifested hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various miraculous transformations for the sake of Maitreya Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, also followed behind those bodhisattvas to provide supportive empowerment.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Even when the Tathāgata performs acts of transformation, that Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, also follows behind the Buddha, assisting in the propagation of the holy teachings through the power of his vows.

Śāriputra! Therefore, you should know that all such things as these are due to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, being fully endowed with the power of wisdom and the inconceivable empowerment of his supernormal faculties.

Chapter Eleven: The Bodhisattva’s Superiority in Ascetic Practice through Maturing Sentient Beings by Means of Receiving Food. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, saying: “Lord of Secrets!”

You may joyfully speak of such matters as the bodhisattva’s ascetic practices, his journey to the site of enlightenment and subjugation of the demonic armies, his turning of the wheel of the sublime Dharma, and his adornment of the buddha-fields.
"I now wish to hear this; I pray that you will explain it for me.
You have personally realized and known such rare and marvelous matters as these.
Thus addressed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, spoke to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati:

"Śāntamati, you should know that the practices of asceticism and other such deeds of a bodhisattva possess immeasurable adornments of merit; even if one were to remain in the world for an eon, exhausting the full span of one's lifespan, one could not fully explain them in detail."
I shall now briefly explain this for you. Śāntamati!

The ascetic practices of a bodhisattva are not of a single kind. A bodhisattva engages in these—ranging from the various forms of moral discipline to such acts as scorching the body with the five fires and all other matters of deportment—solely for the purpose of subduing all māras and non-Buddhists. This is done so that he may become most excellent and supreme, surpassing all those who practice the difficult feats of asceticism and moral discipline.
"Where those non-Buddhists are unable to perform, the Bodhisattva is able to manifest and perform everything, making himself surpass them.
O Śāntamati! There may be sentient beings who see that Bodhisattva standing on one foot, or who see the Bodhisattva raising both [feet]..."
Some saw the Bodhisattva gazing intently at the sun; some saw the Bodhisattva performing the penance of five fires;
some saw the Bodhisattva walking on his elbows; some saw the Bodhisattva standing motionless;
some saw the Bodhisattva with both feet raised upward; some saw the Bodhisattva with his head downward; or they saw the Bodhisattva...

He lay upon thorns; or he was seen by some as the Bodhisattva lying upon cow dung, or sitting cross-legged upon a stone, or lying upon a wall, or lying upon fruits and gourds, or lying upon rafters, or lying upon the bare earth;
or he wore a raincoat, or wore garments of grass, or wore garments of deerskin.
Some covered their bodies with robes, while others remained naked; some turned with the movement of the sun, some wore garments from burial mounds, and some wore garments of tree bark;
some ate weeds and barnyard grass, some ate roots, some ate leaves, some ate flowers, some ate fruits, and some ate stalks.
Some ate from branches; some ate lotus roots; some did not eat for six days;
some ate *kaṇa* beans; some ate *kaṇa* rice; some ate buckwheat; some ate mung beans;
some ate green beans; some ate *śāli* rice; some ate sesame; some ate non-glutinous rice; or some drank only water.
For their sustenance, they may eat a drop of clarified butter, or a drop of honey, or a drop of milk;
or they may never eat at all; or they may dwell among the hosts of Māra, or sit alone, or stand perpetually.

Śāntamati! Regarding these various modes of conduct and other immeasurable difficult practices and ascetic austerities, the Bodhisattva, for the sake of subduing non-Buddhists, is able to manifest himself as sharing in all their painful and evil characteristics.

In this manner, for six years, the Bodhisattva never once violated even a single aspect of his dignified deportment; he manifested the fulfillment of the practice of the prohibitive precepts, refining his bodhisattva activities through diligence, remaining most excellent, supreme, firm, and non-retrogressive.

Thus, for six years he manifested these various signs; yet those of other inclinations and understandings could not see one another, nor could any practitioners of external ascetic disciplines, upon seeing the Bodhisattva’s practice in this way, fail to be completely subdued by it.
Śāntamati! In all places, whatever the bodhisattva does or manifests, he abides entirely in a mind of equanimity, free from all faults.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!
When the Bodhisattva was thus practicing austerities, sixty-four nayutas of devas and humans reached maturity in their roots of virtue within the three vehicles.

Śāntamati, you should know that there were devas and humans who possessed great faith and understanding and performed virtuous deeds; they saw the Bodhisattva sitting serenely within the jeweled pavilion, having entered the *āsphānaka* samādhi and experiencing the bliss therein.

After the Bodhisattva had completed six years, he arose from meditative concentration and taught the Dharma as was appropriate to ripen those among the devas and humans who desired the Dharma and sought it with resolve.
When those gods and humans see this bodhisattva and hear the Dharma he preaches, they find no difference whatsoever in the activities they perform.

Śāntamati, you should know that this is called the "Dharma Gate of the Bodhisattva’s Great Wisdom Accumulation, the Skillful Means of Great Compassion, the Profound Principle of Entering the Inconceivable, the Subduing of All Demons and Heretics, and the Purification of the Wisdom of Ascetic Practices."
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!
During those six years, the Bodhisattva accomplished such extremely difficult deeds as he was destined to manifest.
Having passed the six years, he went to the Nairañjanā River; conforming to worldly custom, he bathed to purify himself, and once his body was washed, he stood upon the riverbank."

At that time, there was a woman from a certain village named Sujātā; she had prepared milk-rice gruel by milking a hundred cows, and with a pure heart, she carried it to the Bodhisattva’s dwelling and offered it to him.

At that time, there were also sixty koṭis of assemblies consisting of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, each of whom prepared exquisite food and drink to offer to the Bodhisattva.
They all spoke these words:
"We pray that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva will accept our food and drink!
We pray that the Mahāsattva will accept our food and drink!"

"Śāntamati! At that time, the Bodhisattva first accepted the milk-rice offered by the woman Sujātā; he also accepted all the food and drink offered by those sixty koṭis of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others."
They could not see one another, and each thought to themselves:
"The Bodhisattva has accepted the food and drink I have offered.
Having accepted it, he shall realize the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."

“O Śāntamati! Because the Bodhisattva universally brings to maturity the roots of goodness for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) in all those beings to whom he gives, this very act constitutes the Bodhisattva’s supreme ascetic practice;
it is the superior practice of skillful means for maturing sentient beings by means of receiving food.”
The Sūtra on the Inconceivable Secrets of the Tathāgata Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Nine.

Chapter Twelve: The Bodhisattva’s Journey to the Site of Enlightenment At that time, having bathed and received food and drink so that his physical strength was fully restored, the Bodhisattva immediately proceeded toward the Great Site of Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa).
Having arrived, he addressed the Devaputra Sudhīmat and the assembly of terrestrial devas, speaking these verses:
“Sustaining the great earth without wavering, The Bodhisattva who has abandoned craving and severed harm Shall now realize awakening beneath this tree; You all should adorn this ground.”
“Excellent! The earth-dwelling devas rejoice; the three thousandfold world-system is universally purified.
They scatter the most supreme and wondrous fragrant flowers, and sprinkle pure perfumed water everywhere until all is cleansed.”
All those with Firm Hands and those who hold garlands, the gods of the Heaven of Constant Joy and others up to the sky-dwellers,
joyfully gaze upon the Honored Bodhisattva, scattering various exquisite flowers as an offering.
The four world-protecting devas and their assemblies, even throughout all four great continents,
pervading the triple-thousandfold world system adorned with golden nets, cover [him] as an offering to the Supreme among Men.
The Lord Śakra within the trichiliocosm makes offerings to the Bodhisattva of great majesty;
just as the celestial palace of Vairocana is exquisitely adorned, so too is the adornment of the trichiliocosm.
The hosts of the Yāma Heaven all rejoice, adorning the space with nets of lapis lazuli;
displaying rare and wondrous treasures throughout the three thousandfold world-system, they extend their offerings to the Sage among Men.
The hosts of Tuṣita Heaven were all filled with joy; they spread nets of true pearls as an adornment.
Pearl necklaces there took the shape of half-moons, and they scattered true pearls extensively like rain.
The King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, together with his celestial host, fashioned a precious net of Jāmbūnada gold;
from the jeweled bells of this golden net issued wondrous sounds, which were heard throughout the trichiliocosm, bringing joy to all who heard them.
All the pure and wondrous jewels among the heavens, With boundless, radiant, and pure light,
Adorned by the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, Are offered to Sarvārthasiddha, the Fearless One.
All the nāgas and gandharvas, the mahoragas, asuras, and the rest,
each within their own palaces, have extensively adorned themselves and beautifully embellished the realm of desire.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!

At that time, when the Great Brahmā King beheld these extraordinary signs of the Bodhisattva’s arrival at the site of enlightenment, he addressed all the sons of the gods in the Brahma assembly, saying: 'O virtuous ones!'"
Do you know this matter?
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abandon his great vows and vast armor;
furthermore, regarding his firm armor, he possesses no intention of indolence or retreat, and is able to skillfully accomplish all the practices of a bodhisattva.
Having cultivated all the *pāramitās* and being well-established on the further shore, they have attained perfect mastery over all the bodhisattva stages;

they are able to completely purify all the aspirations of bodhisattvas, and furthermore, they skillfully penetrate the various faculties and natures of all sentient beings, deeply entering the secret states of all Tathāgatas. All...
Having completely transcended the paths of Māra’s deeds, they have attained indestructible faith in all roots of goodness;
established by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas, they universally demonstrate the path of true liberation to all sentient beings.
Acting as great guides who shatter all realms of Māras and externalists, they are the sole heroes within the trichiliocosm.

Venerable One, you have accumulated the medicinal herbs of the Dharma as a Great King of Physicians; you are clothed in the silken robes of liberation as a Great Dharma King; you radiate the light of great wisdom and raise the banner of the Great Dharma.

The eight worldly dharmas cannot stain you; you are born from a truly pure great lotus. You maintain total retention (*dhāraṇī*) of all phenomena without forgetfulness; you arise from the great ocean, free from all increase or decrease. You are unmoving and unshakable like Mount Sumeru; you are wondrously good and stainless, wondrously good and pure. You are born from the great *maṇi* jewel of self-purified sublime wisdom; you have attained non-obstruction amidst all phenomena; and your mental activities are harmonized and refined, born of the Great Brahmā.

Endowed with such virtues as these, this Bodhisattva now proceeds to the Great Field of Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa), desiring to realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, to subdue the hosts of Māra, and to bring to perfection the Tathāgata’s ten powers (*daśabala*), four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*), and eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). He intends to universally turn the Great Wheel of Dharma for all beings and let out the lion’s roar; he will extensively practice the gift of Dharma for all sentient beings, purifying their Dharma-eye, and using the True Dharma to subdue all heterodox and divergent external arguments. This is done to fulfill his former vows, to draw near to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and to attain abundant mastery over all dharmas.
"O you virtuous ones!
You should arouse a mind of diligent vigor to approach and make offerings to the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King, with a pure mind, further addressed all the sons of the gods of the Brahma assembly, saying:
"O virtuous ones! This Bodhisattva has diligently cultivated the precepts throughout many hundreds of thousands of kalpas; he is the most supreme and pure Mahāsattva.
He now proceeds to the site of Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa), about to attain Perfect Awakening."
"You all should extensively perform such deeds as creating sublime and wondrous adornments throughout all the trichiliocosms.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King spoke in verse:
"The Great Being’s precepts are resolute; He brings vast benefit to humans and devas."
The God among Men makes offerings to the God among Gods; He proceeds to the site of enlightenment, the Great Silence.
Having subdued all hosts of Māra’s armies, He has truly awakened to the wisdom of all-knowledge.
All Buddha-dharmas are perfectly clear and bright; He turns the wheel of the True Dharma to bring benefit and joy.
The Great Wisdom lets out a single lion’s roar; all sentient beings who hear it rejoice.
Causing the eye of Dharma to open through pure causes, the Honored One among Men proceeds to the Bodhi tree.

Having subdued all heterodox and external doctrines, and having fully perfected his vows of the past, he now manifests the accomplishment of the deeds of a Perfectly Awakened One; the Honored One among Men approaches the Bodhi tree.
Excellent! All are harmoniously united and single-minded; they universally adorn every region, so that throughout the trichiliocosm, the entire realm of desire is seen to be magnificently adorned.
Just as the adornments of the desire realm are, so too are those of the form realm;
well done, O pure-minded Brahma hosts, who have extensively adorned the trichiliocosm!
The offerings manifested in the desire realm, as well as all the offerings manifested in the higher realms, scatter the most supreme and wondrous fragrant flowers;
the various musical instruments adorned with jewels are all played and struck.
The multitudes of devas throughout the trichiliocosm, having seen and heard this, rejoice and prostrate in reverence;
even unto the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, each within their own palace, adorns it with vast splendor.
Superior among the superior, and most excellent among the excellent, He universally manifests the adornments of all celestial palaces;
With sixty hundred koṭis of celestial maidens, He establishes the Vajra Seat at the site of enlightenment.
Sprinkle everywhere with scented water, and scatter various exquisite flowers;
arraying all manner of jewels throughout this place, the site of great enlightenment is vast, magnificent, and beautiful.
Words cannot praise all his virtues; he possesses immeasurable kinds of adornment.

This Great Being has resolutely cultivated the precepts with diligence; possessing great majesty and virtue for the benefit and welfare of the world, he is about to proceed beneath the King of Bodhi Trees to subdue the demonic hosts and their evil wisdoms.
The harmonious conduct of all noble ones extensively adorns the trichiliocosm.
Among gods and humans, he is the Honored One, sovereign of the Dharma; by making offerings to him, one obtains boundless merit.
When the assembly of Brahmās hears of this Honored One among men, they marvel at how he has exquisitely adorned the trichiliocosm.
Wondrous flowers and jeweled banners form a magnificent array, Transforming the world into a realm composed of jewels.
Tens of millions of exquisite canopies manifest in the sky, As radiant and most beautiful as the sun and moon;
The blossoms of the śāla trees are supreme among all, Manifesting everywhere like the Nandana Grove.
The Great Sage proceeds along the path with joy, manifesting transformations as magnificent as seven chariots;
golden lotus flowers made of jewels densely cover it, surrounded by sevenfold boundary paths.
The Lord Śakra, Sovereign of Devas, fashioned this adornment; such a marvel among humans and devas had never been seen before.
Just as the Vast and Victorious Hall (Vaijayanta) in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, so too was the adornment of the four great continents.
The heavens of Yāma, Tuṣita, and Nirmāṇarati, together with the splendors of Paranirmita-vaśavartin and Akaniṣṭha,
all exerting vigorous and swift effort, together adorn the supreme site of enlightenment.
Just as there are supreme adornments within the desire realm, so too are the hosts of devas, nāgas, and others;
all are manifested in a single kṣaṇa, and the Bodhisattva proceeds through them.
Tens of millions of celestial maidens from the four quarters Approached the Bodhi tree and surrounded it in a great assembly;
With ointments, powdered incense, and various wondrous flowers, They sprinkled sublime fragrant water everywhere.
The base of the Great Bodhi tree is wondrously adorned, like trees growing in the gardens of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven;
all its various ornaments are such that words cannot praise their manifold merits.
Countless nayutas of those devas, each with their respective adornments, are all exceptionally sublime.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!

Once the Bodhisattva has arrived at the site of enlightenment, as soon as he sets down his two feet with the mark of the thousand-spoked wheels and presses them upon that ground, a vast radiance immediately appears."

This light universally illumines all realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts; when the various classes of sentient beings within them are touched by the light, the sufferings they endure are temporarily stilled.
A great light shone universally throughout the palace of the Naga King Kālika.

At that time, having seen this Bodhisattva’s radiance illuminating [the palace], the Naga King Kālika felt joy, leaping for gladness and exultation; he immediately spoke these verses for his own palace retinue and the assembly of nagas:
"Just as golden light shines with extreme brilliance, This great radiance illuminates my Naga King’s palace."
I have been graced by the light illuminating my body, And my heart is likewise filled with great joy.
Just as I previously beheld this auspicious radiance In the presence of former Buddhas, What I now behold is certain beyond doubt: The Great Fearless One shall appear in the world.
Each of you should take exquisite incense and flowers, unguents, powdered incense, and flower garlands,
as well as pure gold and mani-jewels to form necklaces and superior robes;
furthermore, take various kinds of musical instruments, and banners and canopies adorned with pearls and jewels.
And the wondrous high banners made of jewels, To offer worship to the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
All the wondrous palaces of the dragon kings, Vastly adorned and entirely pure—
You all should give rise to a heart of joy, And together proceed in person to the Buddha’s abode.

At that time, the Naga King Kālika, together with his palace ladies, retinue, and the assembly of nāgas, each holding various kinds of exquisite incense, flowers, garments, banners, and canopies, as well as musical instruments, drums, and songs, leaped up into the air. They sprinkled fragrant water everywhere like clouds and rained down nāga-flowers, nāga-pearls, and other such things.
Thus, by means of the majestic power and supernatural faculties of the dragon kings, they manifested various transformations and proceeded to the place where the Bodhisattva was.
Upon arrival, they immediately prostrated at the Bodhisattva’s feet together with their retinues, playing exquisite music as a mark of devout offering.
Having made these offerings, the Dragon King circumambulated him to the right and stood there, uttering a sublime verse in praise:
"The Honored One among Men emits a great radiance, Universally illuminating all Buddha-fields.
In an instant, the sufferings of the evil realms are all stilled, And our dragon palaces are all bathed in light."
Once the host of nāgas had been touched by the light, they all gave rise to joy and spoke these words:
"There is no doubt that the Bodhisattva will attain Buddhahood; such is this golden radiance."
There were nayutas of nāga maidens who, with reverence, held up exquisite incense and flowers,
as well as superior garments, various banners, and streamers, and went to where the Bodhisattva was to present their offerings.
Now, in this place, flower canopies and all other exquisite and vast adornments,
as well as the medicinal herbs and various groves of trees, all bend low toward the Bodhi tree;
the rivers cease their flow and become still, and the winds stop their agitation, remaining entirely at peace.
Today the Bodhisattva has realized enlightenment, the most supreme subduer of Māra in the world;
the radiance of Brahmā, Śakra, and all other lights—the light of the sun and moon included—is entirely eclipsed.
Those who are touched by this light attain refreshing coolness; because the Buddha has appeared in the world, all rejoice.
Furthermore, there were various wondrous *maṇi* jars, swirling and turning clockwise in the sky;
the hosts of sages and the hosts of nāgas dwelling in the air likewise turned clockwise in that same manner.
Whether gods or humans of the world, each offered worship with the utmost sincerity.
Today the Bodhisattva has realized enlightenment, opening the right path for those who seek wisdom;
today, in the presence of the Buddha, we have increased our majestic radiance and attained excellent benefit.
In the past, I made offerings to Krakucchanda and the great holy lord Kanakamuni;
to Kāśyapa, the supreme victor among men, and even now I make offerings to the Sage Śākyamuni.
Seeking this great spiritual power of bodhi, I have never before seen such a most excellent and rare thing.
Possessing virtue, the most honored among men, you utter the great Brahma-voice like a lion’s roar;
with a resolute mind seeking bodhi, this mind is transcendent and peerless.
The sun and moon might fall, and Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, might be destroyed;
yet that the Honored One of Ten Powers should not attain full enlightenment this day—such a thing could never happen in this world.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!

At that time, the chief consort of the Naga King Kālika, named Jāmbūnada-prabhā, surrounded by a retinue of naga maidens, approached the place where the Bodhisattva was. She carried various exquisite jeweled parasols, various wonderful garments and celestial flower garlands, various skillfully adorned pearl necklaces, various superior and sublime mani jewels, and various kinds of exquisite incense vases, while playing beautiful songs as she went."
Having arrived, he paid homage, scattered various precious flowers as an offering, and stood before the Bodhisattva, reciting these verses:
"Your mind is unmoved and free from agitation, devoid of fear; Without greed, without hatred, and likewise without delusion;
O Unstained Honored One, you can tame that which is difficult to tame; You have abandoned all evils and remain unattached."
I now prostrate to the one of pure liberation, The Great Sage who has extracted the arrows of all doubt;
With the light of great wisdom, he destroys ignorance And is able to deliver the world from all suffering and affliction.
For those in the world who are without refuge or protection, the Bodhisattva skillfully acts as their refuge and protector;
his radiance shines universally throughout the triple world, so that devas and humans rejoice with pure hearts.
A rain of various exquisite flowers falls everywhere in the sky, And fine robes are scattered as vast and magnificent adornments;
Such a supreme sign as this I recognize: Today the Great Sage has attained Perfect Enlightenment.
The Victorious One, valiantly approaching the Bodhi tree, subdued all Māras as the Stainless Honored One;
having cleared away the dark web of afflictions, he realized Great Bodhi with a tranquil mind.
Throughout many koṭis of eons, you have sought awakening in the presence of former Buddhas;
having performed what is difficult to do for the sake of the world, you have now perfected your sublime resolve.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!
At that time, when the Bodhisattva was about to achieve perfect awakening, various worthy sages used their majestic spiritual power to rouse him.
Immediately, a grass-cutter named Śrī stood naturally at the Bodhisattva’s right side, holding pure grass."
This grass was as soft as a peacock’s neck and like *kācilindika* cloth; its color and fragrance were perfect, and each blade curled to the right.
At that time, the grass-cutter took the grass and went before the Bodhisattva to offer it to him, deeply resolving his mind toward the most supreme *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!
At that time, the auspicious grass-cutter, because his past vows were profound and firm, had previously made this aspiration:
'May I spread pure grass at every site of great enlightenment where all the bodhisattvas throughout the Bhadrakalpa attain perfect awakening.'"
Why is this? Śāntamati!

I recall that ninety-one kalpas prior to this present Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

Within that Buddha’s Dharma, a full assembly of one thousand great bodhisattvas practiced the holy life; at that time, the World-Honored One bestowed upon those great bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, there was an elder named Jñānavat who, being present in the great assembly, heard that the World-Honored One had bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon the various bodhisattvas; he immediately resolved his mind toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Then that elder made this aspiration, saying:
"May I, within the bodhimaṇḍas of all the Tathāgatas of this Bhadrakalpa, everywhere spread excellent and wondrous lion-thrones, or offer pure grass."
"Śāntamati, you should know that there is no longer any doubt: was the householder Bahudhīra at that time anyone else?
He was none other than Śākyamuni Bodhisattva himself when he offered pure grass upon attaining perfect enlightenment—he who was the auspicious grass-cutter."

For this reason, you should now know that by the power of his past vows, that auspicious grass-cutter has, at the abodes of various Buddhas, either offered pure grass or spread exquisite lion thrones.
The manner in which the roots of virtue of sentient beings ripen through the power of his wisdom that accords with their various inclinations and understandings is as follows. Furthermore, Śāntamati!

At that time, once the Bodhisattva had arrived at the Bodhi tree, the deity of that Bodhi tree and ten thousand celestial maidens all took up various supreme flowers, ointments, and other offerings, and went before the Bodhisattva.
Each scattered the various exquisite incenses and flowers they held as an offering, and each bowed their heads at the feet of the Bodhisattva, speaking these verses with one voice:
"We take refuge in the majestic and virtuous One, the Great Fearless One; Well-pacified, well-disciplined, and the destroyer of all evils;
Free from faults, courageous, and of great majestic radiance; The pure Guide, untainted by defilement."
Able to rescue all who are helpless from suffering and affliction, The Sole Holy Honored One bestows all forms of happiness;
He can eliminate the diseases of worldly afflictions, Acting as the Great King of Physicians to universally provide healing.
I take refuge in the one of pure and great renown, To whom the devas joyfully scatter flowers like rain;
May you now certainly and swiftly realize Bodhi, And arise with a heart of great compassion to gather all beings.
Having approached the King of Trees and ascended the supreme seat, you shattered all the darkness of Māra;
you awakened to the state of tranquility and realized Bodhi, just as the previous Buddhas had realized and awakened.
Having cultivated pure conduct for ten million eons, you have performed what is difficult to do for the benefit of the world;
O Great Sage, your noble intention is now fulfilled as you sit beneath the King of Trees to attain Perfect Enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!

At that time, the Bodhisattva took pure grass and proceeded to the site of enlightenment. Having arrived, he spread the grass upon the diamond throne himself; thereafter, he paid reverent homage to the King of Trees, the Bodhi tree, and circumambulated it seven times to the right."

After the Bodhisattva had spread the grass, at that moment eighty-four thousand devaputras brought eighty-four thousand exquisite and magnificently adorned lion-thrones and presented them to the Bodhisattva.

That seat was high, vast, magnificent, and exquisitely beautiful, adorned with various jewels; it was covered with nets of precious gems and nets of pearls, further draped with strings of pearls interlaced as a lattice, and furnished with hundreds of thousands of exquisite garments of the highest quality, arranged with marvelous skill.
At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately manifested his body, each occupying one of eighty-four thousand lion thrones.
Those devaputras could not see one another, yet each thought, "The Bodhisattva is seated upon the lion throne I have offered."
Once the Bodhisattva was seated, he realized the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
All these sons of gods gave rise to hearts of joy and purity, and all of them became non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
