Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Dispersing Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of the Transmission of the Sanskrit Canon, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject, under Imperial Decree. Chapter Thirteen: Subduing Māra. "Furthermore, Śāntamati!..."

Once the Bodhisattva had taken his place upon the lion throne at the site of great enlightenment, he immediately emitted from the mark of the white tuft between his eyebrows a light that shone everywhere; this light was named "Awakening and Illuminating All Māras."

At that time, there were ten billion hosts of Māras in this trichiliocosm who, touched by the radiance, each had the hair on their bodies stand on end within their respective palaces, and further felt mental distress within their own abodes.
The radiance so completely eclipsed the demonic palaces with darkness that those demons then thought to themselves:
"By what cause and by what condition have all our palaces become so dark?"
"Is it not that Śākyamuni Bodhisattva has sat at the site of enlightenment and realized the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
At that moment, the hosts of Māras perceived that the Bodhisattva had already sat upon the Great Site of Enlightenment; thereupon, each of the Māras withdrew into their own respective palaces.

Each of those Māras was attended by immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of yakṣas. With various colors, various appearances, and various forms, they rushed back and forth in a state of frantic panic and terror. Surrounded on all sides by those with various heads and faces, various weapons, and various banners and standards, they raised a great, evil sound, howling and shrieking, relying upon the power of Māra to manifest their demonic supernatural faculties.

The leaders of the various māras spanned twenty thousand yojanas in both length and breadth, and their retinues of māra followers were likewise vast, extending eighty-four thousand yojanas; all of them, through the power of the Bodhisattva’s skillful means of conversion and guidance, came together beneath the Bodhi tree.

"Śāntamati, you should know that as soon as those hosts of Māras arrived, they immediately employed their demonic powers to manifest various hideous and foul appearances, uttering many kinds of unpleasant sounds, and with fierce, cruel, and roaring clamor, they intended to subdue, destroy, and harm the Bodhisattva."

At that time, there were among those in the assembly various classes of sentient beings who had not yet abandoned desire; upon hearing the evil sounds, they gave rise to great terror and immediately met their death, or else experienced manifold sufferings in the interval before dying.
Due to the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva, those evil sounds could not be silenced for a long time.
The Bodhisattva then gave rise to a heart of great compassion, pitying their affliction; he immediately extinguished all such evil sounds, ensuring that no sentient beings were harmed or disturbed.
Śāntamati, you should know that this is the supreme sphere of a bodhisattva’s skillful means.
At that time, having heard those various extremely harsh sounds, the bodhisattva does not give rise to alarm or terror.
Why is this? Whatever sounds a bodhisattva hears, whether beautiful or foul, they are all like echoes.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!..."

When those hosts of Māras attempted to harass the Bodhisattva with various evil omens, there were immediately the assembly of worthies and sages who protect the site of Great Enlightenment and cultivate the practice of awakening; they reviled the Māras with sixteen kinds of words, saying:
"O evil ones!..."
"You should desist;
do not persistently manifest such malevolent and hostile traits, nor bring harm to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Why is this so?"

Now you, O Māras, wish to destroy the Bodhisattva; yet the Bodhisattva’s power is greatest and most supreme, capable of destroying you all, like a man of feeble strength confronting one of great might.
Furthermore, you māras wish to surpass the bodhisattva, yet the power of the bodhisattva can surpass you all, like a weak army fighting against a great hero.
Moreover, you māras wish to outstrip the bodhisattva, yet the power of the bodhisattva can outstrip you all, just as the stars are compared to the radiance of the moon.
Furthermore, you Māras wish to destroy the Bodhisattva, yet the Bodhisattva’s power can destroy you all, just as a fierce wind blows away chaff and husks.
Moreover, you Māras wish to crush the Bodhisattva, yet the Bodhisattva’s power can crush you all, just as a great tree is cut down at its roots.
Furthermore, you Māras wish to terrify the Bodhisattva, yet the Bodhisattva’s power can terrify you all, just as a herd of wild animals encounters a great lion.
Moreover, you Māras wish to cause the Bodhisattva to dwell on parched ground, yet the Bodhisattva’s power can dry you up, just as the scorching sun dries the water in a cow's footprint.
Furthermore, you Māras wish to destroy the Bodhisattva, yet the power of the Bodhisattva can destroy you all, like a small frontier kingdom waging war against a great nation.
Moreover, you Māras wish to spy upon the Bodhisattva, yet the power of the Bodhisattva can spy upon you all, like a wicked man escaping his life at the hands of executioners.
Furthermore, you māras wish to disturb the bodhisattva, yet the power of the bodhisattva can instead disturb you all, just as a merchant who has amassed vast treasures is consumed by fire.

Furthermore, you māras wish to cause the Bodhisattva great distress, yet the power of the Bodhisattva can cause you all to experience great distress, like an unrighteous king who has lost his royal throne.

Furthermore, you Māras wish to give rise to thoughts of anger and malice toward the Bodhisattva, yet the power of the Bodhisattva restrains your angry minds, just as an old goose breaks its own wings and feathers.

Furthermore, you Māras desire to kill the Bodhisattva, yet the Bodhisattva’s power restrains your murderous intent, just as a person traveling through a vast wilderness and perilous terrain exhausts their wealth and goods.

Furthermore, you māras wish to cause the Bodhisattva to flee in haste, yet the power of the Bodhisattva can cause you all to run away in terror, like a shipwrecked vessel in the midst of the great ocean.

Furthermore, you Māras wish to cause the Bodhisattva to wither away, yet the power of the Bodhisattva can cause all of you to wither away, just as the blazing fires at the end of an eon incinerate grasses and trees.
"Furthermore, you Māras wish to sever the Bodhisattva, yet the power of the Bodhisattva is able to sever you all, just as a great vajra severs small stones.
"Śāntamati! [the Buddha said.]

Furthermore, those assemblies of noble ones who guard the site of great enlightenment and cultivate the practices of awakening disparage the various māras and praise the bodhisattvas with these sixteen kinds of expressions;
yet, even so, those māras have not been defeated or subdued.

At that time, the Bodhisattva—having accumulated and cultivated sublime practices for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, namely: generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and supreme wisdom; loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and the path; as well as śamatha, vipaśyanā, clear intelligence, liberation, and other such dharmas—extended his right golden arm, which was exceedingly well-formed, supple, delicate, and subtle, and placed it upon the crown of Māra’s head. He then pressed down and stroked Māra’s entire body, giving rise to a mind of great compassion and gazing with eyes of love, with a profound resolve to liberate all sentient beings;
while all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of all worlds stood before him, bearing witness to his right mindfulness and right awareness.
The Bodhisattva immediately pressed the earth with his hand. Once the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva had pressed the earth with his hand, at that moment the great earth shook in six ways:

namely, it moved, moved everywhere, and moved equally everywhere; it quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere; it roared, roared everywhere, and roared equally everywhere; it surged, surged everywhere, and surged equally everywhere; it crashed, crashed everywhere, and crashed equally everywhere; it struck, struck everywhere, and struck equally everywhere. It surged in the east and subsided in the west, surged in the west and subsided in the east, surged in the south and subsided in the north, surged in the north and subsided in the south, surged at the edges and subsided in the center, and surged in the center and subsided at the edges. Thus, these six types of shaking gave rise to eighteen transformations, causing the entire great earth to tremble and sway, manifesting various extraordinary signs in an instant.

At that time, the hosts of Māras—those of wicked, cruel, and savage disposition, who roared and struck with intent to cause harm, and whose karmic natures were such—that upon seeing these signs, all gave rise to fear and trepidation.
Furthermore, by the power of the Bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual authority, a voice was heard from the sky reciting this verse:
"One should take refuge in the Noble Great Being, The supreme sage among all the hosts of seers,
Who extensively bestows fearlessness through great compassion, And is universally able to rescue and protect all classes of beings."
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!
Upon hearing these words, eight million *koṭi-nayuta* of evil yakṣas among the hosts of Māra fell prostrate upon the ground, and they all cried out with one voice:
'Save us from suffering! Save us from suffering! Great Being, save us! "
The remaining hosts of Māras all desired to flee, yet despite exhausting their magical powers, they were unable to advance.

At that time, out of compassion, the Bodhisattva emitted light from his entire body; because they were touched by the illumination of that radiance, the hosts of Māras were all freed from fear and immediately returned each to their own abodes within the palaces.

Śāntamati! When that bodhisattva manifested supernatural powers for the hosts of māras, eight million koṭī-nayuta evil yakṣas all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; furthermore, within the assembly, nine million nine hundred thousand koṭī-nayuta persons resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; and eighty-four thousand devaputras, by the power of their past roots of goodness, all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
14. Chapter on Turning the Wheel of Dharma, Part One of Fourteen: “Furthermore, Śāntamati!

Some devas and humans knew that the Bodhisattva had subdued the armies of Māra; some devas and humans knew that none of the various evil māras had ever come to the Bodhisattva’s abode; some devas and humans first learned that the Bodhisattva had spread auspicious grass and taken his seat at the place of enlightenment; some devas and humans saw the Śākya Bodhisattva seated upon a lion throne adorned with various precious lotuses; some devas and humans saw the Bodhisattva on the ground; some saw the Bodhisattva sitting serenely beneath an aśvattha tree; some saw him beneath a pārijātaka tree, or a kūṭadru tree, or a bodhi tree; and some saw the Bodhisattva beneath a bodhi tree composed of various jewels.
Some devas saw the Bodhi tree as being one tāla-tree height; some devas saw the lion throne as being one tāla-tree height; and some devas saw the Bodhi tree as being seven tāla-trees in height.

Some devas saw the lion throne as being half a tāla tree in height; some saw the Bodhi tree reaching as high as eighty-four thousand yojanas; and some saw the lion throne as being forty-two thousand yojanas in height.

Some devas and humans saw that Bodhisattva subduing the demonic armies; some devas and humans saw a single demonic army; some devas and humans saw a vast multitude of evil demonic hosts; and some saw the Bodhisattva destroying the demonic hosts through his playful supernatural powers (*vikrīḍita-abhijñā*).

Some see the Bodhisattva dwelling in mid-air; some see the Bodhisattva seated upon a lion throne in mid-air; and some see the Bodhisattva seated upon a precious throne beneath the Bodhi tree, realizing the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Śāntamati, you should know that the accomplishment of the immeasurable, most supreme, and pure realms by bodhisattvas is entirely due to their abiding at the most exalted and supreme site of great enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), wherein they manifest various sublime signs endowed with such immeasurable merits.

"Furthermore, Śāntamati! Once the Bodhisattva has established himself in the most excellent and supreme site of great enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and subdued the hosts of Māra, there immediately appear before him the assemblies of Bodhisattvas from immeasurable,
incalculable worlds in the ten directions who had previously practiced the same supreme path of conduct."
They all came to this place and together uttered pure and fearless sounds, namely: sounds of auspiciousness, sounds of happiness, sounds of joy,
sounds of swiftness, sounds of agility, sounds of "well done," sounds of non-emptiness,
sounds of valor, sounds of manliness, sounds of non-retrogression, and sounds of increase.
The voice of auspiciousness; the voice free from feverish affliction; the voice of great compassion; the voice of former aspirations;
the voice of non-wasteful merit; the voice that gladdens the mind; the voice of firm harmony; the voice of the Great Being’s playful manifestation;
the voice of supreme benefit; the voice corresponding to every moment; and the voice of the knowledge of all-knowing wisdom.
...the sound of attaining perfect enlightenment; from those bodhisattvas emerged such pure sounds as these.

At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas gathered from the worlds of the ten directions within that most supreme and excellent site of enlightenment further offered extensive consolation through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of exquisite voices, presented various kinds of sublime offerings, and performed various forms of supreme praise.

At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas who had cultivated virtuous conduct over many lifetimes, together with the great bodhisattvas gathered from the worlds of the ten directions at the sublime site of enlightenment, offered such consolation, offerings, and praise.
Although the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni subdued the armies of Māra, he neither opposed nor complied with them.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva has already transcended the dharmas of opposition and compliance.

When a bodhisattva is endowed with supreme wisdom within a single moment of mind, whatever they know, whatever they see, whatever they attain, or whatever they realize—all of these are fully accomplished.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!

Once the Tathāgata had attained the fruit of enlightenment, immediately all the Buddha-Tathāgatas of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds in the ten directions extended their right hands, pressed upon the Bodhisattva’s body, and comforted him, asking:
'O Son of the Buddha!'"
Are your limbs free from fatigue?
Do you experience pleasant sensations?
Have you realized the fruit through the wisdom of self-nature?
Is it realized through an unobstructed mind?
Is it realized through the wisdom of equality?
Is there no conduct involving artificial ornamentation?
Have you donned the armor of great compassion?
Have you ensured that the lineage of the Triple Gem remains unbroken?
Have you attained mastery over all phenomena?

"Śāntamati, you should know that at that time, those whose roots of virtue were already matured were able to approach the site of great enlightenment (*mahābodhimaṇḍa*) and understand its supreme activities; however, those whose roots of virtue were not yet matured could neither approach it nor understand it."
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!

After the Tathāgata had attained the fruit of enlightenment, for seven days and nights he contemplated with profound discernment the joy of the true Dharma, while gazing intently at the Great Bodhi tree without ever blinking his eyes."

At that time, there were hundreds of thousands of devaputras who extensively offered worship, praised him, and prostrated; furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of devakanyās, each reverently prostrating, praising, and honoring him.
Having beheld the supreme majestic deportment of the Tathāgata, all these goddesses resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!..."
After the Tathāgata had attained the fruit of enlightenment, the four Great Heavenly Kings each brought a precious alms bowl and came to the Buddha’s dwelling to present it as an offering.
As for these four heavenly kings:
These are the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the east, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka of the south, the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa of the west, and the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa of the north.

When the Four Great Heavenly Kings of these four great continents had thus arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, the others did likewise; there were hundreds of koṭis of Four Great Heavenly Kings from hundreds of koṭis of four great continents, each holding a precious bowl, all coming to the Buddha’s dwelling to present their offerings.
At that time, after the Tathāgata had accepted these four hundred koṭis of precious bowls, he immediately used his supernormal powers to merge them into a single bowl.
Each of the Four Great Heavenly Kings individually conceived this thought:
"The Tathāgata has accepted the bowl offered by me; may he receive his meal from within my bowl in due order."
Each and every one of them gave rise to a most supreme, pure, and joyful mind, and did not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!..."

After the Tathāgata had attained the fruit of enlightenment, two merchant leaders—one named Dharapusa and the other named Vāraka—along with sixty thousand other devaputras, all came to the Buddha’s dwelling and were the very first to offer pure food and drink.
These merchant leaders and others had all previously made this vow:
"May we be the very first to offer pure food and drink to the Tathāgata.
Once that Tathāgata has accepted our offerings at the outset, may he give rise to a heart of joy, and may we all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!

When a bodhisattva first ascends to the most supreme and most excellent site of great enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they have not yet perfected all-knowledge (sarvajñatā); now that they have realized the fruit of the path, their awakened wisdom is fully perfected. Yet, they have not yet turned that vast wheel of Dharma to extensively bring great benefit to sentient beings."

Why is this? Because from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until now, sitting at the site of awakening to achieve equal and perfect enlightenment, the bodhisattva desires to bring benefit to sentient beings.

Śāntamati! For this reason, you should now know that as each and every bodhisattva attains the fruit of enlightenment, they likewise act in the same way, all bringing great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!

After the Tathāgata had attained the fruit of enlightenment, there was a Brahmā king named Śikhin, who, together with six million eight hundred thousand sons of gods from the Brahma assembly, respectfully surrounded him while remaining hidden within that Brahma realm. He then proceeded to the presence of the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and with palms joined in sincere devotion, entreated the World-Honored One to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, saying these words:
'I pray only that the World-Honored One..."
I pray, Sugata! May you extensively turn the sublime wheel of Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings,
so that all those present in this assembly who possess the capacity as vessels may fully understand the teachings spoken by the Buddha.
Just as that Prince Dhṛtarāṣṭra made a supreme vow in the past:
"May I, throughout this Bhadrakalpa, after all the Tathāgatas have attained the fruit of the path of Buddhahood, exhort them all to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma."
"Furthermore, Śāntamati! It was not only this Brahmā King Śikhin who requested the Tathāgata to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma. Why is that?"

After the Brahma King Śikhin had first made his request, there were further ten koṭis of Brahma kings, ten koṭis of Śakra devas, and ten koṭis of great bodhisattvas who also all entreated the Tathāgata to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.

At that time, the Brahma King Śikhin, knowing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had accepted his invitation by remaining silent, immediately prepared an exquisite lion throne for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, within the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. It was forty-two thousand yojanas high, exquisitely adorned, endowed with supreme characteristics, and a sight for all to behold; he then set it firmly upon the ground.

Just as the Brahma King Śikhin had first prepared an exquisite lion throne, there immediately appeared ten koṭis of Brahmā kings, ten koṭis of Śakra devas, and ten koṭis of great bodhisattvas, all of whom prepared exquisite lion thrones for the World-Honored One—splendidly adorned, endowed with superior characteristics, and a sight for which all beings longed to behold.
The Sūtra on the Inconceivable Secret Mahāyāna Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Eleven.
The Sūtra on the Inconceivable Secret Mahāyāna Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll Twelve.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Commissioned Translators of the Western Heavens, Court Dispersing Grandee, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of Sanskrit Transmission, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject, by Imperial Decree. Chapter Fourteen, Part Two: Turning the Wheel of Dharma. "At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. Having arrived, he manifested his body, each appearing upon a lion throne within the assembly."
At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, and the great bodhisattvas each saw the Tathāgata individually within the seat they had offered, seated upon it and turning the Great Wheel of Dharma.
All those assemblies gave rise to pure and joyful hearts, and none of them ever regressed from their progress toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, once the World-Honored One was seated upon the supreme lion throne, all the boundless worlds of the ten directions immediately shook, and a great radiance shone everywhere.
"At that time, the World-Honored One entered the samādhi of the Boundless Realm.

Having entered this samādhi, the entire great earth of this trichiliocosm became as level and smooth as the palm of a hand. Furthermore, all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm—whether in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, or devas—every class of being attained peace and happiness. Not a single sentient being was afflicted by greed, hatred, delusion, or any other defilements; they all gave rise to thoughts of mutual compassion, regarding one another as parents."

"Furthermore, when the World-Honored One enters this samādhi of boundless realm, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas from the ten directions all come to assemble in order to hear and receive the true Dharma."

At that time, all those possessing great power throughout the trichiliocosm—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all came to the Buddha’s assembly to listen to and receive the true Dharma.

Śāntamati, you should know that when the Bhagavān desires to preach the Dharma, this entire great trichiliocosm—its vast assemblies of humans and devas from every quarter—will all gather and fill the space completely, leaving not even the measure of a single hair-tip empty, so as to listen to and receive the True Dharma proclaimed by the Bhagavān.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the entire assembly of devas and humans had gathered, arose serenely from samādhi. Giving rise to great compassion, he surveyed the entire assembly with the Tathāgata’s pure eyes of loving-kindness and turned the wheel of the True Dharma.
Whether they be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or anyone else, all are of one and the same Dharma.
Furthermore, Śāntamati!

The wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata is turned for the sake of causing the minds of all sentient beings to rejoice, and furthermore, so that every sentient being in the assembly may individually understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha.

As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was about to turn the wheel of Dharma, first there were immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* bodhisattvas from the ten directions who all came to assemble to hear and receive the true Dharma; immediately thereafter, hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* devaputras from the desire realm and the form realm also came to assemble to hear and receive the true Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words:
"O virtuous ones! The eye is not a permanent phenomenon."
Why is this? If one is to be delivered by means of the teaching on suffering, they hear it said that "this eye is suffering.
If one is to be delivered by means of the teaching on non-self, they hear it said that "this eye is non-self."
If one is to be delivered through the discourse on emptiness, they hear it said that this eye is empty.
If one is to be delivered through the discourse on tranquility, they hear it said that this eye is tranquil.
If one is to be liberated through the discourse on detachment, they hear it said that this eye-dharma is detached.
If one is to be liberated through the discourse on impermanence, they hear it said that this eye is impermanent.
If one is to be delivered by means of the teaching that there is no basis, they hear it said that the eye has no basis.
If one is to be delivered by means of the teaching that things are like illusions, they hear it said that this eye is like an illusion.
If those who are to be liberated by means of the analogy of a dream should hear it, they immediately hear it said that this eye is like a dream.
If those who are to be liberated by means of the analogy of the moon in water should hear it, they immediately hear it said that the eye is like the moon in water.
If there are those who should be delivered by means of the teaching that [the eye] is like a reflection, they hear it said that the eye is like a reflection.
If there are those who should be delivered by means of the teaching that [the eye] is like an echo, they hear it said that the eye is like an echo.

If there are those who are to be delivered by means of such terms as emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, lack of volitional action, non-arising, and non-origination, then upon hearing what is taught, they understand that this eye is empty, signless, wishless, without volitional action, non-arisen, and unoriginated.
If there are those who should be delivered by means of the teaching on dependent origination, they hear this teaching on the eye as dependently originated.
Just as it is taught regarding the eye, so it is likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Furthermore, if there are those who should be delivered by means of the term "dependent origination," they hear that the meaning of what is taught is dependent origination;
the same applies to the meanings of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.

Some hear words concerning emptiness; some hear words concerning the impermanence of the five aggregates; some hear words concerning the impermanence of the eighteen elements; and some hear words concerning the impermanence of the twelve bases.
They may hear words concerning suffering, or words concerning its origin, or words concerning its cessation, or words concerning the path.

Or they may hear words concerning the four foundations of mindfulness, or words concerning the four right efforts, or words concerning the four bases of psychic power, or words concerning the five faculties, or words concerning the five powers, or words concerning the seven factors of enlightenment, or words concerning the eightfold noble path.
They may hear words concerning śamatha, or words concerning vipaśyanā;
they may hear words concerning the dharma of dependent origination;
they may hear words concerning the teachings associated with the śrāvakas, or words concerning the teachings associated with the pratyekabuddhas, or words concerning the Mahāyāna.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati! The wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata is turned for the sake of causing the minds of all sentient beings to rejoice.
Moreover, the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata extensively brings great benefit to all sentient beings."

Suppose there were someone whose wisdom was equal to that of Śāriputra, and they desired to deliberate upon and penetrate this Dharma; even after passing through a hundred kalpas, they would ultimately be unable to enter it, let alone anyone else.

Śāntamati, you should know that from the time the Tathāgata first undertook his practice, until he proceeded to the site of enlightenment, subdued the hosts of Māra, made a lion’s roar with supreme adornment, sported in supernatural powers, and turned the great wheel of Dharma—performing such acts of supreme benefit as these—eighty-four thousand people resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and immeasurable sentient beings attained maturity within the three vehicles.
Chapter Fifteen: The Chapter on Objects of Focus (Ālambana-varga), Part One. At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, teaches the Dharma, could there not be something in what I have said that contradicts what the Tathāgata has taught?
Or is it in accord with it?

What the Tathāgata has spoken is profound and vast; what the Tathāgata has spoken is profoundly secret, difficult for all the world to believe and difficult to understand, its source and depth unfathomable.
"Bhagavān! The minds of all Tathāgatas are true and definitive.

That I have any understanding or comprehension of the profound Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata is entirely due to the supreme wisdom of the Tathāgata residing within my body; it is not through any personal power or agency of my own."
The Buddha said: "Lord of Mysteries! So it is, so it is."
It is as you have said.

Why is this? You should now know that regarding all the dharmas which the Tathāgata establishes through analogies and expounds, every sentient being possesses within their own body the supreme wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Lord of Mysteries!

Because it is impossible for sentient beings, who pervade all places, to accord with the nature of reality (dharmatā) of the Tathāgata according to the secrets taught by the Tathāgata, without being sustained by the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment.
Furthermore, whether one hears, speaks of, or understands the profound secret Dharma taught by that Tathāgata, it is entirely due to the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
"Furthermore, Guhyapati!

When the Tathāgata speaks with right speech, you should know that the Tathāgata’s dharmatā is as it truly is and that the dharmatā is truly eternal; moreover, the Tathāgata’s conduct is as it truly is and that his conduct is truly eternal. Therefore, the Tathāgata, by means of right speech, teaches this true Dharma."
Furthermore, Lord of Mysteries!

All the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, have proclaimed, guided, and extensively revealed this true Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is difficult for all the worlds to believe and difficult to understand.

If those sentient beings, upon hearing such a profound and correct Dharma that is difficult to believe and difficult to understand, are able to immediately give rise to faith and understanding, you should know that these beings have not merely approached and served one or ten Buddhas; you should know they have already approached and served many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas. You should know that such persons are true sages who have diligently cultivated meritorious deeds.
Furthermore, Lord of Mysteries!
Even if Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, were to collapse, there might still be someone who could carry it upon their head or shoulders.

However, it is impossible for those sentient beings who have not planted roots of goodness to give rise to even a single moment of pure faith and understanding toward such a profound and true Dharma; how much less so to receive, uphold, read, recite, or practice it according to the teaching.
Furthermore, Guhyapati!

If there are sentient beings who, having heard the sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna, are able to believe and understand it, you should know that such persons have not merely attended upon and served a single Buddha; they have already attended upon and served many Buddhas, extensively cultivating supreme practices within the Mahāyāna Dharma and planting the seeds of roots of goodness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught the Dharma of cessation.”
"In what sense is this called 'stopping' (*upaśama*)?
From where does this stopping originate?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! What is called ‘stopping’ is a synonym for stopping the afflictions (*kleśa*).
This stopping of the afflictions is a synonym for stopping conceptualization, discrimination, and pervasive imagining (*parikalpa*)."
This "stopping of discursive thought, conceptualization, and pervasive imagining" is a synonym for the "stopping of ideation and mental attention.
This "stopping of ideation and mental attention" is a synonym for the "stopping of perversions."
This "stopping of inversion" is a designation for the stopping of causes and objects of perception;
this "stopping of causes and objects of perception" is a designation for the stopping of ignorance, existence, and craving.
This cessation of ignorance and craving for existence is itself the cessation of the designations "self" and "mine.
This cessation of "self" and "mine" is itself the cessation of the designation "name-and-form."
This "stopping of name-and-form" is a designation for the stopping of the views of eternalism and annihilationism.
This "stopping of the views of eternalism and annihilationism" is a designation for the stopping of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Śāntamati, you should know that if one is associated with views regarding the causes of objects of perception, then all afflictions will likewise follow and arise; all of them originate from the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
If one can bring the view of a self-identity to rest, then all views will cease.
If the view of a self-identity is brought to rest, then all desires and aspirations will likewise cease.
If the view of a self-body is stilled, then all afflictions are likewise stilled. Śāntamati!
It is like a great tree: if its root is severed, then its branches, leaves, stems, and trunk will all wither away.
This view of a self-identity is likewise so: if it is stilled, all afflictions are also stilled.
Śāntamati, you should know that because all sentient beings from the outset are unable to realize this view of a self-identity, the various grasping afflictions arise in its wake.
"If one can awaken to and realize the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), then the various afflictions of grasping will no longer arise in accordance with it, nor will they cause any harm.
The Bodhisattva Śāntamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Since they possess the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
how could they possibly awaken to it? The Buddha said, “Śāntamati!”
If one does not give rise to views such as those of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, one is then able to realize that [such] view of a personal identity exists.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!..."

That view of a self-existent body does not abide internally, nor does it abide externally; it does not abide at all in any place whatsoever. Because it does not abide, one perceives that there is nothing in which to abide.
Śāntamati! This wisdom of non-abiding correctly awakens to that view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, Śāntamati, you should know that the view of a self-existent body is a synonym for emptiness. If one can accord with the patience of the wisdom of emptiness, one sees that there is nothing to be grasped; this is precisely what it means to correctly awaken to that view of a self-existent body.

Furthermore, that which is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is precisely the view of signlessness, wishlessness, and non-action, and of non-arising and non-origination; this view has nothing to be grasped, and this is what constitutes the thorough and correct awakening to that view of a self-identity.

"Furthermore, Śāntamati, you should know that what is called the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is in fact no body; it is neither opened nor closed, for all such things are unreal conceptualizations."
Because that which is discriminated is unreal, it is itself non-discriminative, yet it is not separate from discrimination.
Because it is non-discriminative and not separate from discrimination, it is without activity, without obstruction, and without arising.
Because there is no arising, there is no activity.
Since there is no activity, this is what is called "stopping.
The Bodhisattva Śāntamati said:
“What is meant by ‘proximate tranquility’?
The Buddha said, “Śāntamati! [Listen.]”
A mind that has an object of perception is like a blazing fire; if it lacks an object of perception and lacks activity, it does not blaze. This state of non-blazing is called "proximate tranquility."

Furthermore, just as a great fire burns when there is fuel and extinguishes when there is no fuel, so too is the flame of the mind that takes an object: if there is no object, the fire of the mind naturally extinguishes itself.

Śāntamati, you should know that a bodhisattva endowed with skillful means, within the pure objects of focus of the *prajñāpāramitā*, understands with equanimity the superior dharmas that are the objects of roots of virtue and does not allow them to cease; he causes the defiled dharmas that are the objects of afflictions not to arise; he constantly causes the superior dharmas of the *pāramitās* to increase; he causes the defiled dharmas that are the objects of demonic activities and afflictions to be forever severed and extinguished; he does not abandon the pure objects of focus of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*); he does not grasp at the objects of focus of the inclinations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; he does not forsake the supreme object of focus, which is the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*); he thoroughly investigates the object of focus that is emptiness; and he deeply generates the aspiration and joy for the object of focus that is great compassion for all sentient beings.

Śāntamati, you should know that a bodhisattva endowed with skillful means attains mastery within the dharmas that are the objects of focus for the purity of the *prajñāpāramitā*; they attain certainty through the contemplation of non-arising as the object of focus, yet they do not weary of or abandon the arising of compounded phenomena as their object of focus.

They enter into the object of focus that is the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*), causing all roots of goodness that take conditioned activity as their object to be fully understood; they skillfully discern the object of focus that is signlessness (*animitta*), never becoming weary of the object of focus that is the bodhicitta; they correctly contemplate the object of focus that is wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) with wisdom, yet they do not give rise to weariness or detachment toward the object of focus that is the triple world.
By means of wisdom and skillful means, the bodhisattva operates with mastery within all objects of perception that are unborn.
If they perceive impure objects, they immediately abide in the pure body and mind of the Tathāgata.
If one takes impermanence as the object of focus, one dwells with a mind free from weariness regarding birth and death.
If one takes suffering as the object of focus, one brings happiness to all sentient beings and dwells with a mind of equanimity established in nirvana.
If there is no object of perception for "mine," one dwells in great compassion toward all sentient beings.
If there is an object of perception for greed, one dwells in the mind that clarifies through the pure great medicine among those sentient beings who act out of greed.
If there is an object of anger, one dwells with a mind clarified by the great medicine of loving-kindness toward those beings who act out of anger.
If there is an object of delusion, one dwells with a mind clarified by the great medicine of dependent origination toward those beings who act out of delusion.
If the object of focus is the balanced [defilements], one dwells with the mind illuminated by the great medicine of the perception of impermanence among sentient beings who act with balance.
If the object of focus is freedom from craving, one dwells with the mind transformed through the teachings of the Śrāvakas.
If one is free from the object-condition of hatred, the mind dwells in the cultivation and transformation of the dharmas of the Pratyekabuddhas.
If one is free from the object-condition of delusion, the mind dwells in the cultivation and transformation of the dharmas of the Bodhisattvas.
If the object of focus is form, the mind dwells upon attaining the supreme physical marks of a Tathāgata.
If the object of focus is sound, the mind dwells upon attaining the exquisite voice of a Tathāgata.
If the object of focus is fragrance, one dwells with a pure mind that has attained the Tathāgata’s fragrance of ethical discipline.
If the object of focus is flavor, one dwells with a pure mind that has attained the Tathāgata’s supreme flavor among all flavors—the mark of a Great Man.
If the object of focus is touch, the mind dwells upon attaining the exquisite, soft, and supple touch of the Tathāgata’s hands and feet.
If the object of focus is phenomena (*dharma*), the mind dwells with certainty upon attaining all the qualities possessed by the Tathāgata.
If the object of focus is generosity, one dwells with a mind intent on attaining the supreme marks of a Tathāgata.
If the object of focus is ethical discipline, one dwells with a mind intent on purifying the Buddha-field.
If one takes patience as the object of focus, one dwells in a pure mind regarding the attainment of the mark of the Brahma-voice and the wondrous golden-colored body.
If one takes diligence as the object of focus, one dwells in a mind intent on the deliverance of all sentient beings.
If the object of concentration is the focus, one dwells with a mind of wondrous application arising from the supernormal powers.
If the object of wisdom is the focus, one dwells with a mind that severs the continuity of all afflictions and views in all sentient beings.
If the object of focus is loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one dwells having given rise to a mind free from obstruction toward all sentient beings.
If the object of focus is compassion (*karuṇā*), one dwells having given rise to a mind that protects and upholds the true Dharma.
If one takes joy as the object of focus, one dwells with a mind that delights in teaching the Dharma.
If one takes equanimity as the object of focus, one dwells with a mind that remains detached from all things favorable or adverse and accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings.
If the objects of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are present, one dwells with the mind set on bringing all sentient beings to maturity.
From the *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśamahāyānasūtra*, Fascicle Twelve. From the *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśamahāyānasūtra*.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heavens, the Court Scattered Official, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of Sanskrit Transmission, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Dharmapāla and others, by Imperial Decree. Chapter Fifteen, Part Two: On the Objects of Perception. "Furthermore, Śāntamati!..."
If bodhisattvas wish to counteract the fault of stinginess by means of a focal object, they give rise to and abide in a mind that is capable of relinquishing all that they possess.
If they wish to counteract the fault of violating the precepts by means of a focal object, they give rise to and abide in a mind that upholds the precepts.
If, as an antidote to the fault of malice, one dwells by giving rise to a mind of firm patience;
if, as an antidote to the fault of indolence, one dwells by giving rise to a mind that accomplishes the supreme powers of the Tathāgata through diligence.
If, as an object for counteracting the fault of distraction, one gives rise to the mental abiding that attains the meditative concentration of the Tathāgata;
and if, as an object for counteracting the fault of defiled wisdom, one gives rise to the mental abiding of perfected, unimpeded knowledge.
If one takes the mental attention of a śrāvaka as the object of focus, one immediately gives rise to and abides in a mind that accumulates the Mahāyāna.
If one takes renunciation as the object of focus, one immediately gives rise to and abides in a mind that refrains from all transgressions.
If the object of focus is the miserable realms (*durgati*), one dwells in the mind that arises in each moment to rescue those within the various miserable realms.
If the mental attention (*manasikāra*) has the celestial realms as its object, one dwells in the mind regarding the final limit of both their formation and destruction.
If one takes the human realm as the object of mental attention, one dwells having given rise to a mind that perceives it as unstable.
If one takes mindfulness of the Buddha as the object of mental attention, one dwells having given rise to a mind that perceives being sustained by all Buddhas.
If one takes the mental attention on mindfulness of the Dharma as the object of focus, one dwells having given rise to a mind that is ungrudging regarding the Dharma.
If one takes the mental attention on mindfulness of the Saṅgha as the object of focus, one dwells having given rise to a mind that has attained non-retrogression from the wheel of Dharma.
If one takes the mental attention of mindfulness of relinquishment as the object, there arises the dwelling of the mind that is capable of relinquishing everything.

If one takes the mental attention of mindfulness of ethical discipline as the object, there arises the dwelling of the mind characterized by the factors of enlightenment of the sublime concentration that fulfills one's aspirations.

If one takes the mental attention directed toward the recollection of the devas as the object of focus, one dwells with a mind that gives rise to the praise of the Buddhas' wisdom and their sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
If one takes the mental attention directed toward the body as the object of focus, one dwells with a mind that gives rise to the attainment of the purity of the Buddha-body.
If one takes the mental attention directed toward speech as the object of focus, one immediately gives rise to the dwelling of a mind that has attained the purity of the speech of all Buddhas.
If one takes the mental attention directed toward the mind as the object of focus, one immediately gives rise to the dwelling of a mind that has attained the purity of the Buddha’s equanimous mind.
If one takes conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as the object of focus, one abides in the mind that gives rise to the perfected wisdom of the Tathāgata.
If one takes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) as the object of focus, one abides in the mind that gives rise to the perfected Buddha-wisdom.

"Śāntamati, you should know that although these and other such states may have objects of focus, there are no bodhisattvas who do not abide within the dharma-gate of the manifestation of the knowledge of all-knowledge."

Furthermore, when all bodhisattvas dedicate all objects of focus toward awakening, this is precisely what is called a bodhisattva’s skillful means for realizing all phenomena and penetrating them through observation.
Śāntamati! For example, just as all the great earth throughout the entire trichiliocosm is, according to its various productions, a place for the enjoyment of all sentient beings without exception.

Those bodhisattvas are likewise in this regard: among all objects of focus, there is none that is not a factor of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) shared by bodhisattvas through their skillful means (upāyakauśalya), and there is none that does not bring the dharmas of the path to enlightenment to maturity.
Furthermore, just as all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), so too is the bodhisattva skilled in means:
whatever objects of focus (*ālambana*) they may have, they are all harmonized and conjoined with the supreme characteristics of enlightenment (*bodhi*).
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!
If there are sentient beings who are stingy and engage in evil deeds, the Bodhisattva then brings to perfection for them the pāramitā of generosity and the pāramitā of ethical discipline."
If sentient beings give rise to conduct of anger and indolence, the bodhisattva thereby fulfills the perfection of patience and the perfection of diligence.

If sentient beings give rise to distracted minds and engage in deluded conduct, the bodhisattva thereby brings to perfection the pāramitā of meditative concentration and the pāramitā of transcendent wisdom.
If there are sentient beings who cannot be pitied, the bodhisattva harbors no thought of hostility or harm toward them.
If there are sentient beings who should be benefited, the bodhisattva harbors no thought of mere compliance toward them.
If sentient beings constantly praise him, the bodhisattva harbors no sense of superiority toward them;
if sentient beings do not praise him, the bodhisattva likewise harbors no sense of inferiority toward them.
If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who are afflicted by all manner of suffering and distress, they immediately give rise to a mind of great compassion.
If they see sentient beings who possess all manner of happiness, they immediately give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
If a bodhisattva sees any beings who are coarse and unruly, they immediately give rise to a mind of subduing them.
If they see any beings who are disciplined and compliant, they immediately give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
If a Bodhisattva sees sentient beings who possess the power of conditions (*pratyaya*), they immediately give rise to a mind of protection.

If they see sentient beings who possess the power of causes (*hetu*), they immediately give rise to a mind of gathering and transforming them; having gathered and transformed them accordingly, they then provide instruction.
If he sees sentient beings whose wisdom is clear and enlightened, the bodhisattva immediately proclaims for them the most profound Dharma.
If he sees sentient beings who possess the wisdom of eloquent exposition, the bodhisattva immediately expounds the Dharma extensively for them.
If the Bodhisattva perceives sentient beings who accord with the principle, he then teaches them the Dharma in successive stages.
If he perceives sentient beings who delight in and cling to words and phrases, the Bodhisattva then teaches them the Dharma using concise and abbreviated expressions.
If a bodhisattva perceives that sentient beings delight in taking śamatha as their precursor, he then teaches them vipaśyanā.
If he perceives that sentient beings delight in taking vipaśyanā as their precursor, he then teaches them the methods for entering samādhi.
If he sees sentient beings who delight in upholding the precepts, the Bodhisattva first proclaims for them the non-definitive teachings, and subsequently speaks to them of matters such as the hells.
If he sees sentient beings who delight in extensive learning, he immediately proclaims for them the teachings that are free from doubt.
If he sees sentient beings who delight in samādhi, he immediately proclaims for them the Dharma for entering into wisdom.
If he sees sentient beings who delight in dwelling in the wilderness, he immediately proclaims for them the Dharma of mental tranquility.
If he sees sentient beings who delight in practicing the dhūta austerities, he immediately expounds for them the Dharma of the faculty of noble wisdom.
If he sees sentient beings of dull faculties, he immediately expounds for them the Dharma that accords with hearing.
If they see sentient beings who are firmly attached to the dharma of greed, they immediately proclaim for them the dharma of impurity.
If they see sentient beings who are firmly attached to the dharma of hatred, they immediately proclaim for them the dharma of loving-kindness.
If he sees sentient beings who are stubbornly attached to the phenomena of delusion, he immediately expounds for them the teaching of dependent origination.

If he sees sentient beings whose [three poisons] are in equal measure, he enters into their midst and extensively teaches the Dharma, namely: the teaching on impurity, the teaching on loving-kindness, and the teaching on dependent origination.

If there are those who are to be delivered according to the various dharmas that accord with them, the bodhisattva then proclaims for them the dharma of higher ethical discipline, the dharma of higher mind, and the dharma of higher wisdom.

If he sees sentient beings who should be delivered by means of the Buddha’s supreme marks, he immediately proclaims for them the true dharmas that accord with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
If he sees sentient beings who should be delivered by means of subduing their arrogance, he first closes the door to arrogance and subsequently teaches them the Dharma.

If a bodhisattva perceives that sentient beings who continue to delight in observing the noble marks of a bodhisattva, he will constantly manifest his body for them; however, he does not preach the Dharma to those whose faculties are not yet mature.
If he sees sentient beings who delight in skillful teachings and are ready to be delivered, he explains the Dharma by means of analogies based on dependent origination.

If he sees sentient beings who delight in the profound Dharma and are ready to be delivered, he proclaims for them the teaching that all phenomena are dependently arisen, devoid of self, devoid of a person, and devoid of a sentient being.
If there are sentient beings who are attached to various views, he preaches the Dharma of emptiness for them.
If he perceives sentient beings who give rise to seeking and practice, he immediately proclaims the Dharma of signlessness for them.
If one sees sentient beings giving rise to seeking and aspiration, one immediately proclaims for them the Dharma of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
If one sees sentient beings attached to the aggregates (*skandha*), one immediately proclaims for them the Dharma of being like an illusion (*māyopama*).
If he sees sentient beings attached to the various elements (*dhātu*), he immediately proclaims for them the Dharma of skillful discernment.
If he sees sentient beings attached to the various sense bases (*āyatana*), he immediately proclaims for them the Dharma that they are like dreams.
If he sees sentient beings attached to the desire realm, he immediately proclaims for them the teaching on affliction.
If he sees sentient beings attached to the form realm, he immediately proclaims for them the teaching on the suffering of conditioned formations.
If he sees sentient beings attached to the formless realm, he immediately proclaims for them the teaching that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
If he sees sentient beings who should be delivered by means of the dharma of suffering, he immediately proclaims it for them, causing them to give rise to joy within the noble lineages.
If he sees sentient beings who delight in the Dharma of happiness and are to be delivered thereby, he preaches for them the methods of immeasurable meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
If he sees sentient beings who delight in the dharmas of the heavenly realms and are to be delivered thereby, he immediately proclaims for them the exclusively joyful Dharma.
If he sees sentient beings who delight in and are attached to various marks and are thus ready for deliverance, he teaches them the Dharma of non-self and non-appropriation.
If he sees sentient beings who delight in the Śrāvaka Dharma and are thus ready for deliverance, he immediately instructs them in the methods for attaining realization.

If he sees sentient beings who should be delivered by means of the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas because they delight in it, he immediately proclaims for them the Dharma that is concise in both its phenomena and its meaning.

If he sees sentient beings who should be delivered by means of the Dharma of Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds, he immediately proclaims for them the Dharma of generating the profound mind and great compassion.

If one perceives sentient beings who delight in the long-term cultivation of the bodhisattva path and are ready to be delivered, one then proclaims for them the dharma of being free from weariness within saṃsāra.
If he sees sentient beings who should be delivered by means of the Dharma of non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, he immediately proclaims for them the Dharma of purifying the Buddha-fields.

If he sees sentient beings who should be delivered by means of the Dharma of bodhisattvas in their final birth before enlightenment, he immediately proclaims for them the Dharma of adorning the Great Bodhimanda.
If he perceives sentient beings who would be liberated by delighting in the Buddha-body, he teaches them the dharma of the continuous and non-empty sublime practices of a bodhisattva.

Śāntamati, you should know that all such dharmas are those of great bodhisattvas who possess both wisdom and skillful means, and who have attained mastery within those pure objects of focus; therefore, they extensively teach the dharma of non-emptiness.
The dharma they teach is spoken for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to rejoice.

When this Dharma was being taught, ten thousand people in the assembly gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and five thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Chapter Sixteen: The Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Mahāguhyapati Vajrapāṇi, Part One. At that time, there were bodhisattvas within the assembly who all had this thought:
"How long will it be before this Bodhisattva Mahāguhyapati Vajrapāṇi attains the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
What shall be the name of the Buddha-land where you dwell?
What shall be the name of the Buddha when you have attained enlightenment?
How many shall be the members of your retinue, and how complete shall they be?

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, immediately smiled. It is the natural law that when all Buddhas manifest a smile, there must be a cause and condition.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from his face a vast radiance of various colors—namely blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, and green—which universally illuminated boundless worlds up to the Brahma realm. These multicolored rays of light circled back to the Buddha’s presence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and entered through the crown of the World-Honored One’s head.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati, with palms joined in reverent devotion before the Buddha, inquired with these sublime verses:
“Your golden light is wondrous and stainless; Your tranquil moon-like face is steadfast and serene.
Supreme sun of radiance, you who dispel the darkness— O Sage among Men, for what reason do you now smile?”
Abiding peacefully in the lotus posture of meditative concentration, with the roar of great compassion increasing the power of progress,
and perfumed by the wondrous fragrance of mindfulness, wisdom, and merit— O Sugata, why do you smile from the lotus?
Mindfulness is like a pure vessel, concentration like oil; with compassion as the wick, one lights the lamp to destroy the three defilements.
With the brilliant light of sublime wisdom, the darkness is extinguished—O Sugata, for what reason do you smile with the radiance of your wisdom?
With the light of the wheel of compassion and the wisdom of observation, you have stilled the three impurities and extinguished all darkness;
having purified and opened the eye of knowledge to benefit the world, O Buddha-Sun of wondrous radiance, for what reason do you smile?
The Buddha knows the thoughts of the world of the three realms of existence; his light universally illumines the hearts of all devas and humans.
With eyes of great compassion, the Great Sage gazes upon sentient beings: why does the Great Sage now manifest a smile?
When the Bodhisattva Śāntamati had finished speaking these verses,
the World-Honored One then addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati, saying: “Now this Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets,

has served as a vajra-wielder in the presence of all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of this Bhadrakalpa, performing acts of offering and protecting the True Dharma with a mind of benefit.”
Now, within this secret dharma of mine, you shall perform vast deeds for the sake of all immeasurable sentient beings, universally ripening their roots of virtue for supreme enlightenment.
When they have vanished within the Dharma of the final Tathāgata, Ruci, during this Bhadrakalpa, they will be reborn in the Buddha-field of Akṣobhya Tathāgata in the world-system of Sukhāvatī.

In that world, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya expounded the one hundred and eight secret mudrās for those bodhisattvas; at that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, upon hearing what was taught, entered into their meaning and intent without relying on further application of effort, practicing in accordance with reality as it truly is.

Thereafter, he again drew near to, honored, revered, and made offerings to immeasurable and incalculable Tathāgatas; in the presence of each of those Buddhas, he cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and upheld the True Dharma, extensively bringing immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings to maturity in the dharma of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Thereafter, he further passed through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, fulfilling the factors of enlightenment, and subsequently attained the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. He appeared in the world as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Vajrapada (Vajra-step), the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
The world is named Universal Purity, and the eon is named Pure.

Śāntamati! Within that Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Vajrapadavikrama in the world Universal Purity, it is peaceful, prosperous, joyful, adorned, pure, and beautiful to behold; gods and humans abound, bodhisattvas are numerous, and it is perfectly endowed with the seven treasures in exquisite adornment.
The seven treasures—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, and ruby—abound and fill that world in every direction.
The ground may be measured at eight paces, as level as the palm of a hand, soft and supple like *kācilindika* cloth, and endowed with every pleasant touch.

Wondrous banners and standards are erected, interlaced with jeweled cords; exquisite celestial flowers hang down everywhere, and the most sublime, refined fragrances permeate the air. Music spontaneously plays from the sky; there are no evil realms or manifold perils, and the enjoyments are as supreme as those in Tuṣita Heaven.

Furthermore, in that world, everything one might conceive of—palaces, mansions, gardens, pavilions, food, drink, clothing, and various articles of adornment—is fully provided according to their needs; all these are no different from those enjoyed by devas and humans.
The devas and humans there possess great faith and understanding, and they have deep faith in the Buddha's wisdom.

Furthermore, in that world, even the names of the two vehicles—the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—are never heard; the Dharma taught by that Buddha consists solely of the pure and sublime teachings for Mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, that Tathāgata Vajrapada has a vast retinue of hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas.

Moreover, in that world, the code of discipline is not impaired, lifespans do not diminish, ethical conduct is not broken, and right view is never lost. There are also none who are insane, deaf, mute, lame, hunchbacked, or stammering; nor are there those who are cruel, combative, or deficient in their faculties. All beings are adorned with the twenty-eight kinds of supreme marks of gods and humans.
That Tathāgata’s lifespan was eight intermediate kalpas, and there were no gods or humans who met with untimely death.
Śāntamati, you should know that such were the immeasurable and supreme qualities and deeds of that Tathāgata Vajrapada, as well as others beyond measure.

Whenever that Buddha, the World-Honored One, desired to preach the Dharma, he would immediately emit rays of light; upon seeing this light, those sentient beings would know that the Tathāgata was proclaiming the sublime Dharma.

If there are sentient beings who conceive the mutual desire to go to the Buddha’s abode to behold him and listen to the Dharma, they shall immediately arrive at the Buddha’s presence through the empowerment of that Buddha’s supernatural powers and wisdom; or some may arrive at the Buddha’s presence by means of their own supernatural power, whereupon the great assembly of devas and humans will all gather together.

At that time, the World-Honored One leaped into the air to a height of one hundred thousand *tāla* trees; all four great continents beheld the vast physical marks of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, his voice resounded, manifesting the pure and wondrous sound of the Tathāgata, which brought joy and satisfaction to all sentient beings who heard it.

Furthermore, when the Tathāgata expounds the True Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas, not a single sentient being contradicts the Dharma he proclaims; all those sentient beings possess sharp faculties and are capable of understanding through clear insight.
Furthermore, that world has no king; there is only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Vajrapada Tathāgata, the Supreme Dharma King.
Moreover, all sentient beings in that world are without self and without grasping.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!

Moreover, when that Tathāgata Vajrapada went forth to beg for alms among the devas and humans in that realm, at that time, whether they were devas or humans, they would see the holy image of the Tathāgata standing before them, holding an alms bowl."

Having beheld the holy image, those devas and humans each desired to offer the Tathāgata pure food and drink, as well as bedding and seating according to their wishes and preferences; they prepared all manner of delicacies, numbering in the hundreds, and made every arrangement complete.
That Buddha, knowing the proper time, accepted the offerings as they were presented.
Having received the offerings, the Buddha immediately left the house and returned to the monastery where the Tathāgata resided; the assembly of bodhisattvas likewise entered samādhi accordingly.

“Śāntamati, you should know that the world-system in which that Buddha-Tathāgata resides is endowed with these and other immeasurable, supreme qualities; therefore, it is named the World-System of Universal Purity.”
