The Sixteenth Chapter, “The Prophecy of the Bodhisattva Mahāguhyapati Vajrapāṇi,” Part Two: At that time, when the World-Honored One was bestowing the prophecy upon the Bodhisattva Mahāguhyapati Vajrapāṇi, twenty thousand people within the assembly gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, all vowing to be born in the land of the Tathāgata Vajrapada within that world-system of Universal Purity.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, having heard the World-Honored Buddha bestow this prediction upon him, felt a sense of joy and exhilaration; filled with great delight, he immediately cast his vajra into the midst of space.

When he playfully cast the vajra, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways; the heavens rained down various flowers and drums played music, and furthermore, from the right hands of all those in the assembly, there spontaneously emerged various exquisite and supreme flower garlands of wondrous colors.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, joined his palms with sincere devotion before the Buddha and spoke these verses:
"O Great Dharma King of vast and expansive reach, Inexhaustible treasury of wondrous Dharma,
Desiring to benefit the world, You skillfully discern all phenomena."
Having already abandoned all thoughts of stinginess regarding all phenomena,
practicing in accordance with and relying upon the Dharma, I take refuge in the one who abides well therein.
To the Buddha, the Great Being of purity, whose conduct is perfectly pure, I pay homage.
The fame of the King of Merit is heard throughout the three realms;
Able to constantly maintain inexhaustible wisdom within the three periods of time,
His virtuous conduct is impartial— homage to him who is without obstruction.
The moonlight is most perfectly round and pure; All-pervading purity, further refined and clear.
The sunlight is most brilliantly radiant; A sublime light, a supreme mass of radiance.
The Brahma-voice is most wondrously melodic; A pure sound with profound and subtle resonance.
The Triple Gem is of supreme golden light; therefore, I now prostrate to it.
It constantly manifests a pure and wondrous body, yet is not bound by a physical form;
it constantly utters sublime speech, yet is free from the conceptualization of words.
Though he is a great Dharma Master, he does not give rise to the notion of "Dharma";
he liberates all sentient beings, yet has no notion of "sentient beings.
What can the world do to repay the great kindness of the Buddha?
Among all meritorious benefits, none can repay [the Buddha] as well as going forth from the household life.
Those who hear the Buddha’s instructions find no other dharma to turn toward;
according to the Dharma-gate they have received, they should practice authentically in accordance with the principle.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, together with all the other members of the assembled multitude, each scattered various exquisite flower garlands over the Buddha.

By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the flower garlands he scattered immediately pervaded this trichiliocosm, appearing everywhere as a magnificent array of exquisite floral ornaments surrounding it all, piled up to a height of eight paces.

Chapter Seventeen: Non-duality and Non-discourse. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati approached the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, and addressed him, saying: "Lord of Secrets!"
“Has the World-Honored Tathāgata bestowed a prediction of enlightenment upon you,
O Noble One? Vajrapāṇi replied,
“O Son of Good Family!”
"The Buddha has bestowed upon me a prediction [of enlightenment], which is like the nature of a dream. Śāntamati asked:
"Now that you have received this prediction, what have you attained?"
Vajrapāṇi said: “Because there is nothing to be attained, I have received the prophecy. Śāntamati said:
“What phenomena are not apprehended? Vajrapāṇi replied:

“The self, the person, the sentient being, and the life-span are all not apprehended; those aggregates, bases, and elements are also not apprehended. Furthermore, whether wholesome or unwholesome, with fault or faultless, with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned, defiled or pure, birth-and-death or nirvāṇa—all are not apprehended.”
Śāntamati said: "If dharmas are non-apprehendable, how can there be a prophecy within them? Vajrapāṇi replied:
“Because there is nothing to be apprehended, one receives the prediction of enlightenment within this very state through the wisdom of thorough penetration. Śāntamati asked:
“How could there be two kinds of wisdom to be observed?”
Vajrapāṇi said: "If there were two things to be perceived, then no prophecy could be received.
However, because that wisdom has no duality to be perceived, it is for this reason that all bodhisattvas receive such a prophecy within non-dual wisdom."
Śāntamati said: "If wisdom is such that no duality can be observed, how then can there be a predictor and that which is predicted? Vajrapāṇi replied:
"Whether it be that which predicts or that which is predicted, by way of their equality, nothing at all is apprehended within the non-dual limit.
Vimalakīrti said: "Lord of Secrets!"
"How can there be a prediction within the non-dual limit? Vajrapāṇi replied:
"If that limit is thus, it is itself the non-dual limit."
"It is precisely within that very limit that such a prophecy is thus bestowed."寂慧 (Jikhyi) asked:
"What is meant by 'limit'?"
"Furthermore, in what state is one granted the prediction of enlightenment?

Vajrapāṇi replied, "One is granted the prediction in the state of the limit of the self; one is granted the prediction in the state of the limit of sentient beings, the limit of the life-principle, and the limit of the person."
Śāntamati asked:
"Furthermore, where does the locus of my limit reside? Vajrapāṇi replied:
"The sphere of the limit of self is precisely the sphere of the limit of the Tathāgata’s liberation. Śāntamati asked:
"In what place does the sphere of the limit of the Tathāgata’s liberation reside?"
Vajrapāṇi said: “The limit of liberation of the Tathāgata resides at the limit of ignorance and craving. Śāntamati asked:
“Where, furthermore, does the limit of ignorance and the craving for existence reside? Vajrapāṇi replied,
“It resides at the limit where there is ultimately no birth and no arising.”
Śāntamati said: "Where, then, does the limit of ultimate non-arising and non-origination reside? Vajrapāṇi replied:
"In a place where there is no manifestation," Śāntamati said,
"if there is no manifestation, what is being revealed?"
Vajrapāṇi said: "If there were any disclosure, it would not be non-manifestation. Śāntamati said:
"What is meant by 'no disclosure'? Vajrapāṇi replied:
"All that is indicated is entirely without disclosure."
Śāntamati said: "If there is no revealing instruction, how can there be a teaching? Vajrapāṇi replied:
"If there is an instruction, there is no revelation; if there is no revelation, there is no instruction."寂慧 (Jikhyi) said:
"How can one obtain an instruction?"
Vajrapāṇi said: "Although there is manifestation, there is nothing that is apprehended. Śāntamati said:
“What is meant by ‘manifesting clearly while having nothing to receive’?
Vajrapāṇi replied, “If one does not cling to words and letters, then there is nothing to receive.”
Śāntamati asked, "How does one not cling to words? Vajrapāṇi replied:
"It means 'conforming to the meaning.
Śāntamati asked: "In what way, then, does it mean 'conforming to the meaning'?"
Vajrapāṇi said: "It means that within the very meaning, there is nothing to be seen. Śāntamati said:
"How is it that there is no perception of meaning? Vajrapāṇi replied:
"Whether it be meaning or non-meaning, neither can be found when sought within this."
Śāntamati said: "If neither meaning nor non-meaning can be found when sought, then what is there to be sought? Vajrapāṇi replied:
"Because neither the meaningful nor the meaningless can be found through seeking, there is no dharma that can be sought.
Śāntamati said: "If there is no dharma that can be sought, is it then the case that there is nothing whatsoever to be sought?"
Vajrapāṇi said: “In this, there is not even the slightest dharma to be sought. Why is that?
"Because no dharma can be sought, dharmas are themselves non-dharmas. Śāntamati asked:
"In this context, what is called 'dharma'?"
Vajrapāṇi said: "If even the sound of dharmas cannot be apprehended, how could there be any dharma therein?
O son of good family!"

Thus it should be understood: if one speaks of "dharmas," it means not being attached to nor engaging with words and letters; therefore, it is said that all dharmas are beyond speech and beyond description.
"Good son! If someone says that there is something spoken, that is not speaking.
Because it is not speaking, it is neither a phenomenon nor is it in accordance with reality."
Śāntamati said: "Lord of Secrets!
If that is so, would it not be the case that all the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are also not spoken?"
Vajrapāṇi said: “Śāntamati! Have I not already told you before that the Blessed Tathāgata does not speak a single syllable?”

Because there is no speaking, the Tathāgata, by means of his supernatural powers and the power of his vows, manifests as if there were something spoken in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings.
Jihui said, “If there were indeed speaking, what fault would there be?”
Vajrapāṇi said: "To have something spoken constitutes a fault of verbal karma. Śāntamati said:
“What further fault is there in that vocal action?
Vajrapāṇi replied, “The fault of conceptualizing and clinging to syllables.”
Śāntamati asked, "How,
furthermore, can one be free from faults? Vajrapāṇi replied:

"Among all phenomena, whether there is something spoken or nothing spoken, there is not the slightest phenomenon that can be expressed or made known; because there is nothing to be expressed or made known, one is free from faults."
Furthermore, he neither reveals anything concerning himself nor is he subject to faults.”寂慧 (Jihui) asked:
“What is the root of those faults?”
Vajrapāṇi said: "That fault has grasping as its root. Śāntamati said:
“What is the root of grasping?
Vajrapāṇi replied, “Attachment is its root.”
Śāntamati asked: "What is the root of attachment? Vajrapāṇi replied:
"False conceptualization is the root. Śāntamati asked:
"What is the root of false conceptualization?"
Vajrapāṇi said: "The vision of the superior object of focus is the foundation. Śāntamati said:
"What is the basis of the superior objective referent (adhipatālambana)? Vajrapāṇi replied:
"Form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena (dharmas) are themselves the basis of the superior objective referent."
Sila said: "In what way is there no object of focus? Vajrapāṇi replied:
"When craving is not continuous, there is no object of perception.
Śāntamati, you should know that as the Buddha has taught: among all phenomena, if craving is severed, there is no object of perception."

When the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, had spoken this Dharma, five hundred bhikṣus in the assembly attained liberation of mind, and two hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

18. Chapter on Entering the Great City of the Wilderness and Receiving the Food Offering, Part One of Eighteen. At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, having had his aspirations fulfilled and received the prophecy, felt comforted in his heart and was filled with great joy, exultation, and delight. He stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”

"I now earnestly entreat the World-Honored One to descend to my secret palace where I dwell, to accept a modest offering for a full seven days, and I also invite the assembly of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas."
I pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will graciously accept my invitation. Why is this?
World-Honored One!

Within the great city of the wilderness dwell many beings of diverse species—yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, gandharvas, mahoragas, and others—who, having seen the Buddha, shall obtain benefit and peace for a long night, and have their harsh, resentful, and malevolent minds stilled;
furthermore, they shall cause the four great kings and their retinues to obtain great benefit and abide in security for a long night.

If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, would deign to descend to my palace out of compassion for me, and if the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas would accept this modest offering, it would cause immeasurable classes of sentient beings to increase their roots of goodness and fulfill the aspirations of ourselves as well.
The Buddha then accepted his request by remaining silent.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, knowing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had silently accepted the invitation, felt great joy and leaped for delight. He immediately prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and quickly departed from the assembly to return to his own dwelling in the great city of Kāpila-vastu.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, having arrived at his own palace, gave rise to this thought:
"How shall I now arrange offerings?

Furthermore, by what kind of realm and adornments shall I embellish it, so as to cause the hosts of devaputras of the desire and form realms to conceive a sense of wonder, and to cause all the great bodhisattvas gathered from the worlds of the ten directions to feel great joy, while I too perform wondrous acts of vast offering for the Buddha?"
Having formed this thought, he immediately recollected:
"In the past, at one time, during the night, the Buddha entered a samādhi named 'Tranquil, Inconceivable, and Vast Conduct,' and I also followed the Buddha and entered that same concentration."

To the east, having passed from here as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, one arrives at a world named Boundless Merit Jewel Adornment; there resides a Tathāgata named King of Adornments.
In that buddha-field, the World-Honored One, the Master of Transformation, bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon ten thousand bodhisattvas.
At that time, I beheld that buddha-field, adorned with inconceivable gods and humans, surpassing all other matters of exquisite adornment.
"I should adorn myself according to the characteristics of the adornments of that world-arrayed-with-jewels-of-boundless-merit, and I shall perform an act of worship for the World-Honored One."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, entered the samādhi of the King of Great Adornments; while within that samādhi, he contemplated according to reality and beheld the various exquisite and wonderful adornments of that World Adorned with Boundless Jewels of Merit.
Just as he had visualized it, he exercised his supernormal power to arrange and adorn this great city in the wilderness so that it was no different from that world.

That world of Boundless Merit Adorned with Jewels was sixty-four *yojanas* in length, breadth, and height, equal on all four sides—east, west, south, and north. Its ground was made of blue lapis lazuli, its walls were constructed of great *indranīla* jewels, and it was adorned with hanging pearl garlands and various precious ornaments. There were lotuses made of Jāmbūnada gold, with branches and leaves of various jewels interspersed and draped with jeweled necklaces.

Furthermore, there were countless exquisite celestial robes made of precious jewels; countless necklaces and ornaments of pearls and gems; and countless exquisite silken fabrics. Hanging from these were countless wonderful flower garlands, incense, ointments, and various precious vases. Additionally, countless flowers of diverse colors were scattered all around, so that anyone who beheld them found them exquisitely pleasing to the mind, bringing joy and harmonious tranquility to both body and heart.
There appeared a mass of jewels of boundless merit, further manifesting as infinite colors and forms of adornment.

Moreover, there were many hundreds of thousands of exquisite lion thrones with vast adornments; jeweled pedestals supported the feet, and precious cords were interlaced. Adorned with jewel flowers and draped with nets of pearls, they were piled up all around to a height of eight paces.
Furthermore, countless celestial garments were spread out, and from the sky there hung canopies of jeweled nets.
Such various and wondrous adornments had never before been seen nor heard of in other vast and numerous worlds.
Furthermore, he prepared a hundred kinds of exquisite, rare, and superior delicacies for food and drink.

He also arranged and displayed hundreds of thousands of magnificent lion thrones in the air; upon each lion throne, a wondrous jewel canopy appeared spontaneously in mid-air, each hanging down to provide coverage, exquisitely adorned and complete with all sublime characteristics.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, while in meditative absorption, arranged such sublime and excellent signs.

Having established and adorned the lion throne, he arose from his concentration. When the night had passed and it was morning, having prepared the most supreme and pure food, with a deeply purified mind, he intended to make offerings to the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, and the assembly of bodhisattvas.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla, the Great Master of Fan (Sanskrit-Chinese) and Saṃgha of Purple Robes, Subject and Court Scattered Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, under Imperial Decree, during the Western Heaven Translation Bureau. The Eighteenth Chapter, "Entering the Great City of the Wilderness and Receiving Food," Part Two. At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, having passed the night, addressed the Four Great Heavenly Kings, saying:
"O virtuous ones!..."

"You should know this: I have now invited the Buddha, along with the great bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas, to descend into my secret palace where I dwell, so that for a full seven days I may extend a modest offering;
and because the World-Honored Buddha compassionately takes pity on me, he has accepted my invitation."

Each of you possesses power and capability and has many followers; for seven days and nights, do not give way to negligence, do not allow your minds to become distracted, and furthermore, set aside all other activities and devote yourselves with single-minded diligence to making offerings to the Buddha.

"Furthermore, you must inform all the yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, gandharvas, mahoragas, and all other classes of sentient beings dwelling in this great city of the wilderness, saying by my command: 'You all should know.'"
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva has requested that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, descend here to this great city of Āṭavī for a period of seven days to receive offerings.

You all should restrain all malice and evil, give rise to a pure mind, and further cultivate a sense of vast joy; you must make solemn offerings to the World-Honored One and listen to the True Dharma.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, addressed his eldest son Vajrasena, saying:

"Worthy one! You should now, by means of your own supernatural power, go to that Brahma realm; from the Heaven of the Brahma Assembly up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, you must address each of those devas, saying:"

“Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, the Great Lord of Secrets, requested the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to descend to the secret palace of the great city of Kāśmīra, where he would perform acts of offering for a period of seven days.”
"You gods who wish to see the Buddha should come here quickly.
At that time, Vajrasena, the eldest son of the Lord of Secrets, received his father’s command and acted exactly as instructed.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, again addressed his second son, Subāhu, saying: "Worthy one!

You should now, by means of your own supernatural power, go from the earth-dwelling devas to the sky-dwelling devas—namely, the Cāturmahārājika, Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens—and speak to each of those devas as follows:"

"Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, requested the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to descend into the secret palace of the great city of Āṭavī, where he would perform acts of offering for a period of seven days."
"You gods who wish to see the Buddha should come here quickly.
At that time, the second son, Subāhu, received his father’s command and acted accordingly.

At that moment, in an instant, there appeared vast and countless hundreds of thousands of devaputras from the desire realm and the form realm, filling the air for an extent of hundreds of thousands of yojanas on all sides.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, having passed the night and prepared a most exquisitely adorned bed for the World-Honored One, knelt with his right knee on the ground. With palms joined in sincere devotion toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he spoke these sublime verses as a respectful invitation:
"Welcome, O Most Victorious Honored One among Men! Welcome, O Unsurpassed Being among Men!
O Most Exalted among Men, we pray you descend; O Buddha, Great Muni, the time has come."
Welcome, most excellent among two-legged beings; welcome, supreme among two-legged beings.
O preeminent among two-legged beings, please deign to descend; Great Muni, Buddha, the time has come.

Born from the pure precepts of the Buddha’s great lotus, Constantly nourished by the waters of diligence and concentration, Like bees gathering nectar, you are the refuge of all; O Lotus of Tranquility, we pray that you descend.
First establishing the Four Noble Truths, observing all with eyes of compassion,
ever able to roar the sound of selflessness— O Great Lion Buddha, we pray that you descend upon us.
With precepts as its root and mindfulness as its trunk, The flowers of the factors of enlightenment bloom in constant profusion;
The fruit of the wisdom of liberation is already perfect and complete— O Great King of Trees, the Buddha, we pray that you descend upon us.
Sublime wisdom, profound and vast, Serene waters of meditative concentration, universally cool;
Great Teacher whose manifold practices are perfected and radiant— O Buddha, ocean of merit, we pray that you descend.
Embodiment of auspiciousness accomplished through great compassion, Magnificently adorned by the light of great wisdom,
The blooming lotus to which all beings turn for awakening— May the Buddha-Sun, with its radiant light, descend here.
With right speech you quelled all heterodox doctrines; as a medicinal tree of liberation, you rescued those afflicted by chronic illness.
Even the deer of small faculties were fully enlightened; O Great Mountain King, Buddha, we pray that you descend upon us.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having accepted the sincere and earnest invitation of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, and knowing that the time had come, addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"You should all put on your robes, take up your bowls, and go to attend the invitation of Vajrapāṇi; you shall perform the rites of offering for a period of seven days."
"Excellent! Go now; this is precisely the right time.
He then entrusted those who were guarding the monasteries, saying:

"Within this assembly, all those bodhisattvas and śrāvakas who have already attained supernatural powers shall each travel through the air by means of their own spiritual power, as is appropriate for them."
"Furthermore, those who have not yet attained supernatural powers should follow and enter the Tathāgata’s pure great circular halo, traveling through the air.

At that time, the World-Honored One vanished from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the great city of Rājagṛha; surrounded by Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas in reverent attendance, he emitted a great radiance that shone everywhere. Devas and devīs led the way and followed behind, singing praises, while hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of drums and musical instruments resounded, shaking the great earth, as the heavens rained down various exquisite and wonderful precious flowers.

Within that buddha-field, he extensively manifested various signs such as the great majestic power of a Buddha, the great supernormal powers of a Buddha, the great deeds of a Buddha, the great transformations of a Buddha, the great auspiciousness of a Buddha, the great supreme light of a Buddha, the great dignified deportment of a Buddha, and the great playful displays of a Buddha; traveling freely through the air, he proceeded to that great city of Kāśyapa.
At that time, the World-Honored One was situated in mid-air like a king of geese, moving with serene composure and proceeding with sovereign ease.
The hosts of devaputras from the realms of desire and form saw the World-Honored One from afar, high in the sky like a king of geese turning and gliding with mastery;

they all felt joy, delight, and exhilaration. He was like the sun’s orb first rising, pure and lovely; like the full moon, brilliant and radiant, surrounded by the stars; like Śakra, Lord of Devas, surrounded by his celestial host; like Mahābrahmā, surrounded by the Brahma assembly. Having seen him, the celestial hosts immediately gave rise to pure and rarefied thoughts, each holding various kinds of exquisite celestial incense and flowers to make offerings to the Buddha.

That is to say, they scattered upon the Buddha celestial *utpala* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *pāriyātraka* flowers, *mahāpāriyātraka* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, lovely flowers, greatly lovely flowers, wheel and great-wheel flowers, as well as various land-grown flowers; and other exquisite, most excellent fragrant flowers possessing a hundred or a thousand petals; as well as *arcisprabha* flowers, *rasaprabha* flowers, *samantagandha* flowers, *nityagandha* flowers, *nityapraphulla* flowers, and *manorama* flowers—these and countless other such superior and wonderful fragrant flowers were scattered everywhere over the Buddha.
Furthermore, he established exquisite banners and pennants, and performed hundreds of thousands of sublime musical performances.

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested such marvelous and superior signs as fragrant flowers, banners, canopies, and the playing of drums and music; amidst these various adornments, in a mere instant, he arrived at the great city of Kāśī and first proceeded briefly to the palace of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
The Buddha, along with the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, descended from the sky and entered that palace.
At that time, the great earth shook everywhere; yet it was soft, exquisite, and lovely, and it did not distress any sentient beings.

At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, knowing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had already arrived within the great city of Kalandaka, each came from their respective guarded quarters with their retinues, carrying various kinds of exquisite incense and flowers, and quickly approached the place where the Buddha was.

When the Four Heavenly Kings had arrived, they bowed their heads to the ground in prostration at the Buddha’s feet; they then scattered the exquisite incense and flowers they held over the Buddha as an offering, and with palms joined in sincere devotion, withdrew to stand to one side.
Their respective retinues likewise each prostrated themselves with utmost sincerity at the Buddha’s feet and stood with palms joined.
The Buddha then briefly expounded the essential points of the Dharma for the assembly of the Four Heavenly Kings and their retinues.

At that time, within the gathering, ten thousand yakṣas, rākṣasas, nāgas, gandharvas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others beheld the supreme marks of the Buddha and all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Among the palace ladies and retinues of those Four Great Heavenly Kings, ten thousand celestial maidens gave rise to the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, together with his own retinue, each holding exquisite incense, flowers, unguents, powdered incense, jeweled banners, pennants, and canopies from the world-system Adorned with Boundless Merit, and accompanied by the sounds of drums, flutes, songs, and various musical performances, quickly proceeded to the abode of the World-Honored Buddha within the palace of King Vaiśravaṇa.

Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and then offered the various pure and exquisite offerings of incense, flowers, and other requisites that he had brought, worshiping the World-Honored One with solemn sincerity.

The various retinues played exquisite music and, with solemn reverence and devotion, prostrated themselves in homage as they escorted the World-Honored One, along with the assembly of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas, into their own palace.
Having arrived, he invited them, one by one, to take their seats.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon that exquisite lion throne adorned with various ornaments, and the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas likewise each took their seats.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, addressed Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protecting Devas, and all the other sons of heaven, saying:

"You should each apply yourselves with diligence; rejoice in and assist in the preparation of these magnificent offerings for the World-Honored One, so that you may cause the merit of your giving to increase."
At that time, the assembly of devaputras, having seen this most supreme realm and the exquisite adornment of the lion throne, gave rise to a sense of wonder and all spoke these words:
"By what power has this sublime manifestation been brought about?"
"Is this due to the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, the World-Honored One?
Or is it due to the majestic spiritual power of Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets?
Immediately, a voice was heard from the air, declaring:
"O virtuous ones! This is brought about by the majestic spiritual power of the Great Lord of Secrets.

To the east, passing from here through as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a world named Boundless Merit Jewel Adornment; the Buddha there is named King of Adornments."

When the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, beheld the various kinds of excellent and wondrous adornments of that world, by virtue of the majestic spiritual power of the Lord of Secrets, he caused the splendors of those superior adornments to appear identically within this palace.

At that time, once the World-Honored One had taken his place upon the sublime and wondrous lion throne, all the hosts of yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, gandharvas, mahoragas, and others dwelling in the great city of Āṭavī, immediately came to where the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was. They prostrated with their heads touching the ground at the Buddha’s feet, joined their palms in reverent devotion, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, addressed the Four Great Heavenly Kings and all the other members of the assembly, saying:
"You should all come together to assist me in making a sincere resolve; by offering pure and exquisite food and drink to the World-Honored One, you shall obtain great benefit."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, together with his retinue and assembly, personally prepared the most excellent and hundredfold refined delicacies with hands purified by cleanliness. With a profound and pure bodhicitta, he made offerings worthy of the Tathāgata; generating the most supreme resolve, he presented them to the World-Honored One, as well as to the assembly of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas, so that all were fully satisfied.
When the meal was finished, he further offered pure scented water for washing his hands and cleansing his vessel; then, withdrawing from before the Buddha, he sat down to listen to the Dharma.

At that time, all the yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and others dwelling in the great city of Āṭavī, each with sincere devotion, gazed up at the World-Honored One, joined their palms in reverent homage, and prostrated themselves in worship.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of Sanskrit and Chinese, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Weijing et al., by Imperial Decree. Chapter Nineteen: The Chapter on the World Protectors (Lokapāla), Part One. At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, exhorted the Bhagavān to proclaim the True Dharma, addressing him thus:
"I pray only that the Bhagavān..."

For those sentient beings who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment, one should teach the Dharma as appropriate to lead them into the principles of the Dharma; they shall then immediately resolve to attain great bodhicitta and abide in non-retrogression.

Furthermore, may this assembly of yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, gandharvas, guhyakas, mahoragas, and others, be brought into accord with long-term benefit, happiness, and virtuous conduct; may they attain the most supreme and exalted state among all victors, without ever losing any portion of their wholesome qualities.
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed the entire assembly, including Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, and the rest, saying: "O noble ones!

Listen attentively and apply your minds well; I shall now proclaim this for the sake of all sons and daughters of good family who practice virtuous deeds so that they may fully enter into the principles of the Dharma, universally attain the most supreme and exalted state, and never lose their portion of wholesome qualities."
Thereupon, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Great Secrets, and the rest of the assembled multitude listened with single-minded attention.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly: "O virtuous ones!

If a son or daughter of good family has deeply resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they will immediately be able to possess extensive and pure faith; they will desire to see the noble ones and delight in hearing the true Dharma; they will be skillful in relinquishing without stinginess, with hands that yield inexhaustibly; they will take great pleasure in accumulating and performing meritorious deeds, and their mind of renunciation will be fully perfected.

In the practice of giving, one delights in impartiality, possessing a mind free from obstruction and untainted by defilement; one has faith in the retribution of karma, remains free from all discrimination, doubt, and hesitation, and ensures that the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome actions are never lost or subverted.

Having understood this, one should refrain from all that ought not to be done regarding the conditions of life; namely: one does not kill, does not steal, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, does not engage in frivolous speech, does not use double-tongued speech, does not use harsh words, is not covetous, is not malicious, and does not hold wrong views. One firmly maintains and accumulates these ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*), abandons and refrains from the ten kinds of unwholesome paths of action, universally practices pure faith, and cultivates pure conduct together with śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and those possessing precepts and virtue within the path of the True Dharma.

Regarding all wholesome dharmas, he is extensively learned and diligent in practice; his profound and firm mental attention is conjoined with virtuous conduct. He is tranquil and self-subdued, always speaking words of affection. He refutes the arguments of others, cultivates the good, and abandons evil. Without pride or inferiority, without disparagement or praise, he maintains right mindfulness as it arises and dwells in a state of meditative equipoise. He closes the gates to the three realms of existence, extinguishes all ailments, casts off heavy burdens, transcends doubt, and attains deliverance from all states of being.
One who knows thus should, according to what is appropriate, draw near to, revere, serve, and honor the Buddhas, their śrāvaka disciples, and spiritual friends—whether they be śramaṇas or brahmins.
From those spiritual friends, they hear and receive the true Dharma, which instructs, benefits, and gladdens them;

that is to say, it explains that giving results in the fruit of great wealth, that observing the precepts leads to rebirth in heaven, and that extensive learning brings great wisdom and pure contemplation free from distraction.
It further teaches: "This practice of giving is the retribution for giving; this practice of stinginess is the retribution for stinginess; this observance..."
This morality is the retribution for maintaining morality; this breaking of morality is the retribution for breaking morality;
this patience is the retribution for patience; this anger is the retribution for anger; this diligence is the retribution for diligence;
this laziness is the retribution for laziness; this meditative concentration is the retribution for meditative concentration.
This distraction is itself the retribution for distraction; this superior wisdom is itself the retribution for superior wisdom;
this poor wisdom is itself the retribution for poor wisdom; this bodily wholesome action is itself the retribution for bodily wholesome action;
this bodily unwholesome action is itself the retribution for bodily unwholesome action; this verbal wholesome action is itself the retribution for verbal wholesome action.
This verbal misconduct is itself the retribution for verbal misconduct; this mental good conduct is itself the retribution for mental good conduct;
this mental misconduct is itself the retribution for mental misconduct. This is wholesome and this is unwholesome;
this should be done and this should not be done. Once this karma has been performed, one will obtain benefit throughout the long night.

It is associated with increasingly peaceful and blissful wholesome conduct; having performed such karma, one will not encounter disadvantageous suffering throughout the long night, as it is associated with unwholesome conduct.
Such dharmas as these are heard from a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), who provides instruction, guidance, benefit, and joy.

Furthermore, observing that they were vessels for the Dharma, he immediately proclaimed for them the profound teachings, namely the practices of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

He further taught the profound Dharma of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)—which is without arising, without production, and without self, person, sentient being, or life-span—and explained: "If this dharma exists, then this is obtained; if this dharma does not exist, then this is not obtained."
If this phenomenon exists, that is birth; if this phenomenon does not exist, that is cessation.

This is: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair. Thus, this entire great mass of suffering arises.

If a phenomenon does not exist, it cannot be attained; this is the cessation of phenomena. That is to say: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
Whether these various phenomena arise or cease, not even the slightest phenomenon can be found within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Why is this? Because all phenomena are dependently originated, they lack a master, lack an agent, and lack an experiencer; they proceed solely by way of causes and conditions.
However, within this, there is no dharma that can be transmuted, nor is there non-transmutation, nor any distinct dharma.
The three realms are provisionally designated according to the transmutation of their conjunction; they are merely designated because of the transmutation of afflictions and karma.

Those who are deluded perceive unreal phenomena as real; the wise should know that not even the slightest phenomenon can be found to have an agent. Because no agent can be found, there is no phenomenon that undergoes transformation, yet it is not that there is no transformation.

If one, having heard this profound Dharma as it has been explained, gives rise to no doubt or confusion, that person immediately enters the unobstructed nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-anāvaraṇatā*). They do not cling to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they do not cling to the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, or the mind and mental objects; nor do they cling to visual consciousness up to mental consciousness. They believe that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is fundamentally empty, and they believe that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is fundamentally detached.
“O virtuous ones!

Because that bodhisattva of non-retrogressive faith has faith in this Dharma, he does not lose the opportunity to see the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and serve the pure assembly. In every place where he is born, he constantly sees the Buddhas, hears and receives the true Dharma, and serves the pure assembly; he is always born in an age when a Buddha dwells in the world.”
Once born therein, they arouse diligence and strive earnestly to seek the wholesome Dharma.

By virtue of this diligence, they completely renounce all meaningless affairs within the homes of laypeople—namely, wives, children, sons, daughters, servants, retinues, and their various activities—and they do not give rise to attachment for the pleasures of youth. Instead, they develop a virtuous mind and aspire to go forth with right faith within the pure teachings of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Having gone forth, he draws near to virtuous friends and ascends the path of goodness together with them, thereby attaining all noble aspirations.

He listens to the sublime Dharma and, in accordance with what he has heard, practices it authentically; not relying on verbal embellishments, his transcendent wisdom is perfected as he exerts diligence in earnestly seeking extensive learning.

According to the Dharma he has heard, he extensively explains it for others without seeking anything for himself; regarding the fame, profit, and offerings he receives, he has no mind of attachment; he teaches the Dharma to others with words that accord with reality, and as he hears it, so does he abide in it.
He teaches the Dharma to others as it truly is, causing those who hear it to attain great loving-kindness and to give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.

He never tires of or abandons that extensive learning; regarding his body and life, he is content with few desires, fully perfected in tranquility, increasing in virtuous conduct, and delighting in secluded places.
They carefully contemplate the meaning of the Dharma as they hear it, gathering all principles and meanings without distraction.

They do not cling to the literal phrasing but instead seek the ultimate reality; for the sake of all beings in the world of devas and humans, they diligently cultivate sublime practices, not merely for their own sake.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he diligently seeks the unsurpassed, most supreme wisdom, so that other sentient beings may attain non-laxity within the Buddha’s wisdom.
Furthermore, what is meant by "non-laxity"?

This refers to the initial restraint and regulation of the sense faculties: when seeing forms with the eyes and so forth, one does not grasp at their signs nor become attached to their secondary characteristics; because one knows the flavors and defilements within all objective realms as they truly are, one constantly seeks liberation.

It is the same for sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, and mental objects cognized by the mind. Having understood these through wisdom, one does not grasp at their marks nor become attached to their fine qualities; because one knows taste and defilement as they truly are, one constantly seeks liberation.
This is called heedfulness (*apramāda*).

Furthermore, one who is heedful, having well-subdued his own mind, also appropriately restrains and protects the minds of others; he skillfully pacifies and eliminates the defilements of afflictions and sensual craving, and instead follows after the craving for the Dharma. The discursive thoughts of desire, hatred, and harm cease and do not arise; the unwholesome roots such as greed, hatred, and delusion likewise do not function. Moreover, he is able to restrain all unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, and even deep-seated mental engagements (*manasikāra*) do not arise.
In brief, the complete eradication of all sinful and unwholesome dharmas is called heedfulness. "O virtuous ones!
By diligently practicing such dharmas of heedfulness as these, a bodhisattva attains pure faith and remains free from negligence."
O Great Lord of Secrets!
You should know that the single dharma of faith is vast and pure; it enables one to constantly and exclusively seek wholesome dharmas.
A person endowed with faith is free from the fear of evil destinies in future lives, does not fall into states of regretful mental activity, and is always praised by the noble ones.
"Furthermore, Guhyapati!

Those who practice by abiding in the Dharma are able to attain the True Dharma, the good destinies, and the constant joy of seeing the Buddha; they dwell securely in the Noble Path and attain great mastery."
Having attained mastery, they further cause others to universally fulfill the dharma of mastery, so that they may abide in the mind of enlightenment and attain the wisdom of a Tathāgata.
Furthermore, O Lord of Mysteries!
If a person desires to attain the most supreme and wondrous bliss, they should ultimately cultivate correct practice and the dharma of nirvāṇa.
O Great Lord of Secrets!

All those gathered here in this assembly have come because they rely on the power of their past roots of goodness; they cultivate correct practice well and do not diminish or lose any of their roots of goodness.
How are the roots of goodness prevented from diminishing or being lost?
It is by practicing heedfulness.
Therefore, the roots of goodness possessed by both devas and humans shall not diminish or be lost.

Why is this? Because that heedful mind skillfully guards against all sensory objects, it is able to abandon all defilements of craving and desire, and by cultivating attachment to the Dharma, it can immediately restrain the discursive thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and harm. Furthermore, it can pacify and eliminate all unwholesome states arising from unstable attention, leaving behind greed, hatred, and delusion. It brings to a complete halt the coarse and heavy faults of body, speech, and mind, such that even any decline or loss among all categories of wholesome dharmas no longer occurs.
This is called heedfulness (*apramāda*).

If a person has faith and understanding in the dharma of heedfulness, they will be able to accord with all matters of diligence; because of this diligence and heedfulness, such a person is then able to accumulate and cultivate the merit of pure faith.
By cultivating pure faith and the dharmas of heedfulness and diligence, one is able to practice right mindfulness and right situational awareness (*samprajanya*).
Through right mindfulness and right situational awareness, one does not lose or neglect any of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
"If one possesses pure faith, heedfulness, diligence, right mindfulness, and right awareness, one will be able to diligently cultivate the profound and firm Dharma.
O Great Lord of Secrets!
If a bodhisattva attains liberation within the profound and firm Dharma, they will be able to know existence and non-existence as they truly are.
In this context, what is meant by "existence"?
What is non-existence?
It refers to the fact that when one correctly cultivates the noble dharma of liberation, this is existence;
if one does not correctly cultivate the noble dharma of liberation, this is non-existence.
If there is karma and there is its retribution, this is existence;
if there is no karma and no retribution, this is non-existence.
Within the conventional truth, the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind exist.
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind do not exist;
yet for a bodhisattva, diligence toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) exists,
while indolence toward great enlightenment does not exist.
The five aggregates arising from inversion exist;
phenomena arising without cause do not exist.
Form is impermanent, it is suffering, and it is a phenomenon subject to disintegration—these exist.
That form is permanent, stable, continuous, indestructible, and a dharma that abides—this does not exist.
That feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, suffering, and dharmas subject to destruction—this does exist;
that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent, stable, continuous, indestructible, and dharmas that abide—this does not exist.
When ignorance conditions volitional formations, there is existence;
when ignorance and volitional formations are unreal, there is non-existence. When volitional formations condition consciousness, there is existence; [when they are unreal, there is non-existence].
If consciousness is not real, it is non-existent;
conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form exists.
If consciousness is not real, name-and-form is non-existent.
When name-and-form (nāmarūpa) conditions the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), they exist;
when name-and-form is unreal, the six sense bases do not exist. When the six sense bases condition contact (sparśa), it exists; [when they are unreal, contact does not exist].
If the six sense bases are unreal, contact is absent;
conditioned by contact, feeling exists.
If contact is unreal, feeling is absent.
With feeling as condition, craving exists;
without real feeling, craving does not exist. With craving as condition, grasping exists; [without craving, grasping does not exist].
If craving and grasping are unreal, then they do not exist;
with grasping as condition, becoming exists,
so if grasping and becoming are unreal, then they do not exist.
When there is a condition for birth, there is existence;
when birth does not truly exist, existence is non-existent.
When there is a condition for birth, there is old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair; thus they exist.
If birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress are unreal, they do not exist;
if giving results in great wealth, it exists;
if giving results in poverty, it does not exist.
That one who maintains the precepts is reborn in heaven is possible;
that one who maintains the precepts falls into the evil realms is impossible.
That one who is widely learned and possesses great wisdom is possible;
When extensive learning results in defiled wisdom, it is absent;
when meditative observation is undistracted, it is present;
when meditative observation is distracted, it is absent.
Afflictions that arise from improper mental attention exist;
afflictions that arise from proper mental attention do not exist.
For those who do not give rise to overweening pride, the realization of nirvāṇa exists.
For one with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), receiving a Buddha’s prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is non-existent;
for one who penetrates emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in all respects, it is existent.
For one who clings to a self within, it is non-existent.
Liberation exists for those who practice with diligence through wisdom;
it does not exist for those who seek renunciation while associated with the conceit of "I" and "mine.
Furthermore, if one seeks a real dharma within the unreal five aggregates—conceived as a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span—it does not exist.
"Furthermore, Great Lord of Secrets!

A bodhisattva who practices with diligence and non-negligence, and who applies profound and firm attention, understands existence and non-existence as they truly are; this is approved by all the wise ones of the world."

Having known things as they truly are, although one acts within existence, one does not grasp at it; although one acts within non-existence, one likewise does not grasp at it. Thus, one is able to penetrate the true meaning taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Chapter Nineteen, Part Two: The World-Protectors. "Furthermore, O Great Lord of Secrets!
The Tathāgata has briefly summarized all dharmas by teaching four Dharma-seals. What are these four?

First is the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-anityatā*), taught in order to shatter the notion of permanence held by śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and those long-lived devas who cling to the doctrine of permanence.
Second, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering, in order to shatter the perception of pleasure held by gods and humans who conceive of them as pleasurable.
Third, all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self (*anātman*), in order to shatter the notion of a self held by those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and others who cling to a self.
Fourth is the tranquility of nirvāṇa, which gives rise to the practice of seeking for the sake of those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) in order to shatter that pride.
This term "impermanence" is a synonym for the ultimate non-existence of any permanent phenomenon (*nityadharma*).
This term "suffering" is a synonym for the distancing from longing and seeking.
This term "selflessness" is a synonym for the characteristic of emptiness.
"The tranquility of nirvāṇa" is a synonym for the realization of signlessness.
O Great Lord of Secrets!

If bodhisattvas deeply and firmly believe in, understand, and diligently practice this Dharma, they will not diminish or lose any wholesome qualities and will swiftly bring the factors of enlightenment to full perfection.
At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings who Protect the World came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We four kings are all named 'Protectors of the World. By what Dharma should we be able to protect the world?"
The Buddha addressed the Four Great Heavenly Kings, saying:
"O virtuous ones! You should practice the conduct of the True Dharma, for this will enable you to protect the world."
The practice of the True Dharma consists of what are known as the ten wholesome actions. What are these ten? First, refraining from killing;

second, being content with one's own wealth and pleasure without seeking further measure; third, not giving rise to defiled thoughts toward the wives of others; fourth, not causing division among the assemblies of others; fifth, not uttering harsh speech; sixth, speaking in accordance with reality; seventh, speaking without frivolous ornamentation; eighth, having no expectations for the wealth or pleasure of others; ninth, ceasing and pacifying anger; and tenth, pure right view.
"O virtuous ones!
These ten wholesome dharmas are able to protect the world.
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas that are able to protect the world."

What are the eight? First, being able to practice according to what one has taught; second, honoring teachers and elders in all circumstances; third, proceeding in accordance with the right path; fourth, having a straightforward mind; fifth, having a mind that is always supple; sixth, constantly giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; seventh, not committing any transgressions; and eighth, accumulating all roots of goodness.
"These eight dharmas are able to protect the world.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas that are able to protect the world. What are these six?"

First is the bodily action of practicing loving-kindness: toward one's teachers and preceptors, spiritual friends and fellow practitioners of the holy life, and even toward all sentient beings, one gives rise to thoughts of respect and affection; this is the first bodily action of concord and reverence.

Second is the practice of compassionate verbal action: toward one's teachers, preceptors, spiritual friends, fellow practitioners of the holy life, and indeed all sentient beings, one gives rise to thoughts of respect and affection; this is the second form of concordant and respectful verbal action.

Third, practicing compassionate mental action: toward one's teachers and elders, spiritual friends, fellow practitioners of the holy life, and indeed all sentient beings, one gives rise to thoughts of respect and affection; this is the third form of harmony and reverence in mental action.

Fourth, whatever gains and offerings one receives in accordance with the Dharma—from the most meager, down to the food within one's alms bowl—one shares them equally and impartially with those spiritual friends and fellow practitioners of the holy life; furthermore, one does so with a mind of respect, affection, and joyful intent. This is the fourth [practice] of harmonious respect regarding gains and offerings.

Fifth, regarding the cultivation of ethical discipline (*śīla*), one practices it without interruption or deficiency, fully complete and free from turbidity. One does not give rise to greedy grasping for that which should be received; it is praised by the wise and remains free from all censure. By means of such pure dharmas of ethical discipline, one practices together with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*). Furthermore, one respects, cherishes, and maintains mindfulness toward them. This is the fifth [aspect of] harmonious respect in the cultivation of ethical discipline.

Sixth, regarding the dharmas of right view and renunciation, as well as the stages of superior discernment (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), whatever dharma one practices as a correct application, one should accordingly engage in that same practice together with spiritual friends and fellow practitioners of the holy life; furthermore, one should regard them with respect, affection, and a favorable disposition. This is the sixth [aspect of] concordant view and harmonious reverence.
"Virtuous ones!
These six principles of harmony are able to protect the world.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas that are able to protect the world."
What are the four? First is non-attachment;
because of non-attachment, one does not fall into the evil destinies.
Second is non-hatred; because of non-hatred, one does not fall into the evil destinies.
Third is non-delusion; because of non-delusion, one does not fall into the evil destinies.
Fourth is fearlessness; because of fearlessness, one does not fall into the evil destinies.
O virtuous ones!
These four dharmas are able to protect the world.
Furthermore, there are two other dharmas that can protect the world. What are these two?
First is having a sense of shame (*hrī*), and second is having a sense of dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).
One who possesses these two qualities is able to protect the world.
Furthermore, there is one other quality that can protect the world.
What is this one? It is called true practice.
Because it is true, it is able to protect the world.
Furthermore, speaking well and being free from deceit—these dharmas are all capable of protecting the world.
O virtuous ones!
If you diligently practice such dharmas as these, you will be able to protect the world; having protected yourselves, you will further enable others to protect the world as well.
Chapter Twenty: On Going and Coming. At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:

"I should now, for the sake of this assembly, proclaim the secret mantras and verses, so that the roots of goodness of those in the assembly may correspond with them, and the Dharma of Great Bodhi may long abide in the world."
Having formed this thought, he then addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāguhyapati Vajrapāṇi, saying:

"In the past, I once dwelt within the palace of the Naga King Apalāla, and at the time of my initial attainment of enlightenment at the Great Bodhimaṇḍa; in both instances, I sustained the world with a mind intent on its benefit."
"I shall now proclaim the great mantra syllables; are you able to remember them?
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"I am able to memorize it.
The Buddha said,
"Lord of Mysteries!"
"Now you must proclaim those great mantra syllables.

At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, knelt on his right knee with palms joined, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and then spoke these secret mantra syllables: "Tadyathā..."

Vikiraṇa mahāparivarta svameta dharani garjadu samudravijaye. When the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, spoke these secret verses, all the palaces of Māra shook violently;
the great earth quaked, the great oceans surged, and the entire assembly was struck with terror. They all went to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated, and sought his protection.
At that time, the World-Honored One again pressed the earth with one foot, and the great trichiliocosm shook throughout.
Then the entire assembly turned toward the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"Save us, World-Honored One!"
"Save us, Sugata! We are all trembling with fear and agitation.
The Buddha said:
"Do not fear, do not fear!

This is the majestic and numinous realm of the great vidyā-mantras of all Buddhas, which can cause the great earth to tremble, the great oceans to surge, and even the sun dwelling in the void to waver."
At that time, the World-Honored One briefly expounded the essential points of the Dharma as was appropriate for Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the entire assembly.
At that moment, eighty thousand people within the assembly gave rise to the mind of great bodhi, and immeasurable people dwelt on the stage of those still in training (śaikṣa).
At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, his eldest son Vajrasena, held a net of exquisite jewels over the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"How can a bodhisattva attain non-retrogression regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
If a bodhisattva can fully cultivate ten dharmas, they will attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. What are these ten?

First, they constantly practice unimpeded great loving-kindness; second, they constantly give rise to tireless great compassion; third, they diligently accomplish all tasks; fourth, they skillfully cultivate the samādhi of emptiness; fifth, they manifest and penetrate supreme wisdom; sixth, they skillfully penetrate all things in every place; seventh, they are able to purify the three periods of time through sublime knowledge; eighth, they contemplate actual karmic retribution with unimpeded skillful means; ninth, although they fully understand emptiness, they plant the roots of all virtues; tenth, according to what has been taught, their self-nature is pure, and they skillfully enter the noble path.
“If a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, they will attain non-retrogression regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Vajrasena again addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!”
“What dharmas should a bodhisattva cultivate so that, having heard of the inconceivable gateways of the Buddha, they remain serene and do not give rise to fear?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
A bodhisattva should cultivate eight dharmas, whereby they will remain serene and free from fear upon hearing of the inconceivable gateways of the Buddhas.

What are these eight? First, the increase of superior wisdom; second, the increase of wondrous knowledge; third, being constantly sustained by virtuous friends; fourth, possessing great faith and resolve; fifth, skillfully penetrating the dharma of non-arising which is like an illusion; sixth, having faith and resolve in the dharma of impermanence; seventh, mental activity that is equanimous like space; and eighth, skillfully knowing the signs of the arising of obstacles within all dharmas.
“If a bodhisattva is endowed with these eight dharmas, they will be able to hear of the inconceivable gateways of the Buddha and remain serene, giving rise to no fear or terror.
Vajrasena again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By practicing what dharma can a bodhisattva attain mastery over all their activities?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! A bodhisattva should cultivate four dharmas, whereby they will attain mastery over all that they undertake."

What are the four? First, skillfully cultivating the dharma of non-extinction in the present and possessing the five supernormal powers; second, skillfully contemplating the gates of supreme liberation and possessing the four dhyānas; third, transcending the Brahma world and possessing the four Brahma-abodes; fourth, through the wisdom of skillful means, skillfully cultivating non-arising in all places.
“If a bodhisattva is endowed with these four dharmas, they will be able to attain mastery over all that they do.
Vajrasena then addressed the Buddha again, saying,
“How many kinds of dharma-gates are there for a bodhisattva?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son, there are four kinds of Dharma-gates for bodhisattvas."
What are the four? First is the gate of knowledge, which skillfully enters into the faculties and natures of all sentient beings.
Second is the gate of wisdom, which is able to skillfully discern and proclaim the meanings of phrases.
Third is the gateway of dhāraṇī, which skillfully enters into the retention of all speech and sounds.
Fourth is the gateway of unimpeded analytical knowledge, which is able to skillfully proclaim all inexhaustible teachings.
"These are the four dharma-gates of a bodhisattva.
Vajrasena again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"How many kinds of powers does a bodhisattva possess?"
The Buddha said:
"Good son, a bodhisattva possesses nine kinds of power."
What are the nine? First is the power of concentration, because it arises from great compassion.
Second is the power of diligence, because it is non-retrogressive.
Third is the power of extensive learning, because it gives rise to superior wisdom.
Fourth is the power of faith and understanding, because it brings about perfect liberation.
Fifth is the power of cultivation, because it eliminates distraction.
Sixth is the power of patience, because it skillfully protects sentient beings.
Seventh is the power of the bodhicitta, because it subdues all māras.
Eighth is the power of great compassion, because it brings sentient beings to maturity.
"Ninth is the power of the endurance of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), because it brings the ten powers (*daśabala*) to perfection.
These are called the nine powers of a bodhisattva.
When the Blessed One spoke this Dharma, his eldest son Vajrasena attained the endurance of the non-arising of phenomena.
Having realized this patience, he again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray that the World-Honored One, through the power of his majestic spiritual authority, will establish this True Dharma so that it may long abide within the palace of the Great Secret Lord Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva; and that sentient beings who possess the capacity for the Dharma may obtain the illumination and touch of the light of heard wisdom, such that even after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, it shall be widely disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa and not allowed to disappear."
At that time, having accepted the exhortation of Vajrasena, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāguhyapati Vajrapāṇi, saying: "Guhyapati!

You should now proclaim those secret vidyā-mantras and phrases which I, when first attaining enlightenment at the Great Bodhimaṇḍa, established for the protection of all bodhisattvas and for the subjugation and conversion of the hosts of māras; through these, may the eye of the True Dharma long abide in the world, and may all māras, heterodox views, and external teachings be subdued.

At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, having received the Buddha’s command, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One,
and uttered this great mantra: "Tadyathā (1) hulu (2)."

When this great mantra was spoken, all the kings of mountains trembled, the great earth shook and quaked, and the great oceans surged; all heterodox and external teachings were subdued and brought to submit to the words of the True Dharma, which well protects the precious treasury of the True Dharma.
All the hosts of devas rejoiced in mutual celebration and spoke these verses:
“Having proclaimed the secret great vidyā-mantra, It shall cause the True Dharma to abide long in the world.
The three-thousandfold world system trembles all over; We pray for the Honored One among Men to grant us protection.”
The Great Master, who speaks the words of truth well, universally bestows fearlessness upon the assembled multitude;
through his majestic spiritual power he establishes this Dharma-gate, enabling the True Dharma to abide long in the world.

At that time, the World-Honored One remained in the palace of Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva for seven days. Having extensively brought benefit to immeasurable sentient beings, and having ensured that all categories of living beings throughout the great city of Āṭavī were widely and universally benefited, he departed from his original palace and returned to dwell in mid-air. He was respectfully surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, humans, and devas. Furthermore, countless hundreds of thousands of yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, and others preceded and followed him as attendants. Brahmā, Śakra, the world-protecting devas (*lokapālas*), and others spread nets of light, played exquisite music, and rained down various extraordinary flowers.

At that time, all the buddha-fields trembled; through the Buddha’s majestic virtue, the power of his supernormal abilities, his sustaining empowerment, his miraculous transformations, and his dignified deportment—like a king of geese moving with sovereign ease—he gradually blew [the wind] back and returned to Vulture Peak Mountain.
The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, followed behind the Buddha through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
This concludes the seventeenth fascicle of the *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśamahāyānasūtra* spoken by the Buddha.
