Chapter Twenty-One: The Former Deeds of the Bodhisattva Vīryabalasamudgata At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling with a great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas on Vulture Peak Mountain. In the afternoon, he departed from his original abode and proceeded to teach the Dharma as was appropriate for the great multitude.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, knowing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had already returned to the mountain, set out from the great city of Rājagṛha with his palace ladies, retinue, and sixty thousand people from the city of Rājagṛha. Each carrying various kinds of exquisite incense, flowers, ointments, powdered incense, and other offerings, they proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain, where the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying.
Having arrived, they prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and each stood to one side.
Then King Ajātaśatru came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Whatever I have undertaken, I have settled as was appropriate.
My son came and informed the King, his father:
'Know that the World-Honored One, the Great Teacher, having finished accepting the invitation at the palace of Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, has now returned to Vulture Peak Mountain.'"
I then reflected: "How rare is the Blessed One!

The Buddha acts with great compassion toward all sentient beings; among the multitude of beings, there is not a single being whom the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, ever feels weary of or abandons. Having accepted the invitation and offerings at the Palace of Vajrapāṇi in the Great City of the Wilderness, the World-Honored One has now returned here once more to extensively bring ripening and benefit to sentient beings."

That Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, is most rare and wondrous; endowed with great majestic power, he is able to skillfully proclaim the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata, giving rise to great joy.
Under which Buddha, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha did Vajrapāṇi plant the roots of virtue in the past, such that he is now able to achieve such eloquence?
The Buddha addressed King Ajātaśatru, saying:

"Great King, you should know that those sentient beings who have not planted roots of goodness find it extremely difficult to believe and understand such matters; however, those who have certainly planted roots of goodness are able to give rise to faith and understanding in this regard."
"Great King!
Even if one were able to calculate and determine the limits of worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River,

the limits of that Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, the Great Lord of Secrets— who has personally attended upon and made offerings to the Buddha-Bhagavāns, cultivated the holy life, and attained eloquence— could not be calculated even by all the Buddha-Bhagavāns."
For this reason, Great King, you should know the past causes and conditions.

I recall that in the past, beyond incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and even further back through vast, immeasurable, and inconceivable kalpas, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Bahuśruta (Much-Hearing), Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna (Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct), Sugata, Lokavid (Knower of the World), Anuttara (Unsurpassed One), Puruṣadamyasārathi (Charioteer of Men to be Tamed), Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām (Teacher of Gods and Humans), Buddha, Bhagavān (World-Honored One).
The world was named Supreme Adornment, and the eon was named Indestructible.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the True Dharma for that assembly of pure great bodhisattvas.
That Buddha addressed them, saying:
“O sons of good family!
You should know that if there are bodhisattvas who are able to give rise to great diligence, they will completely relinquish both body and life.”
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Courageous Strength (Vīryabala), who stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Sugata!"
As the Buddha has said,
if there are bodhisattvas who give rise to diligence, they completely relinquish both body and life.
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if a bodhisattva gives rise to indolence, how could they possibly quickly realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?

Why is this? Because those bodhisattvas who are able to arouse diligence do not give rise to thoughts of weariness within saṃsāra; rather, while in saṃsāra, those bodhisattvas should always praise it and take no pleasure in nirvāṇa, solely for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity.

"Bhagavān! Because bodhisattvas practice with diligence for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they possess the faith and resolve of vigor; within the cycle of birth and death, they find their own joy, rather than seeking the joy of nirvāṇa."

Why is this? Because for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, whatever actions a bodhisattva performs according to what is appropriate, they likewise cause them all to obtain happiness according to what is appropriate.
If one were to abide in nirvāṇa, how could one perform [beneficial deeds]?
Therefore, bodhisattvas find their own joy within the realm of saṃsāra, and thus do not grasp at the state of nirvāṇa.
“World-Honored One!

The bliss that a bodhisattva attains within the realm of birth and death consists in this: because they diligently practice for the benefit of sentient beings, they constantly behold immeasurable Buddhas, constantly hear immeasurable pure and true Dharma, and are always able to bring immeasurable sentient beings to maturity.”

Because the bodhisattva dwells within the realm of birth and death, he is able to enter accordingly into the realms of sentient beings, yet within the realm of nirvana, he does not cling to the practice of renunciation.
A bodhisattva who dwells within the realm of birth and death does so out of fear of falling into that which is not his proper realm.
Why is this? For within that which is not his proper realm, he can no longer perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, nor can he abide securely in the realm of the Tathāgata.
Because they cannot abide within the realm of the Tathāgata, they are unable to nurture all sentient beings.
In this context, what is meant by "not being their realm"?
It refers to the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
If one delights in dwelling [in that state], one abandons sentient beings and is unable to bring them to maturity. Why is this?
Because the realm of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is not the realm of the bodhisattva; for the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fear birth and death.

If there were anyone capable of embracing immeasurable birth and death, it would be none other than the pure Mahāsattva Bodhisattvas; therefore, Bodhisattvas are able to dwell within the realm of birth and death.
"Great King, you should know that at that time, the Tathāgata Bahusruta praised the Bodhisattva Vīryabala, saying:
'Excellent, noble son! You have well spoken these words.
Furthermore, you have well honored the various practices performed within the sphere of a bodhisattva, so as not to fall back into what is not that sphere.'"
The Bodhisattva Vīryabala addressed that Buddha, saying:
"What constitutes the bodhisattva’s own domain? That Buddha replied:

“Good son! The bodhisattva’s own realm means being able to embrace immeasurable births and deaths without giving rise to fear; praising the vast and supreme practices of a bodhisattva while taking no pleasure in dwelling in the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; uniting the three realms through unimpeded wisdom; being able to skillfully increase all roots of goodness whether by diminishing or benefiting; accomplishing the foundations of all virtues through increasing wisdom; and further, through the wisdom of exhaustion, achieving inexhaustible meritorious conduct.”
Although they contemplate non-arising, they skillfully accomplish phenomena that arise;

although they know there are no sentient beings, they skillfully bring all sentient beings to maturity; although they know all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, they skillfully embrace the True Dharma;
although they know the self-nature of all Buddha-lands is like space, they adorn and purify Buddha-lands with sublime wisdom; although...
While contemplating that the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is signless, one skillfully and diligently seeks out all the Tathāgata’s sublime marks and signs;
while contemplating that all phenomena are fundamentally unconditioned, one exerts effort in the cultivation of the roots of all virtues through sublime wisdom;
and while contemplating that conditioned phenomena are unreal, one is able to skillfully [engage] in various activities with little seeking and little doing.

For the sake of all sentient beings, they provisionally establish teachings according to what is appropriate; though they contemplate body and mind as detached from clinging, they preach the Dharma with wondrous wisdom without weariness;
though they remain free from bustle and clamor, being born of meditative concentration, they do not cling to the flavor of dhyāna;
and though they have awakened to the most profound dharmas, they employ wondrous wisdom to turn in accordance with the various conducts of all sentient beings.
He skillfully expounds the essential teachings of the Dharma.
Although he knows that all things are non-arising, he uses wisdom to contemplate and universally encompass the three realms of existence.

Although he observes with wisdom that all phenomena are empty, he skillfully protects the fruits he has attained. Although he contemplates the spheres of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he skillfully seeks the dharmas of the Tathāgata’s liberation and tranquility. Although he does not weary of or abandon the practices of the bodhisattvas, he constantly and skillfully contemplates the spheres of all Buddhas.
"Good son! This is precisely what constitutes the gateway to the self-boundary of those bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, Great King!"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vīryabala, having heard this teaching on the Dharma of the pure realm from the Tathāgata Bahuśruta, gave rise to a sense of wonder and addressed that Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!"
You have skillfully expounded this pure, true Dharma, which is the gateway to the self-realm of these great bodhisattvas.
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, it is the entry of a bodhisattva endowed with skillful means into the gateway to the self-realm of all phenomena.

It is like space, which universally illuminates all realms of form and appearance without attachment; all forms and appearances likewise encounter no obstruction, and the realm of space itself encounters no obstruction.
The Bodhisattva endowed with skillful means is likewise so, because he directly awakens to and realizes that all phenomena are his own objective domain.

Furthermore, it is like space, which universally illuminates the objective domains of all forms and images without obstruction; whether there be poisonous trees, medicinal trees, thorny trees, or trees of flowers and fragrances, they all grow within space, yet that space is neither defiled nor pure, neither adverse nor compliant.

The Bodhisattva who possesses skillful means is likewise: from wisdom, he gives rise to the gateways of his own objective realm that encompass all those dharmas—namely, the dharmas of ordinary beings, the dharmas of those in training, the dharmas of those beyond training, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of Tathāgatas.
Why is this? Because all those phenomena are directly realized.
Furthermore, it is like the grasses, trees, thickets, and forests of the world, which fire cannot protect.
Why is this? Because fire, when it ascends, burns everything completely due to its extreme intensity.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: within the self-realm of all phenomena, the light of wisdom shines forth with extreme brilliance.
Furthermore, it is like a body as firm and solid as a vajra, which fire cannot burn, a sword cannot sever, poison cannot affect, and the power of others cannot subdue.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: he cannot be defiled by the habitual tendencies of Śrāvakas, nor those of Pratyekabuddhas, nor the afflictive habitual tendencies of all sentient beings;
for wherever he encounters such habitual defilements, he thoroughly illuminates them all through the power of his diligent cultivation of superior wisdom.
Furthermore, just as a water-purifying maṇi jewel is able to purify all turbid waters, so too is the bodhisattva;
by means of the jewel of supreme wisdom, they are universally able to purify the stains of affliction of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is like a medicine called "Poison-Avoiding," which does not coexist with any poisonous substances yet is able to pacify and eliminate all poisons.

The Bodhisattva is likewise: because they possess the power of skillful means and wisdom, they do not coexist with the afflictions of any sentient beings nor with their own afflictions, yet they are further able to cease and pacify the poisons of the afflictions of all sentient beings.
"All such things as these are the gateways to the self-boundary of all dharmas. "Great King!

You should know that when the Bodhisattva Vīryabala taught this Dharma, eight thousand people gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and two hundred bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
"Great King!
You should know that the Bodhisattva Vīryabala within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Bahusruta at that time—could he possibly have been anyone else?
He is none other than this very Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, present in this assembly."
This Great Being, at that time, was able to don the armor of firm diligence, drawing near to and revering many Buddhas, thereby planting deep roots of goodness.
Chapter 22: The Dialogue with King Ajātaśatru, Part One. At that time, King Ajātaśatru had this thought:
"How heavy is this great vajra held in the right hand of this Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets?"
"However, the Lord of Secrets possesses great power and is able to uphold it well.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, knowing what [the king] was thinking, addressed King Ajātaśatru, saying: "Great King!"
"You should know that this vajra is both light and heavy.
The king asked,
"By what cause is it both light and heavy?"
Vajrapāṇi said: "Because it is intended to subdue those sentient beings who are arrogant and haughty, this vajra is heavy;
because it is intended to demonstrate [the path] to those sentient beings who are free from pride and upright, this vajra is light."

Then the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi immediately placed the great vajra he held upon the ground. At the moment it was set down, by his supernatural power, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways. He then addressed King Ajātaśatru, saying: "Great King!
"You should now lift up this great vajra from within the earth yourself.

At that moment, King Ajātaśatru, relying on his own firm and heroic strength, sought to lift the vajra; yet he exhausted all his power and vigor without being able to move it even by the measure of a single hair-tip.
Immediately conceiving a sense of rare wonder and profound respect, he approached the Buddha, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
In the past, on the field of battle, I once seized a great elephant clad in armor; with a single hand, I grasped it and hurled it to a great distance."
This vajra is of minute proportions; yet even now, though I exhaust my own strength and power, I cannot move it, let alone lift it!
For what reason is this so?
The Buddha said, "Great King!
Do not distress yourself; it is because this vajra-pestle is of the utmost weight."
Then King Ajātaśatru addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
"Kauśika! You should now lift up this great vajra-pestle placed within this ground."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately sought to lift the vajra with his own heroic supernatural power; yet, although he exhausted all his strength, he could not move it even slightly.
Thereupon, a sense of rare wonder and profound reverence arose within him, and he approached the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

When I was engaged in battle with that Asura King, my strength was firm, superior, and fiercely courageous, such that I was without rival; with my right hand, I seized the great chariot belonging to that Vemacitra Asura King, which measured seven hundred yojanas in width, and I then carried it along as swiftly as a rushing wind.
"This vajra has exhausted its own power and cannot move it; is this not because it has been restrained by the vast and majestic spiritual authority of the Blessed One?
The Buddha said, "Kauśika!..."
This is not something restrained by my supernormal power; it is simply because that vajra is of the utmost weight.
Kauśika, what do you think?
"Is Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, exceedingly heavy?
The Lord of Devas addressed the Buddha, saying, "Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is exceedingly and most heavily weighted; no analogy can suffice to describe it."
The Buddha said to the Lord of Devas:
"This vajra is composed of vajra-substance and its weight exceeds even that of Sumeru, the King of Mountains.
Yet, by means of the great power and force of the vajra, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi can hurl and shatter the Cakravāḍa mountains like mere chaff."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"The Buddha has declared that among the assembly of śrāvakas, you are foremost in supernormal powers."
"I pray that the Venerable One will now lift this great vajra-pestle from the earth.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then reflected to himself:
"If I am unable to move this vajra-pestle before this great assembly of gods and humans, would it not be a cause for pride to arise within me?"

Having formed this thought, he exercised his own supernormal power and was about to lift that vajra; immediately, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, the waters of the ocean surged upward, and the great earth everywhere trembled and quaked with terror, yet the vajra alone remained unmoved and unshaken.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and addressed him thus:

"The Buddha has declared me the foremost among the śrāvakas in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). Possessing great majestic power, renown, and authority, I am able to place the waters of the four great oceans within the palm of my hand; I can also turn this trichiliocosm as easily as a person might roll a single coin upon the tip of a finger.
Furthermore, I can cause the sun and moon to halt in the sky, restraining their majestic radiance so that they do not move."

Furthermore, he was able to take up that King of Mountains, Sumeru, and hurl it beyond the Brahma world; he was able to subdue the two great dragon kings, Nanda and Upananda; and he was able to wander for alms throughout that world of Mirage.
"This vajra is minute in size, yet even I am unable to shake it.
World-Honored One,
has my spiritual power not diminished now?"
The Buddha said, “Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

It is not that your supernatural power has diminished; rather, it is because the Bodhisattva’s majestic power sustains him that no Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha can move him, much less any other sentient being.”
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
Even if one were able to shake all the Sumeru Kings within as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, only where the vajra-pestle is placed could it not be moved.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, possessing such great power and majesty, could playfully hurl this vajra—truly it is rare and marvelous!”
The Buddha said,
“Mahāmaudgalyāyana! Suppose all the Sumeru mountains in a trichiliocosm could be merged into a single Sumeru mountain, and could all be made to tremble;”
"Yet this vajra cannot be moved.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was struck with wonder and came forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!"
This Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, possesses great power and is well able to wield that great vajra.
Does this Lord of Secrets possess the power born of his parents?
"Is it through supernatural power?
The Buddha said, "Mahāmaudgalyāyana!..."
The power born of one's parents has a fixed measure according to where it is applied; however, the supernatural powers of the Bodhisattvas are inexhaustible and limitless.
If I were to reveal them, the world of gods and humans would fall into total confusion.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having surveyed all the assemblies, addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, saying:
"You should now personally lift up the great vajra staff placed upon the ground."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, having caused the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system to tremble by his supernatural power, immediately took up his vajra with his left hand, tossed it playfully into the air so that it circled seven times, and once the vajra had completed its rotation in the sky, he immediately caught it and placed it securely in his right hand.
The entire assembly was struck with wonder; they joined their palms in homage to the Great Lord of Secrets and all spoke these words:
"How marvelous, O Lord of Secrets!"
Being able to possess such vast power and majesty, and skillfully wielding the most supreme great vajra scepter, may all sentient beings universally obtain such superior strength.
Then King Ajātaśatru again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many dharmas must a bodhisattva fully cultivate in order to obtain such supreme power?”
The Buddha said,
“Great King! If a bodhisattva cultivates ten dharmas, they will attain this supreme power.”
What are the ten? First, a bodhisattva would rather sacrifice their own body and life than ever abandon the unsurpassed true Dharma.
Second, they maintain a sense of humility toward all sentient beings and do not increase their pride.
Third, one gives rise to a mind of compassion toward those who are weak and inferior, and does not harbor thoughts of harming them.
Fourth, upon seeing sentient beings suffering from hunger and thirst, one bestows excellent food and drink.
Fifth, seeing sentient beings who are afraid, he bestows fearlessness upon them.
Sixth, seeing sentient beings who are ill, he provides medicine to rescue and heal them.
Seventh, seeing sentient beings who are impoverished, he grants them gifts so that they may be satisfied.
Eighth, seeing the stupas, temples, and images of the Buddha adorned with pure and perfect colors.
Ninth, uttering words of joy to comfort sentient beings.
Tenth, seeing sentient beings burdened by heavy loads and afflicted by exhaustion and suffering, and removing their heavy burdens for them.
"If a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten dharmas, they will be able to attain such supreme power.
This concludes the eighteenth fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa-mahāyāna-sūtra*.
This concludes the eighteenth fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa-mahāyāna-sūtra*.

Chapter Twenty-Two, Part Two: The Questions and Answers of King Ajātaśatru. Furthermore, King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many dharmas should a bodhisattva cultivate to obtain the dharma of mastery and proceed toward mastery?
The Buddha said:
“Great King! A bodhisattva should cultivate eight dharmas to attain the dharma of mastery and proceed toward mastery.
What are these eight?

First, uttering beautiful and virtuous speech with a straightforward mind; second, a mind that is always supple; third, a mind that is well-disposed and joyful; fourth, a mind that is always even and upright; fifth, being without flattery; sixth, being without deception; seventh, being without envy; eighth, a mind that is always disciplined and serene.
“If a bodhisattva is endowed with these eight dharmas, they will attain the dharma of mastery and proceed toward mastery.
King Ajātaśatru again addressed the Buddha, saying,
“How many dharmas should a bodhisattva cultivate to be able to abide within mastery?”
The Buddha said:
"Great King! A bodhisattva should cultivate four dharmas to abide in mastery."
What are the four? First, if born among humans, may one become a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin) and encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Second, may one become Śakra and encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Third, he vowed to become Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world, at the time of a Buddha’s appearance in the world.
Fourth, he vowed to become a wealthy and eminent elder at the time of a Buddha’s appearance in the world.
“If a bodhisattva is endowed with these four dharmas, they are able to abide in mastery.
King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“What constitutes the ultimate state of pure faith?
The Buddha said, “Great King!”
"Virtuous friends are the ultimate.
The King asked:
"What is the ultimate purpose of extensive learning?"
The Buddha said,
"Extensive learning has wisdom as its ultimate goal.
The King said:
"What is the ultimate goal of giving?
The Buddha said,
"Great wealth is the ultimate goal of giving."
The King asked,
“What is the ultimate goal of maintaining the precepts?
The Buddha said:
“Observing the precepts can lead to rebirth in the happy realms and serve as the ultimate goal.
The King asked:
“What serves as the ultimate goal for patience?”
The Buddha said:
"Patience consists in protecting sentient beings until the ultimate end.
The King asked:
“What is the ultimate goal of diligence?
The Buddha said,
“The ultimate goal of diligence is the thorough perfection of all Buddha-dharmas.”
The King asked,
"What is the ultimate goal of meditative concentration?
The Buddha replied:
“Dhyāna and samādhi, being close to tranquility, are the ultimate.
The King asked:
“What is the ultimate of superior wisdom?”
The Buddha said, “Jñānottara,
the pacification of all afflictions constitutes the ultimate.
The King asked:
"What is the ultimate purpose of listening to the Dharma?
The Buddha said,
"The ultimate purpose of listening to the Dharma is to sever all doubts and delusions."
The King asked, "What is the ultimate goal of inquiring into the Dharma?
The Buddha said:
"Inquiring into the Dharma while remaining free from all miscellaneous talk constitutes the ultimate. The King asked:
"Dwelling in a quiet and secluded place—what is the ultimate purpose of this?"
The Buddha said:
"To dwell in seclusion and attain meditative concentration and supernormal powers constitutes the ultimate.
The King said:
"What is the ultimate state of visualization?
The Buddha replied,
"The ultimate state of visualization is the transcendence of thought."
The King asked,
"What is the ultimate nature of the sound of impermanence?
The Buddha said:
"The sound of impermanence is ultimately free from all attachments.
The King asked:
"What is the ultimate nature of the sound of suffering?"
The Buddha said,
“The sound of suffering is ultimately characterized by non-appropriation.
The King asked:
“What is the ultimate meaning of the sound ‘non-self’?
The Buddha replied,
“The sound ‘non-self’ has the cessation of ‘self’ and ‘what belongs to self’ as its ultimate meaning.”
The King asked,
"What is the ultimate nature of the sound of tranquility?
The Buddha said:
"Quiescent sound ceasing in accordance with stillness is the ultimate.
The King asked:
"What is the ultimate of profound and firm mental attention?"
The Buddha said:
"To give rise to right view through profound and firm mental attention is the ultimate.
The King said:
“If body and mind are detached, what constitutes the ultimate?
The Buddha said:
“The arousal of meditative concentration and supernormal powers when body and mind are detached constitutes the ultimate.”
The King asked,
“What is the ultimate goal of the Noble Path?
The Buddha replied:
“The fruit of the samādhi in which the Noble Path manifests before one is the ultimate.
The King asked:
“What is the ultimate of faith and understanding?”
The Buddha said,
"The ultimate is the perfection of liberation through faith and understanding.
The King asked:
"What is the ultimate purpose for the appearance of the Buddhas in the world?
The Buddha said,
"The ultimate purpose for the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is the accomplishment of all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma)."
The King asked,
"What is it like for a Buddha to appear in the world?
The Buddha replied:
“Great King! The very moment one gives rise to the bodhicitta, that is the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
The King said:
“How does one generate the bodhicitta?
The Buddha said,
“It is what is called being born from great compassion.”
The King asked,
"How does great compassion arise?
The Buddha said:
"It means to give rise to pure faith.
The King asked,
"How does one give rise to pure faith?"
The Buddha said,
"If one generates the bodhicitta, that is itself the generation of pure faith.
The King said:
"How should one generate that bodhicitta?
The Buddha said:
"To have a profound resolve that does not regress is to generate bodhicitta."
The King asked,
“What is meant by ‘the profound mind that does not regress’?
The Buddha replied:
"This is precisely the great compassion that has arisen.
The King asked:
"How is it possible to give rise to great compassion?"
The Buddha said,
"To give rise to no mind of aversion or abandonment toward any sentient being is itself great compassion.
The king said:
"How does one attain non-abandonment of sentient beings?
The Buddha said:
"It is what is called not being attached to one's own pleasure."
The King asked,
"What is meant by not being attached to one's own pleasure?
The Buddha said:
"It means never to abandon or depart from the Three Jewels.
The king asked,
"How can one avoid abandoning the Three Jewels?"
The Buddha said,
"If one can eliminate all afflictions, one will not abandon or depart from the Triple Gem.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru again approached with profound reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Rare indeed, World-Honored One!
Rare indeed, Sugata!
You have well expounded the pure Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata.”

The Tathāgata is able to skillfully establish the precepts and further accords with the true Dharma taught by all Buddhas and World-Honored Ones; he does not subvert cause and effect and remains far removed from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. He accomplishes all undertakings according to what has been taught, such that the retributions for good and evil deeds are never lost, and he is free from all falsehood, exactly as the Buddha has spoken.
Within such a supreme, vast, and pure teaching as this, who would dare to violate it?
And who could pose challenges or give rise to slander?
Only those who have not planted roots of goodness and are practitioners of evil deeds.

"Bhagavān! In the past, I did not deeply plant roots of goodness nor practice diligent filiality toward the Buddha; thus, I have been unable to repay the Buddha’s profound kindness with my own flesh and blood.
I pray that the Buddha will now bestow his majestic power and protection upon me, so that all my afflictions and all my sinful karmas may be completely extinguished."

"Bhagavān! That youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī is a true spiritual friend who has brought me benefit and happiness throughout the long night. He has pacified all my misdeeds within the realms of existence and illuminated me with the light of the Dharma; yet, I am unable to repay his profound kindness."
“Blessed One, Greatly Compassionate One, Great Spiritual Friend, you are able to explain to me the supreme, correct Dharma that exhaustively fulfills the holy life.
Chapter Twenty-Three: The Noble King Devaputra At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Śāntamati addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, saying:
“O Lord of Secrets! Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, manifests emanations through his transformative power...”
"Is it possible for me to perform various transformative deeds accordingly?
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva said:
"Let the Buddha now appear before us to bear witness for me!"

Whatever transformative activities are performed by all the Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I am likewise able to carry them out in accordance with the Buddhas—namely, the various physical forms, playful displays, and supernormal powers—yet these are ultimately rooted in the profound purity of my mind from previous lives.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śāntamati again addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, saying:

"I now entreat the Great Lord of Secrets: may you, through the empowerment of your spiritual power, provide protection and mindfulness so that this True Dharma may be widely proclaimed and disseminated in the future period, the final age, during the last five hundred years; and may all those great beings who are gathered under this True Dharma obtain this True Dharma and have it fall into their hands."
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva said:
"Good son! All the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have together empowered this true Dharma."

Why is this? This True Dharma is composed of syllables, yet those syllables are neither born nor exhausted, nor do they ever vanish; for neither the syllables nor the meaning they express can be made to disappear.
The Tathāgata’s teaching of this profound, true Dharma cannot be obscured.
Why is this? No phenomenon can arise; if a phenomenon is unarisen, it is likewise unceasing.

Thus it should be known: as the Buddha has said, whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, all phenomena remain eternally abiding—namely, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*)—for the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is pure, such being the very nature of phenomena.
As it has been taught, the dependent origination of all phenomena is likewise not contradictory.
Because the dependent origination of phenomena is not contradictory, it is the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
By virtue of being the True Dharma, it does not disappear.
"What has been thus explained is called the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Śāntamati said,
"Lord of Mysteries!"
"How can one don the armor of diligence to uphold and protect the True Dharma?
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva replied,
"If one does not contradict any phenomena, one can don the armor of diligence to uphold and protect the True Dharma."
"Why is this? Because this True Dharma is not in conflict with any phenomena.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Śāntamati.
"What phenomena are contradictory?
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva replied, "Because the characteristics of syllables are contradictory, the phenomena themselves are contradictory; yet they do not contradict the nature of arising phenomena."
"If one does not contradict them, that is what it means to be a protector of the True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Śāntamati asked:
"In protecting the True Dharma, is there anything that contradicts all the worlds?"
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva said:
“There is, son of good family!”
Why is this? Because worldly beings cling to various views; if there are those who grasp at talk of emptiness, they contradict the world.
Furthermore, if one claims that the world is permanent, blissful, self, and pure, while the world is actually impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure, that too contradicts the world.
Furthermore, worldly beings follow the flow of birth and death while turning their backs on the flow of the True Dharma; this is what constitutes opposition to the world.
Moreover, worldly beings honor the dharmas of the present life, whereas those who protect the True Dharma honor the dharmas of future lives; this is what constitutes opposition to the world.

Furthermore, while worldly beings grasp at the aggregates, sense bases, and elements, those who protect the True Dharma teach that all phenomena are without grasping; thus, they are in opposition to the world.
"Śāntamati, you should know that for this reason, those who protect the True Dharma are at variance with that world.
Śāntamati Bodhisattva said: "O Great Lord of Secrets!"
"How should you uphold and protect the True Dharma?
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva replied,
"As for my upholding and protecting it, it means upholding and protecting through non-self, non-sentient beings, and non-dharmas."
The Bodhisattva Śāntamati asked, "What does this mean?
The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi replied:
"It means: because of the detachment of self, the detachment of sentient beings, and the detachment of phenomena, yet there is no detachment of self, sentient beings, or phenomena.
Because of the detachment of the past, the detachment of the future, and the detachment of the present, yet there is no detachment of the past, future, or present."
Because the three periods of time are detached, yet the three periods of time are not detached;
because the Buddhas are detached, yet the Buddhas are not detached;
because the buddha-fields are detached, yet the buddha-fields are not detached.
"Because phenomena are detached, and because phenomena are not detached.
One who can thoroughly penetrate such phenomena is able to uphold and protect the True Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Great Being!
You have skillfully upheld and protected the True Dharma.”
If one is without attachment and without grasping toward all phenomena, one is then able to uphold and protect the True Dharma.

If one is without grasping and without accumulation regarding the conceptual proliferation of signs in all phenomena, and even if all discrimination and pervasive conceptualization are entirely without discrimination, one is then able to uphold and protect the True Dharma.
At that time, there was a devaputra in the assembly named King of Worthiness (Bhadra-rāja), who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
‘Cessation’ and ‘quiescence’ are what the Buddha has taught.”

If it is as you have described, then all objects of cognition are entirely stilled and there is nothing to be observed; because they are closely quiescent, they no longer combine to give rise to any phenomena.
Although phenomena are quiescent, universally quiescent, and proximately quiescent, he nevertheless upholds the True Dharma of the Tathāgata and does not abandon it.
Although he upholds it, yet regarding all phenomena, there is nothing upheld and nothing abandoned.
While that devaputra was preaching this Dharma, a thousand bhikṣus in the assembly attained liberation of mind, and a thousand devas attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śāntamati addressed the Devaputra Śreṣṭharāja, saying, "How does one attain such eloquence? The Devaputra replied,

"By being able to sever all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), departing from the path of speech, having nothing to record or declare, and because within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) there is no dharma to be grasped— one thus attains eloquence."
The Bodhisattva Śāntamati said:
"O Devaputra! How is eloquence produced?"
The devaputra said:
"Because there is no eloquence, and because one is devoid of eloquence. Why is that? Because..."
"Lacking eloquence" means this is the meaning of non-conjunction.
"Departing from eloquence" means this is the meaning of departing from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Furthermore, son of good family!
Because it is as has been taught, what eloquence could there be to be attained?
If the consciousness that manifests for others does not arise, and if the consciousness that manifests for oneself also does not abide—for this reason, one attains eloquence.
If one discerns all objects of perception with the mind and remains unobstructed, dwelling nowhere within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), one thereby attains eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
Furthermore, because wisdom does not shift among any phenomena, and there is not even the slightest phenomenon that can be known or understood by wisdom, one thereby attains eloquence.
Furthermore, because within the dharma of non-abiding there is neither emergence nor entry, and it transcends all defiled dharmas, one attains eloquence.
Moreover, because all dharmas arise without arising and cease without ceasing, one attains eloquence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śāntamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
This Prince Sudhana possesses great eloquence.”
The Buddha said, "Śāntamati!

This noble King Devaputra has come here from the realm of Akṣobhya Buddha in the world-system of Sukhāvatī, desiring to hear the Great Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, proclaim the secret, sublime Dharma of the Tathāgata."

Furthermore, because this devaputra has attained the dhāraṇī that penetrates the characteristics of all phenomena, he has for a hundred kalpas had no further aspirations or desires; he has naturally acquired unimpeded eloquence, such that his eloquence remains unobstructed in whatever he proclaims.
Chapter Twenty-Four: The Inexhaustible Exposition of Similes for Praising the Merits of Dhāraṇī. Part One. At that time, the Bodhisattva Śāntamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“What is called the dhāraṇī of entering into the characteristics of all phenomena?
The Buddha said, “Śāntamati!

"Entering according to the characteristics of phenomena" refers to the inexhaustible wisdom of entering according to syllables; that is to say, because the gateway of the letter *A* enters into all phenomena.
Furthermore, the letter *A* is the gateway from which all phenomena arise.
Furthermore, the syllable *A* is the initial arising and the final limit of all phenomena.
Moreover, the syllable *A* accomplishes all activities in every place; it follows the engagement of vocal karma, being neither something that is cognized nor something that is not cognized.
Because the gateway of the letter A enters into all phenomena, this is called the dhāraṇī gateway of entering into the characteristics of phenomena.
"Furthermore, Śāntamati!
As for what is called "following and entering," in all places there is not even a minute particle of any dharma that can emerge or enter, because there are no words.
From where does it come? Into what does it enter? And wherein does it abide? Since there is no abiding within words, there is likewise no emergence from which it could depart to any direction.
Furthermore, because letters have no combination, there are no letters that can be recorded or explained; yet this does not mean there is no teaching, nor is there any increase or decrease.
Because there are no letters, there is no such thing as a dharma or a non-dharma that can be conceptually distinguished.
Because there are no syllables, there is no dharma that can arise and no dharma that can cease; no dharma can be established and no dharma can be destroyed.
Śāntamati, you should know that such enumeration of syllables is itself the enumeration of the mind.
As the calculation of the mind, so is the calculation of all dharmas.
As the calculation of all dharmas, so it is non-calculation. Why is this?
Because phenomena cannot be apprehended through calculation;
since there is no calculable phenomenon by which one could calculate, the calculation of all phenomena is unattainable.

In this way, one is able to accord with and enter the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Being thus from the beginning, one accords with and enters non-arising (*anutpāda*); if one enters non-arising, there is likewise no arising. This means that there is not even the slightest phenomenon into which one can enter; therefore, all phenomena are entered without entering.
Śāntamati! If one can thus enter into all forms of calculation, then one’s eloquence cannot be interrupted. Why is this?
Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is uninterrupted,
if one realizes it in this way, one is able to teach the Dharma to others as appropriate, and whatever is taught is directly realized.
By thus entering into the characteristics of all phenomena, one enters into the characteristics of sentient beings.
Because one enters into the characteristics of sentient beings, one skillfully explains all phenomena in accordance with their faith and understanding.

Śāntamati! A bodhisattva who has attained dhāraṇī has a mind free from defilement, pure intention, and immaculate right conduct. His mind is lofty and supreme; his practice is well-established, and his wondrous wisdom is unsurpassed. He attains firm and perfect supernormal powers that cannot be destroyed by the armies of Māra. He subdues non-Buddhists, restrains all afflictions, and unties the knots of enmity. His body possesses power and vigor, and his mind is free from weariness. His eloquence is inexhaustible, his exposition of the Dharma is boundless, and his skillful preaching is limitless. Possessing unimpeded superior wisdom and profound, wondrous insight, he skillfully explains the deep Dharma; his vast learning is like the ocean, and his abiding in samādhi is like Mount Sumeru.
The entire assembly is like the lion king; worldly dharmas are pure like the lotus flower;
nurturing sentient beings is like the great earth; quelling the craving of afflictions is like the great waters; maturing sentient beings is like the great fire;
giving rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings is like the wondrous moon; and shattering [ignorance]...
The darkness of afflictions and delusion is like the Great Sun; he removes the enemies of affliction like one of heroic strength; his mind is well-tamed like a great dragon;
he raises the sound of the Dharma on high like the roar of a great cloud; he universally bestows the rain of Dharma like the falling of a great downpour;
he heals the various diseases of affliction in sentient beings like a great King of Physicians; he acts as a great...
The Dharma King is sovereign like a king; he skillfully protects the worldly dharmas like a world-protecting deity (Lokapāla);
he skillfully observes gods and humans like Śakra, Lord of the Devas; his mind attains mastery and possesses superior power like Brahmā;
he is unattached like a bird in flight; he fears the clamor of the crowd like a monkey or a deer; regarding all things...
They subdue all evils among sentient beings like a compassionate mother; they instruct them in arts and skills and open the gates of learning like a compassionate father;
and they bestow the jewels of the Dharma in an inexhaustible flow like the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.

They shall attain the adornment of merit and be endowed with the primary and secondary marks, such that all who behold them will rejoice; they shall possess the seven treasures and be free from the suffering of poverty; they shall gather those lacking wisdom and praise the wise; by possessing wisdom, they shall be free from all faults; they shall skillfully protect the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others; they shall have mastery in preaching the Dharma and unimpeded supernormal powers; they shall thoroughly understand the inclinations of all sentient beings and accord with the faculties and dispositions of all beings.
He listens to the Dharma without weariness and preaches it without stinginess, seeking no fame, reputation, gain, or honor.

Because he is free from defiled attachment, his ethical discipline is pure; because he is free from malice and harm, the power of his patience is pure; because he is skillfully able to accomplish all tasks, his diligence is pure; because he has attained mastery, his meditative concentration is pure; because his wisdom is immaculate, his transcendent insight is pure; because his holy life is supreme, he possesses the four immeasurables; and through skillful cultivation of supramundane dhyāna and samādhi, he achieves the noble path of unsurpassed enlightenment.
Because they are endowed with such marks and virtues, they shall receive the consecration of the Unsurpassed Dharma King.

Śāntamati, you should know that even a bodhisattva who has merely attained dhāraṇī obtains such immeasurable merit; how much more so when empowered by the spiritual strength (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata, whereby all undertakings are successfully accomplished.
"The merits of the dhāraṇī-bodhisattvas could not be fully exhausted even by praising them with metaphors for a hundred thousand years.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śāntamati addressed the Devaputra Bhadrapāla, saying:
"O Virtuous One!..."
"You have now swiftly attained a great benefit, being able to skillfully praise the immeasurable and boundless merits of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Devaputra King of the Wise addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati, saying:
"O Son of Good Family!
Within ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), there is not even the slightest phenomenon that can be praised. Why is this?
Because phenomena are devoid of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and possess neither shape nor manifest color; therefore, one cannot praise their virtues to reach their limit.
If there were any determinate characteristics within form or manifest color, they could indeed be proclaimed and praised through words.
*The Buddha-spoken Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Inconceivable Secrets of the Tathāgata*, Scroll Nineteen.
*The Buddha-spoken Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Inconceivable Secrets of the Tathāgata*.
The Twenty-fourth:
Chapter on the Inexhaustible Exposition of Similes for Praising the Merit of Dharani, Part Two.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Han Dynasty, the Court Proclaimed Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, the Great Master of Sanskrit, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Weijing, et al., by imperial decree. At that time, the Devaputra Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

All dharmas are without grasping, without self, and without appropriation; they are neither continuous nor discontinuous, yet they are performed according to what is appropriate through skillful means.”
"World-Honored One, those who practice with diligence attain the Dharma through right means manifested before them.

It is, for example, like great water accumulated beneath the earth; one must rely on human effort and diligent application—either by digging pits or by boring wells—and it is only through such diligent exertion that one finally obtains the water."
If there were no pit, how could one obtain water?
It is likewise for those who apply themselves with diligence: through the power of their exertion, they attain penetrating wisdom in all matters.
If there is no diligent effort, from where could wisdom be obtained?
Therefore, those who seek bodhi should always diligently apply skillful means and arouse vigor; in this way, they will be able to directly attain the noble dharmas.
It is like a person born blind in this world, who cannot see the forms and colors that arise before them.
The afflictions that shroud sentient beings are likewise such that they are unable to see the phenomena that arise.
It is also like a person with sight in the darkness of the world: if there is no bright torch, they cannot see any forms or images.

It is the same for one who cultivates the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*): if they lack the instruction and guidance of a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) in preaching the Dharma, they will be unable to give rise to faith and understanding regarding the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is like one who has already perfected the pure divine eye, who does not depend upon the illumination of worldly light.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: one who has already accomplished what was to be done does not rely on others for instruction.
Furthermore, it is like a person dwelling within the womb, who sees nothing at all, nor perceives any growth whatsoever.
It is the same for the bodhisattva who has initiated diligence: although he cultivates the Buddha-dharma, he does not perceive any increase in his realization of bodhi.
It is also like all the trees that grow depending upon the Great Snowy King of Mountains; those trees can never be destroyed or withered while they remain there.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: he diligently practices skillful means to cultivate all the true dharmas born of wisdom, and he neither destroys nor loses them therein.

Furthermore, it is like when a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, and the seven treasures appear accordingly—namely, the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the treasurer treasure, and the military commander treasure.

It is the same for a bodhisattva: if they give rise to the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), the seven treasures also emerge along with it—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, superior wisdom, and skillful means.

Furthermore, just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King governs the realms of the four great continents, regarding all sentient beings with equal love and compassion without any discriminatory thoughts, so too is the Bodhisattva:

through the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they universally gather in sentient beings without any discriminatory thoughts. These four methods of attraction are namely: giving (*dāna*), pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*), beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), and cooperation (*samānārthatā*).
Furthermore, just as when a Wheel-Turning Sage King practices the transformation of the royal dharma, there is entirely no fighting, war, or litigation;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva, who dwells in tranquility and preaches the Dharma, such that there is entirely no conflict or dispute with any heterodox outsiders.
Furthermore, just as in the trichiliocosm, the great Mount Sumeru and its vast oceans were first established, so too it is with the bodhisattva:
when first generating the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), they first establish it upon a foundation of profound and firm great compassion.
Furthermore, just as in the world, when the sun rises, it first illuminates the high mountains;
so too is it with the Bodhisattva, who first gives rise to the light of great wisdom, causing all sentient beings to give rise to roots of goodness and obtain the illumination of wisdom.
Furthermore, just as the great earth receives all seeds, and all grasses, shrubs, and forests grow from the earth and flourish equally, so too is it with the Bodhisattva who has attained dhāraṇī:
with a mind free from attachment, they bestow the Dharma equally upon all sentient beings without ever abandoning any.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Celestial Son Worthy King, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
Celestial Son!”
You have now skillfully used analogies to proclaim the teachings of the bodhisattvas.

O Devaputra, you should know that even if all grasses, trees, thickets, and forests—including their names, characteristics, aggregates of phenomena, aggregates of sounds, and aggregates of forms and colors—were to enter into the mental activities of all sentient beings; and even if all sentient beings were to universally investigate them through the discrimination of all names and characteristics, down to the food and drink they consume as metaphors, and were to praise and extol the merits of a bodhisattva who has attained this dhāraṇī, they could not exhaustively describe them.
"O Son of Heaven!
For those Bodhisattvas who have attained these dhāraṇīs, there is not the slightest thing among all that they speak which is not the word of the Buddha.
Furthermore, all manifestations of the radiance of forms, sounds, scents, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects appear before them."

The eloquence he has attained is not dependent on what he hears from others, nor does he speak while observing the characteristics of others; in all places, it is unimpeded according to its direction, inexhaustible, and likewise boundless.

Without relying on supernatural power to enter all things exclusively, with a body free from heaviness and a mind free from objective referents, they are able to remain before hundreds of thousands of Buddhas as they preach the Dharma, untainted and unattached.

Furthermore, because that bodhisattva is established by the majestic spiritual power of those Buddhas, they attain dhāraṇīs, wisdom, and eloquence; whatever Dharma they preach is untainted, unattached, and free from regression.
"Son of Heaven, you should know that there are three dharmas of non-attachment for a bodhisattva.
What are these three?
First, non-attachment to a self; second, non-attachment to sentient beings; and third, non-attachment to dharmas."
Furthermore, there are three kinds of thorough penetration and purity. What are the three?
First, the purity of the dharma-realm; second, the purity of suchness; and third, the purity of the limit of reality.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of inexhaustible penetration. What are the three?
First, the inexhaustibility of phenomena; second, the inexhaustibility of words and letters; and third, the inexhaustibility of exposition.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of power for attaining the empowerment of penetration.
What are these three?
First, the empowerment of eloquence; second, the empowerment of the meaning of the Dharma; and third, the empowerment of entering the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of joy in accomplishment. What are the three?
First, the joy of wisdom; second, the joy of knowledge; third, the joy of severing doubt.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of swift dharmas. What are the three?
First is the swiftness of mindfulness; second is the swiftness of wisdom; third is the swiftness of practice.

When the Buddha had spoken these praises of the merits of the dhāraṇī and this teaching on the inexhaustible through parables, eight hundred bodhisattvas in the assembly attained entry into the gate of dhāraṇī.
Chapter Twenty-Five: Entrusting the True Dharma. At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One..."

"Through the empowerment of my supernormal power, I shall cause this True Dharma to be widely proclaimed and disseminated in Jambudvīpa during the final period, the latter part of the five-hundred-year era.
The Buddha said,
"Lord of Mysteries!"
"I possess secret protective dhāraṇīs of the sublime Dharma, consisting of mantras and verses; are you able to remember them?
These verses were formerly heard by me in person from the Tathāgata Ratnacandra."
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I also remember it.”
The Buddha said, "Lord of Mysteries!
You should now, for the sake of this assembly, secretly protect the True Dharma so that it may long abide in the world; you ought to proclaim the great mantra syllables of the past."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, joined his palms in homage to all the Buddhas of the ten directions and spoke this great mantra: "Tadyathā, jaya...

When the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, had spoken these secret mantra syllables, this trichiliocosm shook in its entirety.

Then all the hosts of Māras within this trichiliocosm, each accompanied by their retinues, simultaneously approached the Buddha, the World-Honored One; bowing with palms joined, they addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If any Dharma masters are able to bring forth these great mantra syllables from their mouths, we, all the Māras, shall go to serve and honor them, so that the supreme power of these great mantras cannot be destroyed by any gods or humans. We shall constantly provide secret protection, ensuring that no one finds an opportunity to harm them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having surveyed all the assemblies, spoke these secret vidyā-mantra syllables:
"Jaye nṛjaye jayamade."
Śamī śatruṇi riṣṭāni amūni ca.

Vimale-prakramo (15). Then he spoke these verses:

"Subduing others through the True Dharma, Skillfully gathering them in with words of the True Dharma, Constantly protecting and upholding the treasury of the Dharma— These are the great mantra-syllables spoken by the Tathāgata."
He further spoke the great mantra, saying:
"A-mi (1) ma-mi (2) ma-ma-ciṇḍe (3) a-rdhi (4) a-rdha-ni-sat-ta-raṇi (5). These are the mantra syllables for summoning the Four Great Heavenly Kings."
He further spoke the great vidyā-mantra:
“Tiri (1) Tīravate (2) Yūpate (3) Śuvi (4) Śuvāvate (5) Śame (6). “This is the mantra-chapter for summoning the Lord of Gods, Śakra.”
He spoke in verse: "Possessing kindness, charity, compliance, and the power of great patience, he speaks the Great Mantra out of compassion;
fully perfected in both the dharmas of joy and equanimity, he is invoked by Brahmā and Śakra alike."
He further spoke the great vidyā-mantra:
“Araṇi (1) | Varani (2) | Kakṣi (3) | Amuli (4) | Mūlaśuddhane (5). This is the chapter of the great vidyā-mantra for subduing all māras.
He spoke these verses:
“This secret mantra of great brilliance now Shakes and subdues all māras.
Through the empowerment of the Sage of Men’s power, This sūtra is well-expounded and widely disseminated.”
This True Dharma taught by the Tathāgata— know that in the future, at the end of the age,
when the secret empowerment of the explicit words is proclaimed, it shall cause [the world] to tremble and restore it to its former state, just as it is today.
Then the hosts of Māras all assembled and spoke these verses:
“O great wise ones who preach the Dharma, we, the Māras, shall provide secret protection for you,
so that in the final age of the end times, this True Dharma may fall into your hands.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Vajrapāṇi, the Bodhisattva and Great Lord of Secrets, saying:
“You should know that because this true Dharma has now been empowered by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, no one can cause it to waver or be altered.”

Why is this? I recall that in the past, in ages long gone, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Ratnacandra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
The world was named Invincible, and the eon was also named Invincible.
Within that Buddha-dharma, there were two Dharma-preachers of great majesty, renown, power, and influence:
the first was named Wisdom Supreme, and the second was named Truth Bestower.

Those two Dharma masters, in the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnacandra, heard, received, and upheld these great mantra syllables for half an eon, turning the wheel of the true Dharma following that Tathāgata.
“At that time, all the hundreds of koṭis of māras in the trichiliocosm were caused to ripen in the noble dharma of bodhi.
The Bodhisattva Śāntamati then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Does that Tathāgata Ratnacandra currently abide and preach the Dharma,
or has he already entered parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha said:

“Śāntamati! To the east, a million koṭis of buddha-fields away from here, there is a buddha-field named Akṣaya (Unfailing), where a buddha named Ratnacandra (Jewel Moon) currently resides and teaches the Dharma.”
The lifespan of that Buddha lasted for ten thousand kalpas.
Within his buddha-field, there were hosts of māras who were stubborn, evil, and difficult to subdue; that Buddha proclaimed great mantras and verses and completely subdued them.
Having been subdued, they all reached full maturity in the noble Dharma of bodhi.
Lord of Mysteries!
You should now know that I, too, once purified my brahma-conduct within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Ratnacandra and accomplished the holy dharmas of enlightenment.
The Dharma Master Prajñottara at that time was none other than myself.
The Dharma Master Satyadatta at that time was none other than the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.

Śāntamati, you should know that at that time, together with the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, I applied ourselves with diligent vigor and a mind free from negligence. In the presence of that Buddha, the World-Honored One, we paid him deep respect and reverence, making extensive offerings. We listened to and received the secret mantras and verses proclaimed by that Buddha, thereby subduing all māras and upholding the True Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the entire assembly and addressed them all, saying: "O virtuous ones!

Who among you is capable, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, of receiving, upholding, and protecting this supreme True Dharma of my bodhisattva practices accumulated over incalculable kalpas, so that it shall not disappear?"

At that time, there were twelve thousand bodhisattvas in the assembly who, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, rose from their seats, joined their palms in homage, prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and addressed him in verse:
“If a person casts away their own body and life, And seeks no karmic reward for what they have sacrificed,
But does so solely to receive and uphold The most supreme, pure, and true Dharma proclaimed by the Buddha.”
Furthermore, five thousand devaputras, including the noble King Bhadrika, joined their palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We all vow to receive and uphold the Tathāgata’s holy Dharma of Bodhi.”
Then the sons of the gods spoke these verses:
"For the sake of all sentient beings everywhere, I have given rise to a firm and resolute heart of great compassion.
I shall uphold this Dharma-gate, The most supreme and profound teaching spoken by the Buddha."
At that time, Śakra Devendra, Brahmā Śikhin, and Vaiśravaṇa, King of the Gods, spoke these verses:
“This True Dharma is like a wondrous medicine, Capable of curing the illnesses of all sentient beings.
We shall come to protect and uphold it; May the Buddha know the intentions of our assembly.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Lord of Secrets, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I shall receive and uphold the noble Dharma of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which the Tathāgata has accumulated over incalculable eons.”
He then spoke these verses:
"All phenomena are originally without letters; Within that which is without, they are provisionally expressed by means of letters.
Out of compassionate pity, the Holy Honored One has proclaimed them; I shall receive and uphold them, and cause them to spread."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Brahma King Śikhin, saying:

"Brahma King, you should know that there are three kinds of supreme offerings and services for a Bodhisattva; because the Tathāgata receives these supreme services and offerings, he attains immeasurable merit."
What are these three?

First, to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; second, to uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas; and third, to practice according to reality in accordance with the Dharma as it has been heard.
Mahābrahmā!

Regarding these three supreme offerings, even if the Tathāgata were to remain for an eon, or until the end of an eon, or for a lifespan of immeasurable duration, the extent of the merit and reward obtained from such acts of offering could not be fully described.
Why is this? If one wishes to make the supreme offering to all Tathāgatas, one should practice these three kinds of supreme, vast, and pure Dharma-offerings.
"Furthermore, Mahābrahmā!

If there is anyone who can receive and uphold even a single four-line stanza from within the True Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, that person is thereby protecting and upholding the noble Dharma of enlightenment of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present."
Why is this? Because the Bodhi of all Buddhas is born from the Dharma; therefore, the offering of the Dharma surpasses the worldly practice of material offerings.
Among all offerings, the offering of the Dharma is the most excellent, the supreme, the highest, and the foremost.
"Mahābrahmā!

I recall that in the past, within the lineage of the King of Radiance, there was a crown prince named Prajñāvat. Once, during the course of a single night, he personally heard two gāthās being spoken within his dream."
Having heard this and taken it to heart, he then reflected:
"I have now obtained a great treasure trove.
Immediately, he suddenly raised his voice and spoke these words:
"I have now obtained a great treasury of jewels.
At that time, the king, the queen, and their son asked him the reason for this. The prince immediately recounted the aforementioned events in detail, and then spoke these two verses to his parents:
"The wealth and treasures of the world gather and then disperse; Kings, officials, water, fire, and thieves divide them up."
The Buddhas possess the wealth of the sublime Dharma of great learning, which remains unimpaired for many koṭis of kalpas.
Always free from negligence, they teach the nectar-like Dharma; benefiting sentient beings, they give rise to the bodhicitta.
Their profound, firm, and tranquil mind is likewise such that it is the root of all joy, yet remains without grasping.

"O Great Brahmā! At that time, when the Prince spoke those two gāthās he had heard in his dream to his parents, eight thousand people matured the roots of goodness for awakening, and forty-two thousand sentient beings were all reborn in the heavens."

For this reason, one should diligently practice in accordance with the Dharma by means of all the wealth of the pure Dharma derived from extensive learning; for by practicing the True Dharma, one is able to appropriately provide guidance and support for others.
"Furthermore, Great Brahmā!
There are two kinds of dharmas that are capable of producing much. What are these two?
First, one does not inflict harm upon sentient beings; second, one diligently seeks out extensive learning without ever becoming weary or satisfied.
If there are those who can practice these two dharmas, the eye of the True Dharma will not be severed or extinguished.
Mahābrahmā! Throughout the various Tathāgatas of this Bhadrakalpa, you have exhorted them to teach the Dharma and have well protected the True Dharma.
Since those Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the Bhadrakalpa appear in the world only when there are pure sentient beings who encounter them, you must not now grow weary or abandon them.
Why is this? Great Brahmā!

If one is able to receive and uphold the True Dharma for even a single day and night during a period of corruption and evil, the merit obtained will exceed that of one who upholds the True Dharma in a pure Buddha-field for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Therefore, Mahābrahmā!
You should arouse vast and great diligence;
during this age of defilement and evil, you must firmly protect and uphold the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:

"You should now firmly receive and uphold this gate of the Vajrapāṇi-parivarta Guhyaka-jāla-dhāraṇī as it has been spoken here, and in the future final age, you must expound it extensively for others."
I now entrust this True Dharma to you.
In the future age, you must not preach this gateway of the True Dharma to those who possess inferior faith and understanding, lest they become deluded and confused.
Why is this? Because they have not thoroughly penetrated the source and bottom of this True Dharma.

If there are those who have attained mastery within the True Dharma, who have already successfully accomplished all supreme tasks, and who are vessels for the Dharma—for such persons should one preach this gateway of the True Dharma.
Having heard this, he did not give rise to fear or alarm.
Why was this? Because it was from the True Dharma that [his realization] had arisen.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By means of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I shall now receive and uphold this Dharma, and according to my ability, I shall propagate and expound it.”
The Buddha said,
“Ānanda! Do you now see this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi diligently protecting and upholding the True Dharma of the Buddha?”
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
“Indeed, I have seen it.
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! You now do likewise: receive this True Dharma as is appropriate, uphold it firmly, and proclaim it as it should be.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the name of this sutra?
How should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha said:

“Ānanda! This sūtra is titled ‘The Vajrapāṇi Chapter’; it is also titled ‘Proclaiming the Secrets of the Tathāgata,’ also titled ‘Inconceivable Buddha-Dharmas,’ and also titled ‘Immeasurable Accumulation of Merit.’”
"You should uphold this name. Furthermore, Ānanda,

you should know that if there is one who abides in the Bodhisattva vehicle and is beheld by the Buddha-eye, they may take vast quantities of various jewels to fill all Buddha-fields, even piling them from the earth up to the Peak of Existence, and practice extensive giving without seeking reward."

If, moreover, there should be someone who, without a mind for profit or gain, expounds this True Dharma to others as they have skillfully practiced it, their merit would be greater than that [of the former].
This teaching is called the Tathāgata’s secret, immeasurable mass of merit.

When the Buddha spoke this "Chapter on Entrusting the True Dharma," there were ten billion people in the assembly who gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; ninety-six thousand bodhisattvas attained the stage of *kṣānti*; eighty-four thousand people attained the purity of the *dharma-cakṣus*; one thousand six hundred bhikṣus attained liberation of mind; and one thousand six hundred bhikṣuṇīs also attained liberation of mind.

The immeasurable Buddha-fields of the ten directions all shook; hundreds of thousands of devas and humans in the void played celestial music and rained down various exquisite flowers. Having offered these acts of worship, they all spoke these words:
“May this True Dharma abide long in the world and be widely proclaimed and disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa.”

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Great Secrets, along with the assembly of bodhisattvas such as Śāntamati, the assembly of devaputras such as Rājādhirāja, the great kings such as King Ajātaśatru, as well as the other bodhisattvas, Ānanda and the other great śrāvakas, and all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and so forth—hearing what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
